News.title: Furious Brit tourist and partner who fled hotel inferno offered just £87 in compensation between them
News.content:
A BRITISH tourist and his partner who fled a hotel inferno have been offered just £87 in compensation between them.

Josh Robbins and Shelby A’Court took an all-inclusive Tui package trip to a £1,800-a-week complex in Croatia.



Yet they had to flee for their lives as flames closed in at the Gava Waterman Milna Resort on the island of Brac.

The couple said they and dozens of others were left to fend for themselves by staff.



They ran to a nearby dock and got away thanks to locals who turned up in a flotilla of boats.

Mortgage adviser Josh, 26, from Dorset, said: “We thought we were going to die.

“We want all our money back and compensation for what we went through but we’re being told it was an ‘act of God’ and we should claim insurance.

“Tui have now offered £87 — or a little more if we accept a voucher.

“I asked them to email the offer.

“I’ll send it to my legal adviser.”



The hotel denied claims guests were abandoned, insisting reception staff aided the evacuation.

Tui was asked to comment.

News.title: Cost of foreign holidays to soar by £100s thanks to Net Zero just days after PM approved UK ‘tourist tax’
News.content:
MEETING Net Zero ­targets could put hundreds of pounds on the price of holiday flights, experts warn.

Jetting to Benidorm on the Costa Blanca would be £150 more by 2050 — and a plane to New York £400 more expensive.



It comes as Labour mayors plan a tax of up to five per cent on overnight stays here.

The flight price hike warnings comes after the Climate Change Committee (CCC), which advises the Government, says the industry should pay for pollution-cutting measures, which will probably be passed on to passengers.



Tim Alderslade, of industry body Airlines UK, said it could “price ordinary people out of the joys of travel”.

CCC chair Nigel Topping, however, said the “polluter pays principle must apply”.



He added: “If aviation is to grow, it must take responsibility for the emissions it creates.”

The CCC said the expansion of Heathrow cannot proceed unless the aviation sector cuts emissions.

To do so, it said, firms must invest in more efficient planes and green fuels.

The Department for Transport said it was investing £219million in sustainable aviation fuel production and £43million in cleaner technologies to back greener aviation.



It said expansion could boost the economy by £40billion and support 60,000 local jobs.

It added: “We will carefully consider the CCC’s advice.”

The Government aims to hit Net Zero by 2050.

News.title: Shock moment driving instructor ploughs into cycling grandma sending her flying & seriously injuring her
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a driving instructor ploughs into a cycling grandma leaving her with devastating injuries.

Rebecca Tanton was sent flying when she was struck by a car travelling 55mph in Lincolnshire two years ago.



Horror footage shows the moment Jon Dick smashes his Ford Puma into the mother-of-three on Manby Road on October 7 2024.

In one rear view clip, she is seen flying through the air as she is launched from the bike before she crashes to the tarmac.



She is then seen sprawled on the side of the road as a car behind is forced to swerve out of the way.

Dashcam footage then shows Mr Dick in the driver’s seat as the car jolts after hitting Ms Tanton before he slows to a stop, realising what had happened.

Ms Tanton told the Daily Mail her “life is changed completely” adding: “I am simply existing in constant pain, while Jon Dick is still walking around freely – and he has shown no remorse whatsoever.”

“From the moment Jon Dick carelessly drove his car into me, he took away my freedom, independence and love of life,” she added.



She claimed that the driving instructor had never apologised for the incident that left her fighting for her life.

Ms Tanton said she remembered “very little of the aftermath”.

She suffered catastrophic injuries and was raced to hospital for an emergency blood transfusion.

Her pelvis and the bones on the right hand side of her body were left completely shattered by the crash.

The grandmother also suffered a horror facial injury and underwent emergency plastic surgery that evening to stop her haemorrhaging blood.



Over the course of the following weeks, Ms Tanton recovered in ICU where she had seven metal plates screwed into her bones.

When her wounds started to heal, she contracted sepsis as a result of the plates.

An emergency operation to stem the infection resulted in an accidentally torn bladder and was forced to wear a catheter for three months.

And as she recovered, she was forced to make funeral arrangements for her 33-year-old son who tragically passed away from brain cancer.

She said the funeral for the beloved marine pilot had to be postponed until she was in a stable condition, adding she was “barely able to walk” due to her injuries.



Before the crash, Ms Tanton was an avid cyclist riding 40 miles a day while she also enjoyed horse-riding and swimming.

Now, Ms Tanton faces the constant threat of her sepsis returning due to the metal plates fused to her bones.

If it does return, doctors say she has a one-in-three chance of survival.

In December 2025, Jon Dick was found guilty of causing serious injury by careless driving and was handed a suspended prison sentence and two-year driving ban.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

In her victim statement she said it had been a “living nightmare” for her and her family.



The Sun has contacted Mr Dick for comment.

News.title: Britain on ‘energy cliff’ after woke Net Zero drive left us exposed to Russia and China, ex-MI6 chief warns
News.content:
BRITAIN is on the edge of an “energy cliff” after prioritising woke Net Zero policies over taking on Russia and China, ex-MI6 chief Sir Richard Dearlove will warned.

The spymaster will tonight blast ministers in a landmark speech after accusing the Government of handing Beijing the tools to turn Britain’s lights out.



Sir Richard, who ran MI6 from 1999 to 2004, will deliver his warning in a lecture to the Global Warming Policy Foundation in London.

He will say: “We have as a nation negligently wandered close to a cliff edge and the adversaries I have described stand ready to help us over it.”



Sir Richard claims ministers have spent too long focusing on climate change and eco policies.

He will say the country’s biggest threat is not global warming but Vladimir Putin’s Russia and Xi Jinping’s China.



Both are willing to use Britain’s reliance on foreign equipment and undersea cables as weapons, he added.

He said the Kremlin’s GRU spy agency has spent decades building the capability to sever cables, pipelines and electricity interconnectors.

Sir Richard is to say: “We are not the victims of a conspiracy to make us vulnerable. We have quite casually done this to ourselves.

“Such peacetime dependencies give China strategic leverage.



“Water, sewage, gas networks, rail and underground transport, traffic lights and communication are all mains-connected.

“We have very little industry left to protect and we cannot rebuild non-existent industries which lie in foreign jurisdictions beyond our reach.”

And, taking aim at Ed Miliband, he adds: “Does the Foreign Secretary, the arch prophet of net zero, have any grasp of the country’s predicament?

“His present focus on new West Bank Israeli settlements suggests that his attention is elsewhere.”



He will go on: “To hear the Prime Minister state in Parliament that ‘national security can’t come at the expense of social security’ leaves me in a state of pessimism and extreme concern.

“The first responsibility of government is the safety of the nation.

“However successive governments have forgotten this, and Britain is now caught in an energy trap of its own making.

“The task is urgent. The government should have this amongst its very top priorities.

“Stated simply, we need an energy policy which moves us back a safe distance from the cliff edge.”



Professor Gwythian Prins, of the London School of Economics, said: “As a former head of MI6, Sir Richard’s warnings are of chilling importance.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“No-one can now pretend that our enemies China, Russia and Iran are not using our self-harming delusion with ‘net zero’ to attack the core of national security by Active Measures.”

News.title: Labour U-turn as ministers vow pensioners won’t be hit by tax when state pension tops £13,000
News.content:
LABOUR was yesterday forced to promise the elderly will not be hammered by a “granny tax”.

Chancellor John Healey is drawing up Budget plans to ensure pensioners are not punished when the triple-lock pushes the annual state pension above £13,000 next year.



Tax becomes payable at the current threshold of £12,570.

But if a pensioner has no other income they will not be penalised.



Retirees with other money sources will still pay tax.

New figures showed the state pension is likely to go up by 3.9 per cent next year, the same rate as wages.



Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds initially refused to rule out the retirees paying tax on the state pension next year.

But pensions Minister Torsten Bell said pensioners who only just exceed the personal allowance will not have the “administrative burden” of paying small amounts of tax this Parliament.

One Andy Burnham ally, economist Andy Haldane, told LBC that money markets “now suspect that this is a traditional tax-and-spend socialist government with better TikTok videos”.



Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith hit out, saying: “Pensioners will spend their last years filling tax returns or on the phone to HMRC.

“Labour will tax everything – from your holiday to Granny’s pension.”

The government faces huge fiscal pressures from high borrowing costs, the Iran war fall-out and welfare costs, such as the state pension rise under the triple lock mechanism.

News.title: Locals furious as motors from ‘dangerous’ car dealership spill out into street blocking roads and causing ‘gridlock’
News.content:
LOCALS have been left furious after a “dangerous” car dealership started using surrounding roads to park its stock.

Residents in Watford, Hertfordshire, say the actions of staff at a Jaecoo and Omoda dealership is causing “gridlock”.



The dealership has received more 130 enforcement visits in the last month, with claims the motors are blocking pavements and taking up spaces.

But the local council is struggling to take action as some of the cars are unregistered or have no number plates, making it a police matter.



Models including the Jaecoo 7 SUV, which retails from around £30,000, could be seen parked on the street and pavement without number plates.

Neighbour Elsie Humphries, 87, said she wanted to give staff at the dealership “one where the sun don’t shine” because of their behaviour.

She said: “They’re on the pavement where people walk down, so they have to go out into the road to come.

“They say if they haven’t got a number on the front they can put a car where they want.”



Annie Secunda, 83, said her retirement housing community’s local bus stop has been blocked by the dealership’s cars, meaning buses are forced to stop in the middle of the road.

She said: “I’ve got nothing against the cars, I’ve got nothing against the people – but it’s just the inconsideration that they show for everybody else.

“Elderly people have to walk around in the road to get on the bus.”

Nearby resident Glody, 30, said new deliveries of cars were arriving “every day”.

He said: “It’s pretty dangerous – the roads around this area are pretty narrow, and if cars are taking up the footpath, people have to walk in to the road.



“At the end of summer they started to deliver more vehicles, I’ve started seeing a lot more vehicles outside, even on the footpaths.

“It seems like it’s just come out of nowhere. It’s a big problem. They seem like they own the place.”

Peter Taylor, elected mayor of Watford, said: “Local residents are understandably annoyed that this business is flouting parking restrictions around the dealership.



“The council has increased the number of patrols to try get them to change their behaviour.

“In the last month there have been over 130 visits and we will continue to serve Penalty Charge Notices to vehicles parked illegally where they have registration plates.

“We have visited the dealership and made them aware of our serious concerns.

“We are also working with the Police and Hertfordshire Highways to see what more can be done to stop unregistered vehicles being parked where they shouldn’t be, as this falls outside of our parking enforcement team’s jurisdiction.”

Endeavour Automotive Group, which operates the dealership, said: “We are aware of concerns regarding vehicle parking and deliveries at our Omoda & Jaecoo location on Lower High Street, Watford, and we take these matters seriously.



“As vehicle volumes increase at certain times of the year, we recognise the impact that parking can have on local residents, pedestrians and surrounding public spaces.

“We are continuing to review the matters raised with our site management team, including vehicle delivery arrangements, parking, and the way any concerns from residents have been handled.

“To help address the issue, we have secured additional compound space – three compounds in total – to ease pressure on the site and provide further vehicle storage capacity.

“This is aimed at reducing the need for vehicles to be parked on surrounding roads, while also helping to remove cars from grass verges and keep pedestrian pathways clear and accessible.

“Here at Endeavour Automotive, we are continuing to work with our teams and logistical partners to ensure vehicles are stored responsibly and in accordance with local parking regulations.



“We also expect all colleagues to deal with residents and members of the public in a respectful and professional manner at all times.

“We remain committed to being a good neighbour within the community and will continue to review our operations to help reduce any disruption to local residents, pedestrians and visitors.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A Hertfordshire Constabulary spokesperson said: “We appreciate the frustration this situation is causing for residents and understand the concerns around accessibility, road safety and disruption in the area.

“We are actively working with Watford Borough Council, the dealership and other partners to resolve these issues being experienced by the local community.”

News.title: The only way out of the giant mess Britain’s economy is in is for Labour to crackdown on skivers
News.content:
Sicknote UK

THE Welfare Party’s creation of a world where work is increasingly optional is crushing hopes of a return to prosperity.

Yesterday’s unemployment and benefit figures were dismal.

Britain’s sickness benefits bill has ballooned to a record 7.6million claims — including 4.1million on disability PIPs and 3.5million on the health element of Universal Credit.



Shockingly, that is up by ONE MILLION in just a year.



A FIFTH of all working-age adults have now disappeared from the jobs market altogether.

Meanwhile, more than 200,000 jobs have been lost since Labour took power.

Private sector wages are rising at just 2.9 per cent. But in the public sector — where the Government has spent billions on pay bribes to striking doctors, teachers and train drivers — wage increases are DOUBLE at six per cent.



Labour’s addiction to State power means that pay gap will only get wider and the cost to a shrinking number of taxpayers even higher.

Does anyone in Government understand the massive economic problems the country now faces?

Yesterday, allies of Chancellor John Healey desperately briefed he didn’t know how bad things were until arriving in the Treasury. Really?

With debt and welfare spiralling out of control and growth near zero, Britain has been facing a slow-motion economic car crash for well over a year.



The only way out of the giant mess is for Healey to crack down on the skivers’ benefits jamboree.

He then needs to show he is committed to freeing up the strivers by cutting taxes and putting more money back in their pockets.

So far, there’s been precious little sign that Labour has the stomach for the fight needed to deliver either.

Lou blow

SIR Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves’ answer to the crippled public finances was to target business.

But driving up National Insurance on employers and making the minimum wage unaffordable only ended up pricing a million young people out of jobs.



Yesterday, First Minister Lou Haigh unveiled another genius plan.

This time it’s to saddle firms with another costly headache by bringing in new laws which will allow all staff greater flexible working.

That includes the right to demand more working from home. Bosses will be compelled to waste time holding meetings over any requests — and come up with reasons for refusing.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It won’t do anything to boost growth or productivity, one of the Government’s main aims. In fact, it might well have the opposite effect.

But it’s not a bad return for the union chiefs who pushed for ever more onerous workers’ rights in return for donating millions to Labour.

News.title: Desperate hunt for boy, 3, who vanished from village playground as cops ask locals to search their gardens and sheds
News.content:
FIND HIM Desperate hunt for boy, 3, who vanished from village playground as cops ask locals to search their gardens and sheds

A DESPERATE hunt has been launched for a missing three-year-old boy who vanished from a village playground.

Noah was last seen at 3pm on Tuesday in Brantham, Suffolk, as officers urge locals to search their gardens and sheds.



The child was separated from his grandfather after visiting a playground in Merriam Close who was unable to catch him before raising the alarm.

Noah is said to have then run off down an alleyway beside the playground towards a new build housing estate and a large fishing lake known as Decoy Pond.



The area is also surrounded by woodland, thick bushes and fields leading down to the main railway line between Ipswich and Liverpool Street, London.

Trains which normally go down the track at up to 100mph appeared to slow down to around 20mph when they were passing through the area on Tuesday night.

The River Stour is on the other side of the railway track from where Noah disappeared.

Suffolk Police described him as white with curly, ginger hair and wearing a white Bluey t-shirt, shorts and white trainers when he disappeared.



Scores of people scoured the area on Tuesday to try and find any trace of the missing youngster.

Firefighters were also seen looking under cars and over garden walls close to the playground.

Many were seen walking around the village and searching the banks of the River Stour by torchlight.

A search and rescue helicopter joined the hunt and high speed trains were ordered to slow down to avoid the risk of the boy being hit.

But the mood among those searching for him became increasingly desperate as darkness fell with no sign of Noah.



One woman who was searching said: “We are just praying that he might have got tired and be curled up somewhere asleep.”

Another woman who joined the search and gave her name as Kerry, 35, said: “People have been searching for more than four hours now and have found nothing.

“Nobody is giving up, but it is looking really bad. There’s no sign of him anywhere. I heard that he was with his granddad and he just outran him.”



The mother-of-four added: “I think he was being looked after while his mum was at work. Then this happens. His granddad couldn’t keep up with him. It’s just a question of trying to find him before it gets pitch black.”

A youth who said he was a cousin of Noah said: “It all happened in just a moment. My granddad was telling him to stop and he just ran off.”

Noah’s father Rhys Woods posted a message on Facebook, saying: “I am the father of Noah the boy who is currently missing.

“We really do appreciate all of the help in searching for our boy, could we ask for search parties to not enter the Decoy Pond area. This has been searched thoroughly since mid afternoon.

“Also the amount of bodies makes it hard to pick up the infra red signal we need (Noah’s). Thank you again for all your help, and I’m praying we find him.”



A spokesperson for Suffolk Constabulary said: “Emergency services are currently in Brantham conducting searches.

“Residents in the area are asked to check their gardens, sheds and outbuildings.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A spokesperson for HM Coastguard said: “We are assisting Suffolk Constabulary with an incident at Brantham by sending an HM Coastguard helicopter and Coastguard Rescue Teams from Felixstowe and Holbrook.”

Anyone who thinks they have seen Noah is asked to contact Suffolk Police, quoting CAD 203 of 15 September.

News.title: Water companies trigger 'deeply concerning' 84% surge in complaints to industry watchdog
News.content:
Water companies trigger 'deeply concerning' 84% surge in complaints to industry watchdog

Inflation busting price hikes by water companies in April last year fuelled a sharp rise in complaints to both the firms themselves and the industry watchdog

View 2 Images A jump in water prices prompted a leap in customer complaints

Britain’s water watchdog says it is “deeply concerned” after it saw a record 84% surge in complaints about suppliers last year.

‌



The Consumer Council for Water said it dealt with more than 15,100 cases from customers after they failed to resolve the issue with their firm. The increase, from around 8,200 the prior year, marked the biggest increase in its 20 year history.

‌



It came as the overall number of complaints made by households directly to their water company surged by 56% to more than 321,300 - equivalent to almost 900 every single day last year.

‌



The huge tally comes amid angry about water companies for soaring prices at the same time as they are seen to be failing to tackle a leaks and sewage crisis.

View 2 Images Rising water bills have added to the cost of living squeeze for many households

Water firms accused of dumping sewage in rivers and seas over 43,000 hours over summer READ MORE :

The sharp rise was primarily driven by growing concerns over bills, with complaints made to water companies about billing increasing by 72% and almost doubling among the cases brought to CCW.

‌



It came as households were hit with inflation-shattering water bill increases of up to £224 a year in April last year - the biggest wave of hikes since privatisation - with suppliers claiming it was needed to fund long overdue investment in the country’s creaking network of pipe and sewage plants.

Mike Keil, chief executive of CCW, said: “It’s deeply troubling to see such an unprecedented rise in complaints. These numbers reflect just how dissatisfied many people still are with the state of the water sector and the enormous task water companies face in rebuilding consumer trust.

“People have been hit with significant bill rises and are impatient to see the benefits where they live – whether that’s a more reliable service, cleaner rivers or effective and empathetic support when they are struggling to pay their bill. Companies need to be clear and open with their customers about how they are investing people’s money to deliver real improvements.”

‌



The watchdog assesses each company’s performance on the number of complaints it receives for every 10,000 households it serves, and the effort customers have to put in to get their complaint resolved.

Thames Water and South West Water rated “poor” for both measures, making them the worst performing companies. Portsmouth Water and Bristol Water were the only companies to score “good”.

The results come amid mounting pressure on the government to bring the water industry back under some form of public control.

‌



A Parliamentary debate this week heard claims that doing so could save £22billion over five years from not paying dividends and interest on loans.

Labour MP Paul Davies, who led a Westminster Hall debate, said ditching the “disastrous” privatised model would also go some way to restoring the public’s faith in the sector.

He cited a YouGov survey that found 82% of Brits feel the water industry should be publicly owned. up from 59% in 2017.

Article continues below

Water Minister Emma Hardy said Andy Burnham becoming PM would “open up options that were previously not available - more things are on the table. We are working through things right now across government.”

News.title: Huge gaps in job vacancies for young people across Britain fuels Neets crisis
News.content:
Huge gaps in job vacancies for young people across Britain fuels Neets crisis

Think tank, The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), found a sixfold gap between job openings for young people in some areas of the country than others

View 4 Images The battle for work can be six times harder in some parts of Britain than others for young people, think tank the IPPR found (Image: Getty Images)

Out-of-work young people face stark differences in their fight for a job depending on where they live, research has revealed.

‌



A report from think tank The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) highlighted vastly more young job hunters for every vacancy in some areas of the country than others. For example, there was around one suitable job opening for every 22 young people in Rotherham in South Yorkshire. That compared to one for every four youngsters in the Cotswolds.

‌



Nine of the 10 areas with the highest number of suitable vacancies per young adults are in the South, whereas four of the worst areas are in the Midlands, with the rest in Yorkshire, Scotland, Wales, and the East of England.

‌



The findings come against a background of almost one million 18 to 24-year olds not in education, employment, or training - or Neets.

The report highlights the fact that it is not simply a question of an individual’s qualifications or willingness to look for work that makes it harder for some than others to break into the world of work.

UK economy could get £14bn boost by tackling youth employment Neet crisis READ MORE :

View 4 Images Former Labour minister Alan Milburn is conducting a review into how to best tackle a Neets crisis (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire)

‌



One option is to try to secure an apprenticeship, a routine proving increasingly popular but where there is a battle for places. However, the IPPR found the availability of apprenticeships can differ greatly by sectors, with health and social work among those offering the most, while the likes of arts and entertainment providing far fewer opportunities.

Its report calls on the government to fund jobs in areas with too few entry-level opportunities, reform apprenticeships to prioritise young people, and create a universal youth employment service. The recommendations come amid a review by former Labour minister Alan Milburn on how to also tackle the Neets crisis.

View 4 Images Job vacancies across the economy have fallen to just over 700,000

‌



Lord David Blunkett, former secretary of state for education and employment, said: “I was 16, with no qualifications, little knowledge about further education but with a burning ambition to be independent and fend for myself.

"Born without sight and brought up on a council estate in Sheffield, my route forward was neither straightforward nor assured. I know, therefore, something of what it means to stand at the threshold of adult life without a clear path ahead.”

He went on: “Young people have an immense amount to give. With national ambition, local leadership and the willingness to invest, we can ensure that birthplace does not determine a young person’s future. We can renew the promise that should lie at the heart of any decent society: that no young person will be discarded, that the door to opportunity will remain open, and that everyone will have the chance to build a life of purpose.”

Article continues below

View 4 Images Former Labour minister Lord Blunkett called for national effort to "ensure that birthplace does not determine a young person’s future" (Image: Derbyshire Live / Getty Images)

Henry Parkes, principal economist at IPPR, said: “Too much of the debate about youth unemployment starts from the assumption that the problem lies with the young person.

"Our local data shows just how wrong that is. There is a more than six-fold gap in the availability of suitable vacancies depending on where you live.”

News.title: Man fights for his life after horror third-floor balcony fall in Sydney
News.content:
Man fights for his life after horror third-floor balcony fall in Sydney

Emergency services rushed to a unit complex on Cooper Street, Waterloo, as part of ongoing police investigations. After police arrived a 32-year-old man attempted to exit the unit via the balcony and fell.

View 2 Images He was taken to Royal North Shore Hospital in a serious but stable condition. (Image: 7News)

A man is fighting for his life after falling from a third-floor balcony in Sydney.

‌



Emergency services rushed to a unit complex on Cooper Street, Waterloo, as part of ongoing police investigations. After police arrived at around 1.30pm local time yesterday a 32-year-old man attempted to exit the unit via the balcony and fell.

‌



The man, who has not been named, was treated by NSW Ambulance paramedics for serious injuries before he was taken to Royal North Shore Hospital in a serious but stable condition.

‌



It is not known why the man attempted to exit the unit via the balcony after refusing police entry. A critical incident team from Leichhardt Police Area Command will investigate the circumstances surrounding this incident.

View 2 Images A 32-year-old man attempted to exit the unit via the balcony and fell. (Image: Getty Images)

‌



A New South Wales Police spokesperson said: "A critical incident investigation is underway after a man was seriously injured after falling from a third-floor balcony in Sydney’s south.

"Just before 1.30pm today (Tuesday 15 September 2026), police attended a unit complex on Cooper Street, Waterloo, as part of ongoing police investigations. On arrival, officers attached to South Sydney Police Area Command attempted to speak with a 32-year-old man who was inside the unit and refused police entry.

"Whilst police remained outside the unit, the man attempted to exit the unit via the balcony and fell. Police subsequently located the 32-year-old man and rendered assistance until the arrival of NSW Ambulance paramedics.

Article continues below

"The man was treated by NSW Ambulance paramedics for serious injuries before he was taken to Royal North Shore Hospital in a serious but stable condition. A crime scene was established and a critical incident team from Leichhardt Police Area Command will investigate the circumstances surrounding this incident.

"The investigation will be subject of an independent review by the Professional Standards Command and oversight by the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission."

News.title: Bomb squad rush to Sheffield street as homes evacuated and 100m cordon in place
News.content:
Bomb squad rush to Sheffield street as homes evacuated and 100m cordon in place

A number of homes have been evacuated after bomb disposal experts were called to a house in High Green, Sheffield

View Image An Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) team was called to Mapplebeck Road in High Green, Sheffield (file image) (Image: DAILY RECORD)

A number of homes have been evacuated after a bomb disposal team was scrambled to a house in Sheffield.

‌



South Yorkshire Police said a 100m (328ft) cordon was put in place around a property on Mapplebeck Road in High Green on Tuesday evening. An Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) van was pictured at the scene.

‌



Officers have been at the property since Friday, with specialist teams carrying out a forensic search. "Following a discovery this afternoon [Tuesday], it has been deemed necessary to evacuate nearby properties to enable emergency services and specialists to ensure safety," the force said.

‌



It comes after a 36-year-old woman appeared in court on Monday charged with Section 4 of the Explosive Substances Act 1883. She was remanded in custody.

Article continues below

Road closures are in place on Mapplebeck Road, Griffiths Road, School Road, Worrall Road, Beechwood Road, Hawthorne Road, Entwhistle Road and Greenwood Road.

No injuries have been reported. Residents who were asked to leave their homes have been directed to a nearby rest centre.

News.title: Urgent search for missing boy, 3, who vanished from playground in Brantham
News.content:
Urgent search for missing boy, 3, who vanished from playground in Brantham

Police are urgently appealing for help to locate three-year-old Noah, who was last seen near a playground in Brantham, Suffolk, after becoming separated from a relative

View 2 Images Noah, three, vanished in Brantham, Suffolk

A three-year-old boy has vanished after becoming separated from a relative near a playground in Suffolk.

‌



Police are urgently appealing for help to locate Noah, who was last seen at approximately 3pm this afternoon, Tuesday September 15.

‌



The youngster became separated from a relative after visiting the playground in Merriam Close, Suffolk Police said.

‌



Noah is reported to have run off down the alleyway beside the playground towards the new build housing estate.

View 2 Images Police are urgently appealing for help to locate three-year-old Noah, who was last seen near a playground in Brantham, Suffolk. (Image: Google Maps)

‌



He is described by police as white, with curly ginger hair, and was wearing a white Bluey T-shirt, shorts and white trainers.

Searches are currently being carried out by emergency services in Brantham, with residents in the area asked to check their gardens, sheds and outbuildings.

More than 100 people are said to have joined the searches on Tuesday evening, the BBC reports.

Article continues below

A spokesperson for HM Coastguard said: "We are assisting Suffolk Constabulary with an incident at Brantham by sending an HM Coastguard helicopter and Coastguard Rescue Teams from Felixstowe and Holbrook."

Anyone who believes they have seen Noah is asked to contact Suffolk Police, quoting CAD 203 of 15 September.

The force can be contacted on its website or by calling 101. Alternatively, you can use the Live Chat service by clicking the icon at the bottom right corner of the Suffolk Police homepage here.

News.title: 'Pain endured by the families of victims of Lucy Letby must now force change'
News.content:
'Pain endured by the families of victims of Lucy Letby must now force change'

The deaths of three babies at the hands of Lucy Letby could have been prevented if police were called in sooner, an inquiry prompted by the child serial killer’s crimes has found

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

Every parent who places a desperately ill newborn into the hands of a hospital does so with absolute trust. The Thirlwall Inquiry has laid bare how catastrophically that trust was betrayed at the Countess of Chester Hospital. Babies who should have been protected were left exposed by a system that failed at every level. Warnings were missed, suspicions were ignored, and parents were kept in the dark for years. Lady Justice Thirlwall’s verdict of a “complete failure to protect babies” should haunt the NHS. Nothing can undo the suffering of those families, or answer the unbearable question of how many lives might have been saved. But their pain must now force change. Safeguarding cannot be treated as paperwork, guidance or someone else’s responsibility. It must be the first duty of every hospital, every manager and every clinician. When concerns are raised, action must be immediate, independent and unavoidable. No hierarchy, reputation or fear of embarrassment can come before a child’s safety.

‌



Pensions reform must be fair

A £500-a-year rise in the state pension will be welcome to millions of retirees still struggling with food, energy and council tax bills. The Government has promised that pensioners whose sole income is the state pension will not be dragged into paying income tax simply because their income exceeds the £12,570 threshold. That reassurance matters. But the picture is less clear for those with modest workplace pensions, deferred payments or additional state pension entitlements, who could still face an unexpected tax bill. Ministers must spell out exactly who is protected and who is not. There is also a bigger debate coming. The triple lock has protected pensioners well, but its cost is climbing sharply. Any future reform must be fair, sustainable and, above all, protect the poorest pensioners first.

Fox gives those with Parkinson’s hope

Michael J Fox has spent decades turning a cruel diagnosis into hope for millions. His Emmy speech, and the tears it brought, showed the courage behind that fight. By refusing to surrender to Parkinson’s and raising £1.58 billion for research, he has given sufferers something precious - hope.

News.title: Met Office names 29 areas facing heavy rain on Wednesday - see full list
News.content:
Met Office names 29 areas facing heavy rain on Wednesday - see full list

Weather maps issued by the Met Office have turned blue as a band of low pressure will sweep eastwards throughout Wednesday, leading to downpours for many regions

View 3 Images Rain is forecast on Wednesday (Image: Met Office)

These striking weather maps show large swathes of the country will face heavy rain on Wednesday.

‌



The downpours will sweep eastwards throuhout the day, with western Scotland likely to experience the worst of the weather. The Met Office, which has issued the maps, says the cloud will thicken and temperatures will be below average for the time of year.

‌



It will be a stark contrast to the sunny start to the week, during which the mercury hit 27C in Exeter, Devon, on Monday. It was also a sunny start to the week for most, with 6.7 hours of sunshine recorded in part of Flintshire, north Wales.

‌



View 3 Images Northern Ireland and Scotland look set to receive the brunt of the miserable weather (Image: Met Office)

But nearly 30 areas will see rainfall on Wednesday, forecasters believe. By 7pm, the rainfall appears to be focused over Scotland, with Perth and Kinross, the Highlands, Stirling and Lanarkshire all braced to bear the worst of the miserable conditions. In Northern Ireland, Down and Antrim will also see patches of rain, the maps indicate.

The most severely affected areas could experience 4mm of rain per hour, while 2mm is anticipated more broadly, according to the weather maps.

‌



By 8pm, the heavy band of rain will have shifted to drench Moray, Aberdeenshire and Fife in Scotland, with up to 4mm of rainfall possible, reports the Express.

The rain will also have extended to cover Dumfries and Galloway, as well as Cumbria. The latest weather maps suggest conditions will have deteriorated further in Northern Ireland, with Tyrone and Armagh in particular forecast to experience heavy showers. Conwy and Gwynedd in north Wales are also predicted to see rain showers.

By 11pm, Met Office weather maps turn yellow in places, indicating extremely heavy rainfall. Dumfries and Galloway, South Ayrshire, Stirling and large parts of the Highlands could all see up to 8mm of rain per hour.

‌



View 3 Images Take care on the roads during morning rush-hour as they may be wet (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire)

Thursday also appears unsettled too, though the worst-hit areas then will be across the south of England. The Met Office says it will also be breezy then, with strong westerly gusts on the cards.

The fiercest of the gales will be across the western coast of Scotland, including North Ayrshire and Argyll and Bute. Using the weather maps, we have listed below the areas likely to see rain on Wednesday.

News.title: Delta flight from Dublin to New York forced to divert after emergency at 35,000ft
News.content:
Delta flight from Dublin to New York forced to divert after emergency at 35,000ft

The Delta Air Lines flight left Dublin and began flying towards New York before declaring an emergency over the Atlantic and making a U-turn just 90 minutes in

View 2 Images A flight from Dublin to New York was forced to make a U-turn over the Atlantic Ocean (Image: PA)

A flight from Dublin to New York was forced to make a U-turn over the Atlantic Ocean after declaring an in-flight emergency shortly into its journey.

‌



Delta Air Lines flight DL45 departed Dublin Airport at 1:15pm on Tuesday before heading towards its scheduled destination at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

‌



The plane climbed to an altitude of 35,000 feet, but just 90 minutes into its more than seven-hour journey, it issued a squawk 7700 code - the general emergency signal used by air traffic controllers and pilots.

‌



View 2 Images A flight from Dublin to New York was forced to make a U-turn over the Atlantic (Image: Graham Hughes/NurPhoto/Shutterstock)

Flight tracking data showed the wide-body Boeing 767-300ER jet making a sharp U-turn back towards Ireland.

Article continues below

Air traffic control prioritised the returning jet for an immediate diversion back to Dublin Airport, where emergency ground crews were placed on standby ahead of its landing at around 4:15pm.

A Delta Air Lines spokesperson told the Mirror that the flight returned to Dublin following a medical situation involving a passenger.

The spokesperson said: "Delta Flight 45 from Dublin to New York-JFK returned to Dublin due to a customer medical situation onboard. We thank our crew for their professionalism and our customers for their understanding".

News.title: Baby 'cot cams' plan after inquiry finds Lucy Letby crimes could have been prevented
News.content:
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has said officials will "urgently develop plans" to introduce live-streaming cameras on England's baby wards after an inquiry into Lucy Letby's murders and attempted murders.

Inquiry chair Lady Justice Thirlwall called for a series of urgent reforms to neonatal units, including CCTV for all cots and incubators, and restricting access to insulin.

Thirlwall said some of the babies Letby killed could have been saved if managers at the Countess of Chester Hospital had taken action earlier.

Her report criticises a "complete failure to protect babies" and a "profound failure of management, governance and safeguarding" at the hospital.

Thirlwall said this was because "no one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt."

She said it would never be possible to know exactly how many lives could have been saved if safeguarding procedures had been properly followed.

One of the senior doctors who tried to raise concerns about Letby with hospital managers, consultant paediatrician Dr John Gibbs, now retired, told the BBC the Thirlwall Inquiry report was "grim reading".

In a rare interview he said he accepted that consultants must bear "collective" responsibility for some of the failings identified in the report, and said he wished they had been "brave enough to follow our suspicions and escalate things to the police earlier".

Chief executive and registrar at the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC), Paul Rees, said he was "truly sorry for the NMC's failings" in the Letby case and that "we also did not act quickly enough to suspend Lucy Letby".

News.title: Dan Thomas resigns as Reform Wales leader after arrest on suspicion of assault
News.content:
Reform UK's Dan Thomas has quit as the party's Welsh leader, after he was arrested on Sunday on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

Gwent Police confirmed that a 45-year-old man from Aberbargoed, in Caerphilly, was bailed pending further enquiries.

In a statement issued by his party, the Member of the Senedd for Casnewydd Islwyn said he was "standing down" from his position due to personal reasons.

He said he had been "released without charge" and had "done nothing wrong".

Thomas was appointed Welsh party leader by Nigel Farage in February.

Plaid Cymru, which runs the Welsh government, said: "Reform UK is descending into chaos."

Thomas did not take part in First Minister's Questions earlier today.

He was first elected to the Senedd in the elections in May, where his party went from having two politicians in Cardiff Bay to 34.

Reform came second behind Plaid Cymru in the vote, with Thomas becoming leader of the opposition in the Senedd.

Thomas said: "It has been the honour of my life to have been the leader of Reform Wales and see this party go from zero to 34 elected members and become the largest opposition group in Welsh history.

"With deep regret, I am now standing down from this position due to personal reasons.

"Over the weekend, I was reported to the police and was released without charge."

He added: "I will continue to serve my constituents in Casnewydd Islwyn and will fully back whoever the group selects as its next leader."

The news came on the same day that Reform MS Sarah Cooper-Lesadd defected to Plaid Cymru.

News.title: Former England footballer Raheem Sterling admits dangerous driving on motorway before crash
News.content:
Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has admitted dangerous driving on a motorway before he crashed a Lamborghini in May.

The 31-year-old, from Berkshire, also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis.

Sterling, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court, was arrested after crashing near the M3 in Hampshire on the morning of 28 May.

Sterling has 82 England caps, the last of which was won at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

News.title: Warning of space arms race as US confirms weapons in Earth's orbit
News.content:
The US has confirmed it deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit, the first time it has acknowledged such offensive capabilities.

Russia and China responded by warning of an arms race in space.

However, according to the BBC's Defence correspondent Jonathan Beale, this is already happening.

Details of how the weapon operates have not been disclosed by US officials.

News.title: Thirteenth Met Police officer sacked after Charing Cross Panorama film
News.content:
Another Metropolitan Police officer has been dismissed following BBC Panorama's undercover investigation into the force's Charing Cross station.

PC Mason O'Connor was sacked after a hearing found he had breached standards of professional behaviour, relating to a comment he made to a female colleague, the Met said.

O'Connor was reported to a "proactive wider investigation" following the broadcast of the programme in October 2025 and he has become the 13th officer to be sacked since then, the force added.

Other officers who were covertly filmed for the documentary were seen calling for immigrants to be shot, boasting about excessive use of force and joking about rape and sexual assault.

Met Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said at the time that this behaviour was "totally unacceptable".

A disciplinary panel on Tuesday heard that O'Connor had, while off-duty at a pub, told a female colleague that he hoped she would be raped on her way home.

He was found to have breached standards of professional behaviour for authority, respect and courtesy, equality and diversity, and discreditable conduct, the Met said.

As well as the 13 officers the Met has sacked, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said another two men, both former officers, had also been found to have committed gross misconduct.

The policing watchdog added it was still investigating the conduct of a further 15 officers or police staff in the wake of the Panorama film.

"This is one of our largest ever investigations in terms of the number of officers investigated," said the IOPC's Amanda Rowe.

"The sheer number of fast-tracked disciplinary proceedings show how seriously the IOPC and the Met, who held the misconduct hearings, are treating this matter," she added.

News.title: State pension likely to top £13,000 a year as UK wage growth slows to 3.9%
News.content:
The state pension is expected to top Â£13,000 a year, reigniting the debate about its long-term affordability and generational fairness.

The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to rise by Â£488 a year in April, based on the latest official earnings figure released on Tuesday.

The so-called triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest.

Labour made a manifesto pledge to keep the triple lock until 2029, however economists have warned about the cost of the policy ahead of the Budget although pensioner groups say many people still face poverty in old age.

News.title: Two dead after car hits group of pedestrians
News.content:
Two people have died and four have been seriously injured after a car crashed into a group of people in Doncaster.

South Yorkshire Police said officers were called to White Rose Way when a black Mitsubishi L200 hit a group of pedestrians at 11:00 BST on Sunday, before hitting a black Audi and silver BMW on the opposite carriageway.

The force said two of the pedestrians had died at the scene while four other people were taken to hospital with serious injuries.

The driver of the Mitsubishi, a 30-year-old man, was arrested on suspicion of two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, two counts of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and driving while unfit and later released on bail.

News.title: Trump criticises Supreme Court after justices block mail-in ballot restrictions
News.content:
The US Supreme Court has rejected President Donald Trump's plan to restrict voting by mail before November's midterm elections, in a setback for the White House.

The justices upheld a federal judge's order that temporarily blocked the US Postal Service (USPS) from moving forwards with new requirements for postal ballots.

Trump called the decision a blow to his political party. "Republicans just got another bad decision from the United States Supreme Court," the president wrote on Truth Social.

One legal group said in response that the decision would prevent the USPS from "sowing chaos in our elections".

The ruling is unlikely to be the final word on the matter. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a conservative, agreed with the ruling, but indicated he might later rule in Trump's favour as litigation in the case continues.

Trump, who argued the rules would combat electoral fraud, signed an executive order in March that directed the USPS to deliver ballots only to voters on lists of citizens.

Legal challenges argued that the move violated states' constitutional rights to run elections.

Election officials from 24 Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia also warned that the proposed changes were not ready for implementation and could prevent ballots from reaching voters.

Meanwhile some Republican-led states, including Florida, Louisiana, and Montana, supported the president in court filings.

Justice Kavanaugh wrote in the opinion that there was "at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority". But he argued that "applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious".

Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, also conservatives, dissented. They wrote that the challenge to Trump's order was a "Hail Mary pass" that was unlikely to be successful ultimately.

In a Truth Social post, Trump criticised the top court's Monday decision, as well as other key rulings against him such as striking down his executive order to limit birthright citizenship, and also a key element of his tariff policies.

"The Supreme Court has really let our Country down!" he wrote, alleging some justices were "totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America".

"These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," the president wrote.

News.title: Letby hospital consultant says inquiry makes for grim reading
News.content:
One of the senior doctors who tried to raise concerns about Lucy Letby with hospital managers has told the BBC the final inquiry report makes for "grim reading".

Consultant paediatrician Dr John Gibbs worked at the Countess of Chester Hospital throughout the period in 2015 to 2016 when Letby murdered seven babies, and attempted to murder seven more, on the neonatal unit.

He said that he accepted that consultants must bear "collective" responsibility for some of the failings identified in the report.

"I wish we consultants had been brave enough to follow our suspicions and escalate things to the police earlier," he told the BBC.

"When I say, 'we consultants', I am responsible as well and if my other consultant colleagues didn't go to the police, I should have."

The Thirlwall Inquiry was launched after former nurse Letby was convicted in 2023, and the final report was published on Tuesday.

In the 822-page document, Lady Justice Thirlwall described "a complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital".

The report found that the police "should have been notified earlier than they were" and that hospital managers had repeatedly dismissed consultants' concerns.

Reflecting on the findings for the first time, Gibbs said: "I wasn't expecting it to be an easy read and it certainly isn't. I'd imagine it's an extremely difficult read for the parents of the babies concerned.

"As I admitted when I appeared before the inquiry to give evidence, I feel we failed the babies and I apologise to the families for that."

Gibbs, who began working in Chester in 1994 and is now retired, agreed with the report's finding that hospital executives had multiple opportunities to act and potentially save babies' lives while the deaths were happening.

"But it was during that 11 months after Lucy Letby was moved off the unit, before the police got involved, that it was a very difficult atmosphere, very tense, very stressful dealing with the managers," he added.

Managers "were determined to ensure that we accepted Lucy Letby had been wrongly suspected of doing any harm," the senior doctor explained.

He also spoke of the failures of his and his wider team, specifically referencing a doctor who disregarded blood test results that suggested a baby had been poisoned with insulin in August 2015.

While one of his colleagues had missed the relevance of the results when they came back from the lab, it had been a collective team failure, Dr Gibbs concluded.

"Others of us were on call and covering the neonatal unit over the next week or two before the baby moved out of the unit. We all had the opportunity to review the notes."

News.title: Southport attack victims, survivors and families hit by data breach
News.content:
An investigation is under way after a data breach involving court files relating to victims, survivors and families of the Southport attack, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has said.

The unauthorised access by courts staff was identified during a review of the department's digital systems. For a limited number of people, the information accessed included sensitive and personal data, but the MOJ did not state how many people were affected.

An spokesperson said the MOJ was "appalled", but there was no evidence personal data had been shared with third parties and the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) had been told.

The prime minister has asked the Lord Chancellor to oversee the matter.

An MOJ source said its independent Data Protection Officer had assessed the matter and found that, for a limited number of people, the information accessed included sensitive and personal data likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms.

Those affected are being notified directly, the department said.

News.title: Political donors could face tougher residency rules
News.content:
MPs have supported the government's proposals by approving amendments to the Representation of the People Bill. The bill is currently being scrutinised in the House of Lords.

Speaking as the bill was debated by peers, Communities Minister Baroness Taylor of Stevenage said: "We are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring that the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy."

Baroness Taylor said this was "in addition to introducing a robust regime that ensures that donors contributing above the Â£100,000 annual cap must demonstrate a genuine and ongoing connection" to the UK.

Tax is one area that already has residency requirements. The criteria includes someone being declared resident for tax purposes if they have lived in the UK for at least 183 days in the tax year.

Challenged on whether the government was targeting Reform donors, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said policy on donations is "never about one political party or one particular set of issues".

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "Fundamentally we need to make sure that people who want to influence British politics, who want a say in British politics have a stake in Britain.

"That should apply to everyone and will apply to everyone, so I wouldn't make it about any particular donations or anything that's been in the public domain."

When the government set out its plans to cap foreign donations in March and July, it did not mention the idea of an enhanced residency test for political donors.

Asked repeatedly by reporters whether the idea of tightening residency rules had only been discussed after Delo and Harborne's most recent donations to Reform, the prime minister's official spokesman would not give a timeframe.

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart accused the government of "playing whack-a-mole", as she said Labour's residency requirements "aren't good enough".

She said: "We must urgently go further and introduce a universal donation cap to stop Trump's America becoming Farage's Britain."

On Monday, Farage criticised the government's attempts to retrospectively declare some donations illegal.

He told the BBC: "If the government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There would be a response the other way.

"We or the Conservatives would say 'if you're going to stop legitimate donors like this, we would say to the trade unions, you can't give money'."

Farage argued such a move would "collapse" the system of political funding and lead to taxpayers having to fund political parties, a system he said would be opposed by the British public.

Since 2020, Labour has received almost Â£43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees.

News.title: Fall in small boat Channel crossings down to law enforcement, agency says
News.content:
Law enforcement activity has been a "key factor" in reducing the number of small boat Channel crossings, the National Crime Agency (NCA) says.

The number of people arriving in the UK in the first half of 2026 was down 41% on the year before, government figures show.

The NCA said the drop followed a "significant increase in arrests and seizures", although added "fluctuating demand" for crossings, and the French authorities preventing boat launches had also played a role.

However, Mihnea Cuibus, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, says it is "impossible" to disentangle the effects of government policy and other factors on small boat arrivals.

While recent policy changes appear to have led smugglers and migrants to alter their behaviour, Cuibus says fewer unauthorised arrivals into the EU and developments in key origin countries - such as improved security in Syria - may be partially behind the decline.

"It is hard to know how much restrictive measures contributed to reducing [arrivals] in 2026," he continues.

He said limitations on refugee family reunion and a reduction in the asylum grant rate could also have had an impact.

The Conservatives have previously said the weather played a huge role in the fluctuating numbers of crossings from France and Belgium.

NCA director general of operations Rob Jones said the agency was "devoting more resources to tackling organised immigration crime than ever before".

"That is bringing results.

"However, we are not complacent, and the job is by no means done," he continued.

"We must continue to keep up the pressure on these criminal gangs, as they continue to put lives at risk in the Channel."

News.title: British woman abducted in Malawi, police say
News.content:
Police in Malawi are investigating the kidnapping of a British national who was abducted in the southern African nation's main city, Blantyre.

Nusrat Osman, 47, was seized at around 12:30 local time on Friday by four men who had been travelling in a grey Nissan Dualis, according to a police statement.

The authorities have offered a reward of more than $17,000 (Â£12,600) for "credible information" that could lead to the rescue of the mother of two young children and the prosecution of the perpetrators.

Osman was reported to have been working for a local auditing firm.

A Malawi news outlet reported that Osman's husband was in anguish about the disappearance.

"I don't know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor and I have no issues with anyone," he was quoted by Nyasa Times as saying.

Police said the motive behind the abduction was unknown and that so far the kidnappers have not contacted the victim's family or the authorities.

The UK Foreign Office told the BBC that it was aware of reports that a British national had been abducted in Malawi and was in touch with local authorities.

News.title: Search launched for boy, 3, missing at playground
News.content:
Emergency services and members of the public are searching for a three-year-old boy who went missing at a playground.

Noah Woods was with a relative at the small park at Merriam Close in Brantham, but "became separated" from them as they left at about 15:00 BST, Suffolk Police said.

The toddler, who is partially deaf, autistic and non-verbal, was reported to have run down a nearby alleyway towards a newbuild housing estate.

"We ask local residents to please check their outbuildings, gardens and sheds, and report any sightings to police on 999," Supt Pete Partridge said.

A helicopter has been pictured flying over the scene, which is near the estuary of the River Stour and close to the Essex border.

Police described Noah as white, with curly ginger hair, and said he would not respond to his name being called.

News.title: Harry and Meghan change children's school over security concerns due to traffic
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have changed their children's school only days after they first started over security concerns about traffic during the school run.

The schools' names have not been disclosed, but it is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had been concerned that the distance and the heavy traffic on the original school run route had made it difficult to make secure.

It's understood that the security for the children meant travelling with another car, and that driving in convoy proved difficult in the busy school run traffic.

The checks on the route are believed to have initially taken place before term time, but with the school traffic it was deemed not safe enough.

A source close to the couple said: "The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family's security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements."

They added: "The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.

"This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there."

It has also emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their return to live in the UK.

It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.

It will assess any risks they face in their new home and the type of trips taken by the couple and their family, such as regular travel routes and school runs.

News.title: AI poses huge risks to national security without guardrails, minister says
News.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) poses "huge risks" to the UK's national security and society without the right protections, a senior minister has warned.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh - Prime Minister Andy Burnham's de facto deputy - told the TUC congress on Tuesday that the government needed to "heed the warnings" of those "at the forefront" of developing the technology.

She added the government was "ready to work with international partners" to prioritise public safety and national security.

Fears about the potential dangers of AI have ramped up in recent days after executives and current and former staff in the field warned the tech could endanger humanity.

On Monday, a spokesman for UK Prime Minister Burnham welcomed the open discussion among those developing the technology of the risks and rewards.

Speaking at the TUC congress on Tuesday afternoon, Haigh acknowledged the "enormous potential" of AI for public services, businesses and science.

While she said the UK needed to make the most of this, she added: "There are clearly huge risks to our national security and society if the right guardrails are not put in place...

"We have a solemn duty to mitigate the risks and ensure that it is for the benefit - not the detriment - of our society."

In an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier on Tuesday, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said people should not be complacent about the risks of AI - but also not "hyperbolic".

It comes as MPs in the UK are seeking new laws on AI after a report found the technology was responsible for numerous abuses of human rights.

"Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose," Labour MP and committee chair Alex Sobel said.

News.title: Multiple inmates stabbed during brawl at notorious New York jail housing Luigi Mangione and Nicolas Maduro
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Multiple inmates have been stabbed and slashed during a major brawl at the federal jail in New York City that is currently housing UnitedHealthcare CEO killer Luigi Mangione and disgraced former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

Federal officials confirmed to The Independent that the massive fight took place on the morning of September 6 at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, New York. The New York Daily News first reported on the brawl, which their sources said was gang-related.

Members of the Trinitarios gang fought another gang on the seventh floor of the jail’s west building, the Daily News’ sources said, adding that a total of at least 20 people had joined in the brawl.

“Several incarcerated individuals were medically assessed and treated for minor injuries at the facility, while other incarcerated individuals sustained injuries requiring outside medical treatment,” Donald Murphy, a spokesperson for the Federal Bureau of Prisons, told The Independent.

Murphy did not confirm the exact number of inmates involved in the fight and the number of those wounded remains unknown. The exact injuries that the wounded inmates sustained are also not clear.

open image in gallery Multiple inmates were stabbed and slashed during a major brawl at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, New York, which is currently housing UnitedHealthcare CEO killer Luigi Mangione and disgraced former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, earlier this month ( Getty Images )

Murphy told The Independent that jail employees were able to contain the incident without being injured themselves, adding, “At no time was the public in danger.” The incident is still under investigation.

MDC Brooklyn, as the jail is commonly referred to, is known for holding infamous inmates like Mangione and Maduro.

Mangione, 28, is currently awaiting sentencing in the jail after he admitted last month to fatally shooting UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson on the streets of Manhattan in 2024. Thompson’s murder shocked the nation as the New York City Police Department tracked down the Ivy League graduate, with some admiring the killer for what they saw as a stance against the health insurance industry.

“I shot Mr. Thompson and he died,” Mangione said in court on August 14. “I understood that my actions would place him in fear of death or bodily injury. I knew what I was doing was illegal.”

open image in gallery Mangione, 28, is currently awaiting sentencing in the jail after he admitted last month to fatally shooting UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson on the streets of Manhattan in 2024 ( Getty Images )

Maduro, 63, and his wife Cilia Flores, 69, are currently awaiting trial at the jail on drug trafficking charges, following a stealth mission by American forces to capture the couple from their Caracas home in early January. Their trial is set for next June.

Both have pleaded not guilty to charges stemming from an alleged conspiracy to transport thousands of tons of cocaine to the U.S.

Maduro “and his co-conspirators have, for decades, partnered with some of the most violent and prolific drug traffickers and narco-terrorists in the world, and relied on corrupt officials throughout the region, to distribute tons of cocaine to the United States,” their indictment reads.

open image in gallery Maduro, 63, and his wife Cilia Flores, 69, are currently awaiting trial at the jail on drug trafficking charges, following a stealth mission by American forces to capture the couple from their Carcas home in early January ( Getty Images )

MDC Brooklyn has a history of violence, including the reported February 2025 stabbing of Karl Jordan Jr., who was convicted and then acquitted of the 2002 murder of New York rap star Jam Master Jay. Jordan survived the attack.

In September 2024, the Justice Department announced charges against nine inmates in five separate cases involving violence at MDC Brooklyn, including the murder of Uriel Whyte on June 7, 2024, and the murder of Edwin Cordero on July 17, 2024.

“Violence will not be tolerated in our federal jails,” Breon Peace, United States Attorney for the Eastern District of New York, said at the time. “As the only federal pretrial facility in New York City, MDC-Brooklyn houses pretrial inmates accused of some of the most serious crimes in our region.”

“Let these charges serve as a warning to those who would engage in criminal conduct behind bars, and anyone else who facilitates those crimes: your conduct will be exposed, and you will be held accountable,’ Peace said.

News.title: Another Met officer dismissed after BBC Panorama investigation into Charing Cross scandal
News.content:

Another Charing Cross police officer has been dismissed from the Met almost a year after BBC Panorama exposed inappropriate conduct in the force.

A total of 13 serving officers in the Metropolitan Police force have lost their jobs since an investigation was launched by the Independent Office for Police Conduct in October. Investigations continue into the conduct of a further 15 members of police staff.

BBC Panorama published an undercover investigation into Charing Cross Station last year where officers were covertly filmed and seen calling for immigrants to be shot, boasting about excessive use of force and joking about rape and sexual assault.

Met Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said at the time that this behaviour was “totally unacceptable”.

A hearing for PC Mason O’Connor took place on Tuesday following allegations that while off-duty in a pub on October 2024 he said to a female colleague: “I hope you get raped on your way to Waterloo”.

The matter was reported following Panorama’s documentary as part of a proactive wider investigation into any other concerns about officer conduct at Charing Cross.

open image in gallery Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley (James Manning/PA) ( PA Archive )

The hearing found the allegation proven and that PC O’Connor breached standards of professional behaviour for authority, respect and courtesy, equality and diversity, and discreditable conduct.

It comes weeks after allegations were proven that PC Lloyd Hunter made comments that trivialised the use of force, suggested that he would enjoy using force on members of the public and that he “hated” homeless people.

A hearing took place for PC Hunter on 27 August after comments he made during an off-duty drink in November 2024 by the BBC.

Although not featured in the broadcast, extra unaired footage was later shared with the IOPC whose investigation into the behaviour of a number of officers at Charing Cross continues.

PC Hunter was found to have breached standards of professional behaviour for authority, respect and courtesy, equality and diversity, and discreditable conduct.

Commander Simon Messinger from professionalism, said: “Two more officers have now been dismissed for their appalling comments and attitudes.

“I hope this sends a very clear message about the standards we expect from all our officers and the Met’s determination to improve our culture across the organisation.

“We continue to support the ongoing IOPC investigation.”

Both officers will be added to the College of Policing’s barred list to prevent them re-joining policing or working for a number of other police-related bodies.
