World.title: Lindsay Clancy hires Karen Read attorney for high-stakes double jeopardy fight after murder mistrial
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Massachusetts mother accused of strangling her three young children to death is bringing in the attorney who fought Karen Read’s retrial as she makes a bid to have her own case thrown out.

Lindsay Clancy, whose closely watched murder trial ended in a reported 11-1 split in favor of finding her not criminally responsible, has added veteran Boston attorney Martin Weinberg to her defense team.

Weinberg entered a limited appearance Tuesday to file and argue a forthcoming motion seeking dismissal on double-jeopardy grounds, according to a Plymouth Superior Court filing obtained by Fox News Digital.

The filing states Weinberg will represent Clancy in connection with the dismissal motion and "related matters."

LINDSAY CLANCY'S LAWYER REVEALS POST-MISTRIAL STRATEGY AS RETRIAL LOOMS

The filing does not say when Weinberg will submit the motion. Clancy’s case is next scheduled to return to court Sept. 29.

LINDSAY CLANCY JUDGE CALLS MISTRIAL, THEN GRANTS DEFENSE ONE HOUR STAY FOR APPEAL

Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial Sept. 4 after jurors spent seven days deliberating but said they could not reach a unanimous verdict.

Several jurors later revealed that 11 members of the panel supported finding Clancy not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, while one juror voted to convict.

LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON SIGNALS HE'S OPEN TO A DEAL, HOPES DA WILL 'REVISIT' CASE

Clancy’s longtime defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, signaled immediately after the mistrial that he would fight any attempt to put her on trial again.

The defense is expected to argue that the way the mistrial ended bars prosecutors from taking another shot at the case. Prosecutors can generally retry a defendant after a jury deadlocks, but Clancy’s attorneys are expected to claim that the circumstances surrounding her mistrial make a second trial improper.

KAREN READ’S LAWYER SAYS CLANCY DEFENSE ATTORNEY MAY BE ‘CUT FROM A DIFFERENT CLOTH’ AS DELIBERATIONS DRAG ON

Weinberg mounted a similar fight for Read after her 2024 trial ended without a verdict.

Read’s attorneys said jurors later told them they had unanimously agreed to clear her of second-degree murder and leaving the scene of a deadly crash, despite remaining divided on a manslaughter charge.

PATRICK CLANCY SPEAKS OUT AFTER HUNG JURY IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE, ADDRESSES PROSPECT OF ANOTHER TRIAL

Weinberg argued that Read should not face those two charges again. A judge rejected the request, finding that the jury never formally returned not-guilty verdicts and that Read’s attorneys had agreed to the mistrial.

The battle continued in state and federal court before Read was retried in 2025. She was acquitted of second-degree murder, manslaughter and leaving the scene of a deadly crash but convicted of misdemeanor operating under the influence.

DR PHIL SAYS LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL A 'TEACHABLE MOMENT' ON POSTPARTUM PSYCHOSIS: 'THERE WAS A FAILURE HERE'

Clancy is accused of strangling her three children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan, with exercise bands inside the family’s Duxbury home in January 2023.

She then jumped from a second-story window in an apparent suicide attempt, leaving her paralyzed, authorities said.

ACCUSED NC KILLER MOM PLANS INSANITY DEFENSE — AS RETIRED JUDGE SAYS MORE MAY FOLLOW LINDSAY CLANCY STRATEGY

Clancy does not deny killing the children but pleaded not guilty because her attorneys say she was not criminally responsible at the time. Her defense argued she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was heavily medicated when the children died.

Prosecutors countered that Clancy carefully planned the killings, sending her husband, Patrick Clancy, out of the house before attacking the children.

LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR WHO BACKED THE DEFENSE ALSO PUBLICLY CHEERED KAREN READ'S ACQUITTAL

Clancy remains in custody at Tewksbury Hospital. Prosecutors have not publicly announced whether they intend to retry her.

Sullivan also ordered the identities of the 12 jurors and six alternates who served in Clancy’s trial to remain private indefinitely amid safety concerns and the unauthorized disclosure of jurors’ personal information.

The judge wrote that jurors had been identified without their permission and that at least one juror had asked for the protection to be extended indefinitely.

"Based on the circumstances of this trial and the fact that the case continues to receive daily, divisive attention in Massachusetts and beyond, the Court concludes that there is a real and present ‘risk of [personal] harm to the jurors [and] to the integrity of their service,’" Sullivan wrote in the order obtained by Fox News.

Sullivan also found "a risk of immediate and irreparable injury" if the juror list were made public. The order does not prevent jurors from identifying themselves or speaking with the media if they choose.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In a separate order, Sullivan temporarily extended the protection covering the names of the larger pool summoned for jury duty from July 20 through July 24. Those names will remain impounded for another 10 days because of concerns about juror safety.

World.title: Ex-WWE star touts NXT roster, names tag team he'd like The Headbangers to go up against one day
World.content:
WWE NXT has truly featured the pro wrestling stars of tomorrow and it’s been evident over the last year just how fast some of the talents are thrust into the main title picture.

On Monday, Lola Vice made her WWE main roster debut and earned a shot in the women’s Money in the Bank ladder match in October. Sol Ruca held the Women’s Intercontinental Championship for 57 days this year. Stephanie Vaquer and Giulia, who got a cup of coffee in NXT, each held titles when they were called up. Je’Von Evans is in the Men’s Money in the Bank ladder match, Bron Breakker is a tag team champion and Oba Femi feuded with and likely ended the career of Brock Lesnar.

Former WWE star Mosh, who spoke to OutKick Dropkick last week and opened up about his Live Fortunate premium lifestyle brand, said he’s gotten to spend some time with the NXT stars and named a few wrestlers to watch and a tag team he’d like to see The Headbangers (Mosh and Thrasher) possibly get into the ring with one day.

"Well, the obvious is the guys on top. Kelani (Jordan) is amazing. Jaida (Parker) is amazing. Then you have Kam Hendricks, who's going to be another great superstar," he said. "And then, you've got Grayson Waller, who came in and made a huge impact by calling out the locker room.

"Tag teams, I love Hank and Tank. If there's ever an opportunity for us, for The Headbangers, to wrestle Hank and Tank, I would absolutely love that. Birthright is a great group. They all have the wrestling gene in their blood. There's so many. You have Harlem Lewis and Harley Riggins who are in Evolve. I get the names crisscrossed. There's so many guys there that are coming up that are ready."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Mosh said that’s one of the things he enjoys about NXT – the environment that’s being built around the up-and-coming talent.

"That's one of the things I love about NXT is that the culture they've built there is unbelievable and the environment is crazy great," he added. "As soon as they start plucking people from the NXT roster and put them on the main roster, the next person steps right in and there's no lull. They step right in, they know what's coming up, and they know what's going on.

"And then the other part I love too is guys from the main roster still go down to NXT to work out and train. Then they get in there with these kids and they talk to them and go, ‘This is what you've got to expect when you come up here. This is kind of what you need to do to be next in line for it.’ That's one of the things that I love about it."



Mosh, whose real name is Chaz Warrington, is leading the Live Fortunate brand. He told OutKick Dropkick about his perseverance and being able to keep a steady hand even in the toughest of situations.

World.title: Senate moves to rein in college sports 'Wild West' with sweeping new rules for players, schools
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Senate took a major first step to advancing standardized, federal guardrails on college sports as name, image and likeness (NIL) has transformed the landscape of collegiate athletics.

Lawmakers moved the Protect College Sports Act, led by Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., onto the next phase, opening up the opportunity for the Senate to advance the bipartisan bill later in the week.

"I think most people acknowledge that the current landscape of college sports is a mess," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said ahead of the vote. "It needs to be addressed."

SENATE ADVANCES LANDMARK PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT, IGNORING SEC AND BIG TEN OPPOSITION WITH CLOCK TICKING

At its core, Cruz pitched the legislation as a means to corral the chaos that has unfolded in college athletics since the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) made its landmark decision in 2021 to allow student-athletes to benefit financially while playing collegiate football, basketball and many others.

"Some have asked why should Congress get in the middle of this? The answer is simple: because Congress screwed it up in the first place," Cruz said during a press conference on Monday.

"It has been the federal antitrust laws applied in litigation after litigation after litigation that have had the effect of tearing down essentially all the rules," he continued. "So right now it is the Wild West."

CRUZ AND CANTWELL REFUSE TO BEND TO SEC AND BIG TEN CONCERNS IN REVISED COLLEGE ATHLETICS LEGISLATION

The Protect College Sports Act would broadly add restrictions to the transfer portal for student-athletes, create a uniform eligibility framework of five years, recruiting and tampering guardrails that establish when schools or agents can contact or recruit a student-athlete, a federal standard for NIL rules, and a revenue-sharing cap.

Opponents of the bill, including Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., contended that the Protect College Sports Act would take away bargaining power from student-athletes and create exemptions from antitrust laws for colleges.

"The ‘chaos’ is that (mostly black) athletes now have bargaining power and white coaches and sports industry execs hate it," Murphy said on X.

KATIE UHLAENDER: ATHLETES RISK PAYING THE PRICE IF PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT IS PASSED

And the Congressional Black Caucus, led by Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-N.Y., announced that it would not support the bill, charging in a statement that it would not support the legislation while "Black political representation is under attack across the country," following the Supreme Court’s decision on the Voting Rights Act earlier this year.

"Several months ago, before the Senate ever reached this moment, the Congressional Black Caucus made clear that Congress should not rush to provide sweeping new federal protections and legal certainty to powerful athletic institutions while those same institutions remained largely silent as Black voting rights and Black political representation came under unprecedented attack," the group said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Cantwell acknowledged the pushback, noting that "several are friends and allies."

"Let me be clear, voting rights are sacred, and I will stand in that fight with anyone," she said on the Senate floor. "But I cannot agree that the way to wage it is to hold thousands of student-athletes' scholarships, health protections and future hostages to a Supreme Court decision they did not make."

World.title: Clancy-fixated Illinois mom sang 'Wizard of Oz' tune after allegedly killing 2-year-old son: report
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Corie Walsh, the woman who obsessed over the Lindsay Clancy case and allegedly killed her 2-year-old son, sang a rendition of a Wizard of Oz classic while being questioned by investigators, according to reports.

Walsh, 40, who allegedly told officers she killed her son because she believed he was the "devil" and the "anti-Christ," belted out "Follow the Yellow Brick Road" from the movie classic, according to court documents obtained by The Sun.

She is charged with three counts of first-degree murder in the death of her son, Barrett Walsh, who was found hanging lifeless from a rafter in the basement of their suburban Chicago home.

ILLINOIS MOTHER CHARGED WITH MURDER IN DEATH OF 2-YEAR-OLD SON IN CASE DRAWING COMPARISONS TO LINDSAY CLANCY

The boy was discovered by his two siblings on Sept. 1 as they returned home from school. Upon arrival, responding police officers found a neighbor performing CPR on Barrett.

While speaking with detectives, Walsh reportedly went on an unhinged rant and singing her own version of "Follow the Yellow Brick Road."

LINDSAY CLANCY DESCRIBED A MALE VOICE ORDERING HER TO ‘KILL HER CHILDREN AND KILL HERSELF’: TESTIMONY

Walsh’s attorney, Andrea Lyon, said her client was "psychotic" and rejected any connection between her interest in the Clancy case and the alleged killing.

"She was psychotic. And this is not a first-degree murder," Lyon told reporters.

Before the killing, Walsh had become "very invested" in the Clancy murder trial, which involved the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children.

She had discussed the case in text messages with her friends as recently as the morning she allegedly killed her son.

Fox News Digital's Greg Wehner contributed to this report.

World.title: Democrat rebels defy Jeffries to hand GOP critical win just before midterms
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A pair of moderate House Democrats defied House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., on Tuesday, rescuing Republicans from an embarrassing final week before the November midterms.

Reps. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., voted with Republicans on a procedural hurdle known as a "rule vote," aimed at allowing the House to consider a slew of other bills this week.

It’s an embarrassing blow to Jeffries’ leadership; it is almost unheard of for the minority party to break ranks and help the majority pass one of their rules, even if lawmakers on that side support the underlying legislation.

LINDSEY GRAHAM'S FINAL MISSION TO PUNISH PUTIN CLEARS SENATE AFTER YEARLONG FIGHT

Golden’s spokesman told Fox News Digital that the congressman’s vote was to advance a Russia sanctions bill that would have effectively been killed had the Tuesday evening rule vote failed.

"Congressman Golden has been a consistent supporter of America’s allies in Ukraine. He didn’t want to see the Russia sanctions bill die in a rule vote after passing with overwhelming bipartisan support in the Senate," the spokesman said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Gluesenkamp Perez’s office as well.

The congresswoman posted on X, "I’m proud to represent one of the largest Ukrainian communities in America-people who have lost fathers, mothers, sons and daughters in the fight to defeat fascism. I’ll always stand with my community’s values, and am grateful for the 86 senators who voted to send this bill to the house. My vote today gets us one step closer to enacting these sanctions into law and I look forward to voting tomorrow to cut off the flow of Russian oil money fueling this war."

JEFFRIES THREATENS 'SERIOUS RESPONSE' AFTER DEMOCRATS HELP GOP ADVANCE ANTI-SOCIALISM VOTE

It’s not the first time the two voted against their own party on a rule, having done so several weeks earlier. The pair have been known to break ranks with fellow Democrats before, but their decision to do so on procedural votes incited particular fury among fellow Democrats.

It also spurred questions over whether Jeffries will be able to control his caucus if Democrats take back the House in November, and he is elected to be the next speaker.

HOUSE DEMS OVERWHELMINGLY REJECT ANTI-SOCIALISM RESOLUTION AFTER 2 MODERATES DEFY JEFFRIES

Jeffries and his top deputies said in a statement the last time the pair broke ranks on a rule, "The decision by two of our colleagues to blindside the entire House Democratic Caucus and join with the Republican majority to pass a procedural rule on the brink of failing represents a significant breach of trust. It is an action that necessitates a serious response, and we have asked the Committee on Caucus Rules to take this up in short order."

It’s not clear if any punishment ensued, however.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Golden is notably retiring from Congress at the end of this year. Gluesenkamp Perez is facing her toughest election yet against a Republican challenger in her Washington state district, which voted for President Donald Trump in 2024.

World.title: EXCLUSIVE: Haitian illegal alien gang member who went viral yelling ‘Biden forever’ during ICE arrest deported
World.content:

EXCLUSIVE: A Haitian gang member and illegal alien who defiantly told Fox News cameras "I’m not going back to Haiti" and shouted "Biden forever" during his viral U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrest has been deported to Haiti by the Trump administration after spending 19 months in federal custody.

Wisteguens Jean Quely Charles was deported on an ICE flight originating in Louisiana, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed to Fox News.

Sources told Fox News that Charles was extremely combative aboard the aircraft and made crude, profane and threatening remarks about President Donald Trump and his family during the deportation flight.

DHS CHIEF MULLIN CLASHES WITH TAPPER OVER HAITI DEPORTATIONS AFTER SUPREME COURT TPS RULING

An image obtained exclusively by Fox News shows Charles aboard the plane. The photo was provided by an ICE source and was not included among the images officially released by DHS.

The deportation completes a dramatic reversal from Charles' arrest in Massachusetts on Jan. 22, 2025, when Fox News cameras captured him insisting he would not be returned to Haiti.

"I’m not going back to Haiti … you feel me?" Charles said during the arrest. "F--- Trump," he added. "Biden forever bro."

Fox News witnessed the arrest as ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officers took Charles into custody in Massachusetts, just days after Trump returned to the White House.

EXCLUSIVE: ICE NABS MULTIPLE CONVICTED KILLERS IN SINGLE DAY AMID NATIONWIDE IMMIGRATION SWEEP

DHS identifies Charles as a member of the Back Block Money Gang and says he had accumulated 17 criminal convictions.

His criminal history included convictions for assault and battery on a public employee, resisting arrest, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, possession with intent to distribute a Class D controlled substance, possession of controlled substances, carrying a dangerous weapon, carrying ammunition without a firearm identification card and trespassing, according to DHS.

Charles remained in federal custody for approximately 19 months after his arrest as his immigration case proceeded.

A Department of Justice (DOJ) immigration judge issued Charles a final order of removal on Nov. 7, 2025, according to DHS.

ICE MAKES NATIONWIDE ARRESTS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS, MURDERERS, PEDOPHILES IN HOLIDAY BLITZ

DHS publicly announced Charles' deportation after Fox News obtained details of his removal, specifically referencing the viral video of Charles praising former President Joe Biden during his arrest.

"This illegal alien gang member from Haiti had quite the rap sheet," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement, citing Charles' convictions for assault and battery on a public employee, resisting arrest and drug trafficking.

Mullin also criticized the immigration policies of the Obama and Biden administrations and credited the Trump administration with carrying out Charles' removal.

"Once again: if you’re here illegally, we will find you, arrest you, and remove you from the United States of America," Mullin said.

HOUSE REPUBLICAN BREAKS WITH TRUMP, SAYS ENDING HAITIAN TPS RISKS US HEALTHCARE 'CRISIS'

DHS said Charles had originally received Temporary Protected Status (TPS) during the Obama administration in February 2013, and was admitted to the U.S. in July of that year, according to DHS.

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services terminated his TPS in July 2022, according to DHS.

The White House separately provided Fox News with a statement following Charles' deportation.

"This gang member and criminal illegal alien loved Obama, Biden, and open-border Democrats who let him enter our country with TPS and allowed him to terrorize American citizens," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

"Thanks to the Trump administration, he is now off our streets and back in Haiti," she continued, while contrasting Trump's immigration enforcement policies with those of Democrats.

DHS also posted a tongue-in-cheek photo of President Donald Trump at his viral McDonald's campaign trail stop waving goodbye to accompany the news.

The deportation came more than a year and a half after Charles predicted the opposite as ICE officers placed him under arrest in front of Fox News cameras.

"I’m not going back to Haiti," he said at the time.

Charles was deported by ICE to Haiti on Thursday, DHS said.

World.title: Finneas and other acts exit Ed Sheeran tour in protest of Macklemore being dropped
World.content:
Finneas and other musical artists have withdrawn as supporting acts for Ed Sheeran as of Tuesday in protest of Macklemore being dropped from the tour after the rapper says New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft organized a boycott against him.

Macklemore, whose real name is Ben Haggerty, joined Sheeran’s “Loop” tour in New Jersey earlier this month. He made remarks to the Metlife Stadium crowd that included the phrase “Free Palestine” before performing his protest anthem “Hind’s Hall.”

He announced Monday that he was no longer on the tour after Kraft called Sheeran and threatened to cancel Sheeran’s planned tour if Macklemore was still performing.

All of the opening acts listed for Sheeran’s upcoming tour dates have now announced their departures.

Finneas put out a statement saying he decided to withdraw from his upcoming tour dates with Sheeran. He wrote on Instagram that he stands “with Palestine and its people.”

“Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” Finneas wrote.

This is not the singer’s first public display of support for Palestinians amid the Israel-Hamas war. He and his younger sister, Billie Eilish, joined fellow celebrities last year to promote a benefit concert to support relief efforts called “Together for Palestine.”

Finneas’ statement came roughly an hour after one of Sheeran’s other openers, Irish singer Aaron Rowe, announced he was dropping out.

Rowe posted his statement to Instagram as well, saying in part that he could not stand by while billionaires silenced voices speaking up against “Israeli genocide” and those who highlight the “savage murder of children.”

“Ed has been a friend to me and has changed my life, I could never thank him enough for this,” Rowe wrote. “But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine, and violent occupation.”

A United Nations commission said that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza in findings from an independent inquiry published last year. Israeli government officials have denied the allegations, calling them “distorted and false.”

Beoga, Sheeran’s house band, also said the group was departing the tour. The Irish band described itself as being friends with Sheeran for over 10 years who “never saw ourselves playing in stadiums of that size and that opportunity is not lost on us.”

“It’s important that everyone knows that the real enemy is the zionist lobby,” the band’s statement said. “They have worked tirelessly to silence artists who want to speak freely about a genocide happening before our eyes, for fear of retribution.”

The band’s statement went on to criticize Kraft and express support for Macklemore and his message. It added that the real issue is that Palestinians have been killed.

Beoga’s Instagram post was captioned “Saoirse don Phailistín,” which translates from Irish to “Freedom for Palestine.”

Danish band Lukas Graham issued a statement apologizing to fans but confirming that the group was departing Sheeran’s tour. The statement called on the band’s roots as a small community in Denmark where “speaking your mind was part of everyday life.”

“Having more money didn’t make your opinion worth more than anyone else’s,” the statement said. “Money doesn’t give you the right to own the conversation.”

“We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed, about children who deserve to group up,” the band said. “Wherever they live. Whatever flag flies over them.”

Sheeran put out a statement Tuesday morning as backlash against him grew, clarifying that it was not his decision to remove Macklemore from the tour. The “Shape of You” singer said he spent a week trying to build bridges after venues began to reach out to him to say they would pull his shows if Macklemore was still a supporting act.

“I was informed that this stance was based on how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance, rather than everything that was said,” Sheeran said. “I spoke with venues at length all week to try and build a bridge. One of those people was Robert Kraft.”

But Sheeran says it was his concert promoter who held the contract with Macklemore and the promoter who chose to drop the rapper. He expressed his respect for Macklemore’s “strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes.”

Messina Touring Group, the promoter for Sheeran’s tour, told Rolling Stone Monday that it was informed that multiple venues “will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup.” The statement said cancellations would “impact hundreds of thousands of fans,” confirming that Macklemore would no longer perform on his previously scheduled dates.

The company did not respond to multiple requests for comment from NBC News regarding Macklemore’s removal from the tour.

In his own statement on Monday, Kraft did not deny Macklemore’s accusations.

He said the decision to bar the artist from Gillette Stadium was based on Macklemore’s “recent actions” on stage and “a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community.” Kraft added that the decision was not about trying to stifle Palestinian advocacy or diminishing the suffering of Palestinians.

“I would welcome the opportunity to sit down with Macklemore and discuss the facts, because ultimately our goal is the same — peace for all people, an end to suffering, and an end to all hate,” Kraft said.

World.title: Trump’s handpicked Kennedy Center board again votes to close venue, calling it ‘unsafe’
World.content:
President Donald Trump’s handpicked Kennedy Center board voted Tuesday to immediately shutter the performing arts center, citing its “dire” financial and structural shape.

The vote came shortly after a federal judge in Washington rejected the board’s latest effort to add Trump’s name to the building’s facade. A spokesperson for the center said it would appeal.

Trump said on social media after the vote that renovations wouldn’t happen unless his name was added to the building.

“The closing will take place immediately, however, the Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board’s approved name,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place.”

“In the meantime, 17 Million Dollars, raised by President Trump, has been put into The Kennedy Center account to keep it afloat,” he added. Congress appropriated $250 million for the project last year.

The board had cited a partial ceiling collapse in the center’s Grand Foyer this month as evidence that the center needed to be immediately closed for repairs.

A construction consultant and the center’s director “consider the main building to be unsafe for continued occupancy, and anticipate further risk to the public and employees if the building is not immediately closed and renovations begun,” the board said in a draft resolution to close the center for two years.

It was the third time since February that the board has voted to close the center for renovations for two years. Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, an ex officio board member, has challenged those efforts in court, saying the board hadn’t done its due diligence before it decided it needed to close the venue.

The center was initially scheduled to close July 5.

A tarp remained on the facade of the Kennedy Center on Sept. 2. Finn Gomez / Getty Images

Attorneys for the board have said the legal action has kept them from doing necessary repairs, but the judge presiding over the case noted at a hearing Tuesday — as he had previously — that his earlier order preventing full closure allowed for emergency repairs.

Trump, who was elected chairman last year by the board he appointed, joined the closed-door meeting virtually and spent several minutes criticizing both Beatty and the judge who blocked his name from being added to the facade, according to a source who dialed into the Zoom meeting and who opposes the closure.

That person described Trump as getting into a shouting match with Beatty, whom he blasted as an “obstructionist” who didn’t know how to get things done. Beatty countered that Trump was unprofessional, and at one point each accused the other of incompetence, the source said.

During the tirade, Trump also suggested without evidence that the judge, Christopher Cooper, is compromised because his wife, an attorney, represented former President Joe Biden, the source said. Trump also suggested there was something untoward about the judge’s wife’s not using her husband’s last name, the source said.

Attorneys for the center are expected to ask the judge to lift his block on closing the center this week. A source familiar with Beatty’s legal strategy said her attorneys will oppose the move and argue that the repairs can be done without shutting down the center.

In a separate resolution that was originally scheduled to be taken up Tuesday, as well, the Kennedy Center said that it “is in a dire financial position” and facing potential bankruptcy after it “exhausted its fiscal resources” — and that only Trump can rescue it.

The board had said that to do so, he would have to be recognized for his efforts on the exterior of the building.

“The Kennedy Center is in such a precarious fiscal position that it will not be able to support its payroll obligations, nor routine maintenance contracts within a matter of weeks,” said the draft resolution, which was made public in a court filing. “While actively considering alternative means of fiscal survival, President Trump has offered to step in and raise the necessary funds to keep the Center from bankruptcy during its much needed renovation.”

“With certain fiscal collapse within weeks, the board seeks to determine what recognition and acknowledgement will comply” with the judge’s earlier order banning the center from being renamed the Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

The board didn’t vote on the resolution at the meeting because members said they needed to focus on the closure issue.

The trustees had voted last month to instead add the words “renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump” to the building and to rename the center’s grounds President Donald J. Trump Plaza by Sept. 8. The new draft resolution offered numerous similar suggestions.

In a ruling issued just ahead of the board vote, Cooper, the judge, found the effort to add Trump’s name to the facade in a different way was also illegal.

“Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing. The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted,” Cooper said.

He also noted the board’s threat about fundraising — and its claim that the center might need to be razed if Trump’s repair plan isn’t followed — with skepticism.

The “government offered ‘no proof that current or future donations hinge on President Trump’s name being on the building’ and ‘no competent evidence that removing the Trump name would prevent the Center from fulfilling its artistic mission, as it has done for the last sixty years,’” he wrote.

Instead, Cooper suggested, the opposite could be true.

“The renaming of the Center coincided with declines in revenue and contributions, as artists cancelled performances, the Washington National Opera ended its 50-year residency, and ticket sales and viewership of the Kennedy Center Honors broadcast dropped precipitously. The Board also has access to the $257 million that Congress appropriated for necessary capital improvements,” he wrote, but that’s “beside the point for present purposes.”

And while cultural institutions often honor big donors by naming buildings or features after them, Cooper said, “Congress had other ideas for the Kennedy Center.”

“It limited such memorials and donor recognitions to discrete (and discreet) areas, so as not to detract from the Center’s function as an ongoing memorial to President Kennedy. The current Board’s apparent disagreement with that approach does not change the law,” he wrote.

Cooper said he could “not license a violation of those authorities under threat that some unidentified donors will withhold their largesse if the Board is not allowed to have its way. It can even less reward a decision by Board members, including the Chair, to curb the Center’s fundraising efforts because they cannot abide statutory restrictions on displaying his name.”

Beatty praised Cooper’s ruling in a statement, saying: “The law is extremely clear: The John F. Kennedy Center is named for President Kennedy — and no one else. But President Trump is holding the Kennedy Center hostage unless he can put his name on this sacred memorial.”

“This unlawfulness is as breathtaking as it is wrong, and it needs to stop,” she said.

Her attorneys, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group, said in a joint statement, “Legal sanity has once again prevailed over Trump’s vanity.”

Roma Daravi, vice president for public relations at the Kennedy Center, said in a statement, “We intend to appeal today’s Court ruling and move forward with recognizing Chairman President Trump’s historic contributions to the revitalization of America’s Cultural Center.”

World.title: Iran war driving up inflation for Americans, CBO report says
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The war with Iran is driving up inflation, and borrowing costs may increase for Americans, according to a new report released Tuesday by the Congressional Budget Office.

The report found the war was responsible for more than one-third of the increase in inflation this year, and inflation will likely continue to grow in the first quarter of next year. The CBO specifically blames the war for more than 40% of inflation during the second quarter of 2026 and an estimated half a percentage point of higher inflation during the first quarter of 2027. Interest rates are likely to rise as a result, making borrowing costlier, the report found.

Interest rates are likely to keep rising as a result, making borrowing more costly, the report found. The rate on the typical 30-year mortgage was under 6% before the war started; it was at 7.22% on Tuesday, according to Mortgage News Daily. Wall Street, likewise, expects the Federal Reserve to raise its key interest rate Wednesday in a bid to tamp down inflation.

The main driver of increased inflation is fewer oil and natural gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, the CBO report says. The average price of a gallon of gasoline in the U.S. is up 45% since the beginning of the war, hitting $4.32 as of Tuesday. Diesel, which is essential to the economy as it fuels farm equipment and other commercial vehicles, has increased 66%, to a record $6.26.

The Congressional Budget Office is a nonpartisan federal agency controlled by Congress that conducts analysis related to the federal budget and the economy.

The estimate comes a day after the Pentagon’s watchdog found the Iran war resulted in a shortfall of U.S. munitions and “bottlenecks” in supply chains.

The CBO report estimates it will be five years before the Pentagon is able to replace munitions expended during the war, which it estimates had cost roughly $38 billion as of Aug. 1. That cost estimate does not include the price tag for repairing damage Iran inflicted on “hundreds of buildings and structures at U.S. bases” in the Middle East.

The Pentagon didn’t cooperate with requests from CBO, according to the agency.

“For 47 years, American Presidents and countless other world leaders talked about the threat posed by Iran, but no one had the courage to address it,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement. “President Trump took decisive action to ensure that Iran could never harm our homeland, our troops, or our allies again. The United States Military has more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of the Commander-in-Chief’s strategic goals and beyond.”

One of the reasons the CBO says it could not estimate the cost of damage to U.S. military bases and other facilities in the region is that the Defense Department hasn’t shared “information about the value of damaged or destroyed equipment and property” with the office or what repairs the Pentagon plans to make, the funding for which could in part be picked up by the countries where the facilities are located.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., called for an end to the war in a statement, describing it as “a one-two punch that’s burning a hole in Americans’ pockets and burning a hole in our munitions supply, hurting our military readiness.”

The report estimated it would cost $13.1 billion to replace missile defense interceptors alone, and the overall cost to replace munitions expended through Aug. 1 would be $21.7 billion. It will take roughly $2 billion to $3 billion per month to maintain the war’s status quo, and more if the conflict escalates, the report found.

World.title: U.S. and China face grave AI risks, but mutual distrust stalls cooperation
World.content:
BEIJING — The United States and China are both gripped by safety fears as they reckon with their rapid advances in AI, but intensifying competition and deep mutual distrust could derail the kind of cooperation experts say is vital to head off the strategically vital technology’s greatest dangers.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly at the center of the rivalry between Washington and Beijing, and it is expected to be a major topic of discussion at a summit in Washington next week between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

The summit comes as AI leaders and researchers in the U.S. warn that companies should “slow the pace” of AI development, citing recent incidents involving autonomous agents. Trump has dismissed such concerns as a “hoax” while agreeing with executives such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that the U.S. must maintain AI dominance over China through export controls and other measures.

00:00 00:00 How exactly could AI cause widespread danger? 02:35

China, which tightly regulates AI and largely avoids the existential worries the technology provokes in the U.S., has interpreted calls to slow its development as targeted squarely at its own progress. U.S. companies say the Chinese AI sector is being driven in part by large-scale “illicit distillation” of their most advanced models.

Chinese officials, who say distillation is a conventional practice that U.S. companies also use on Chinese models, in turn accuse America’s AI executives of trying to stave off competition.

Senior Col. Zhu Qichao, a noted voice on Chinese military AI and national security, called for “cooperation” with the U.S. while warning against “vicious competition.”

“Because with the development of emerging technologies, it definitely comes with many possibilities,” said Zhu, the director of the Institute for Defense Technology and Strategic Studies at the People’s Liberation Army National University of Defense Technology.

“On one hand, it benefits humanity, but on the other hand, there are also considerations regarding risks,” he told NBC News on Tuesday at the Xiangshan Forum in Beijing.

AI and the worries around it were a major focus at the annual defense forum, where rooms were packed with scholars, military officials and commentators from the U.S. and other countries, many of which are being pressured to pick sides in the U.S.-China AI race.

Wu Xinbo, left, at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum on Tuesday. Johannes Neudecker / dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images

Though Trump and Xi agreed at their May summit in Beijing to hold high-level AI talks, no such talks have been publicly confirmed ahead of Xi’s visit next week.

Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, said China was wary that the talks could be used to further slow its progress.

“On the other hand, I think both sides need to sit down to talk about the risks posed by AI development,” he said at the forum, adding that “it will take a long way before the two sides can really forge some important consensus on this issue.”

For U.S.-China cooperation to work, the U.S. needs to be open to both sides benefiting, said Francesca Giovannini, executive director of the Harvard Belfer Center’s Initiative on Managing the Atom.

“The United States operates on a very specific type of theory. And the theory is, whoever wins the AI race wins everything,” she said in an interview at the forum. “So if this is your zero-sum game idea, you won’t be conceding anything.”

China is unlikely to agree to a slowdown at the behest of U.S. AI companies, said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at the Asia Group, an American strategic advisory firm based in Washington.

“I don’t think what happens in the U.S. really matters to China,” he said Tuesday in a phone interview from Hong Kong. “They want to do AI at their own pace, and to a very large degree a lot of people in the industry, in the government, they have a very proud sense that this is finally the chance for China.”

China, which sees its “open-weight” AI models as a tool for diplomacy, has promoted the technology as a global “public good” that should be managed by the international community. At a summit in India on Sunday, Xi offered the 11-member BRICS group of nations help developing open-source AI and urged them to join China’s global AI governance initiative.

But China is also keenly aware of the risks it faces from its own AI success, with Xi telling a Shanghai conference in July that authorities must “ensure that AI is always under human control.”

The industry must make mandatory filings and submit security assessments to officials, with many of the companies having to submit technical filings to an algorithm registry. The government has also imposed rules requiring watermarking and safety requirements.

Foremost among the risks are potential threats to China’s ruling Communist Party, which worries the technology could be weaponized against it and has imposed ideological controls to ensure products fall in line with socialist values, for example.

“Hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives misuse generative AI technologies — such as deepfake audio-video, AI-generated graphics and text, and intelligent bot farms — to manufacture political rumors, spread harmful information, and incite confrontation at low cost and on a massive scale,” Chen Yixin, the Chinese minister of state security, said in an article Sunday in the state-backed China Cybersecurity Magazine that called for greater party control and government oversight of AI.

Anthropic said last week that Chinese AI labs had secretly routed requests to its Claude models. Don Feria / AP Content Services for Anthropic

Chen said AI could enable misinformation campaigns and cyberattacks on China’s critical infrastructure and, in an apparent reference to the U.S., warned that countries with “advantages” in AI could restrict other nations’ access to their technologies.

He also warned of espionage and data leaks, days after Anthropic released a report that found Chinese AI labs had secretly routed requests to its Claude models, some of which contained sensitive information from individuals, major companies and state-affiliated actors.

Like the U.S., China increasingly views AI as a national security issue, down to the individual researchers working on it. On Tuesday, China tightened travel curbs on its citizens, barring some whose work has implications for national technology security from leaving the country.

The new rules add to an extensive AI regulatory regime that includes restrictions on AI companions over mental health concerns, mandated labeling of AI-generated content and a requirement that trained models must use data conforming to Chinese values.

Experts say it could take a major crisis for the U.S. and China to finally work together on AI, much like the 1962 Cuban missile crisis pushed the U.S. and the then-Soviet Union to start negotiating on nuclear weapons.

AI is expected to be a major topic of discussion at the U.S.-China summit in Washington next week. Alex Wong / Getty Images

AI has already had profound military implications, including for targeting, and could be integrated into systems supporting the nuclear chain of command, said David Finkelstein, vice president of the Center for Naval Analyses.

“This is scary stuff, and I think that this is an area where the two sides ought to be sitting down and talking to each other,” he said at the forum.

U.S.-China competition is inevitable, but there is still room for the two sides to negotiate because their respective positions “are not necessarily very much entrenched,” said David Santoro, president and chief executive of Pacific Forum International, a Honolulu-based think tank.

“There are still ways that we can better understand each other and hopefully come up with mechanisms so we can better control this emerging technology,” he said in an interview at the forum.

Santoro said he was “not very optimistic,” however, about the prospect for a major agreement in the near term.

“I don’t know that we will be able to get to a position where we agree on something substantive,” he said. “But at least the first step has got to be talking to each other.”

Eric Baculinao and Erin Tan reported from Beijing and Mithil Aggarwal from Hong Kong.

World.title: Kash Patel defends FBI’s new policy on bestiality at Senate hearing
World.content:
FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday found himself defending a new policy at the bureau that does not immediately disqualify potential hires who have engaged in bestiality.

At a Senate Judiciary Committee oversight hearing, some senators grilled Patel about the new standards, which he said were established so as not to discriminate against potential victims of sex trafficking who were forced to perform acts of bestiality.

His explanation elicited curious responses, one from Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., who asked Patel why he would “even get into bestiality.”

Patel quickly emphasized that “we’re not into bestiality,” to which Kennedy said, “I know you’re not,” prompting a chuckle from Patel, who said he was trying to explain the policy.

Kennedy asked, “If Joe participated in bestiality, not as animal but as the human, don’t you think he ought to be disqualified?”

“If he voluntarily did it, sure. But if he was trafficked into it ...,” Patel responded.

Kennedy went on to ask how a person would “involuntarily do it.” Patel said human traffickers forced people into types of conduct like bestiality and “degrading acts of all kinds” in “a lot of cases.”

He said people at the bureau who suggested the policy change “explained to me and showed me cases in which people were forced into it and had applied to the FBI, and so I thought they should be considered. It’s not an automatic disqualification.”

Patel said that the previous policy addressed prostitution, trafficking and bestiality and that for bestiality, the rules “automatically disqualified any individual who participated on either side of it.”

“Either side of what? The bestiality?” Kennedy asked. “So you disqualified the animal?”

“Well, I don’t think — we have great canines, but we’re not going to disqualify them,” Patel said.

Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., also inquired about the policy change, asking Patel whether he believed applicants who had engaged in bestiality were qualified candidates whom the FBI was losing.

“Applicants who have engaged in bestiality means they were victims of bestiality because they were forced to do so. And at this FBI, we are not going to criminalize and prevent victims from serving the United States of America and the premier law enforcement agency in the world,” Patel responded, adding he had “eliminated the bureaucracy that prevented these great Americans from serving, or at least being considered to serve.”

The oftentimes tense hearing included Democrats’ pressing Patel on broader topics about his leadership at the bureau and grilling him about his suit against a reporter for The Atlantic and firings and departures at the FBI since he took over.

While Patel was mostly praised by Republicans in the room, he drew heat from Kennedy over the change in hiring practices.

“You’re not telling us today that if a human being had sex with an animal that they can still be an FBI agent, are you?” Kennedy asked. “They can’t be, can they?”

“They cannot,” Patel responded.

“In fact, they ought to be in jail, right?” Kennedy said.

“They all are,” Patel said.

World.title: Delaware holds U.S. Senate primary and more races to watch today
World.content:
Delaware voters headed to the polls on Tuesday to choose their nominees for U.S. Senate, House and a number of local races — the last primary contests of the 2026 midterm election cycle.

Delaware state law dictates that state and local primaries be held the second Tuesday after the first Monday in September in general election years, pushing the primary back into the third week of September this year.

Here are the major races to watch:

U.S. Senate

Democratic Sen. Chris Coons, who was first elected to the seat in 2010 to fill an opening when Joe Biden became vice president, is expected to sail to victory on Tuesday. He faces three nominal primary challengers, including former business executive Eric Hansen, who will appear on the ballot as "E. No-Trump Hansen."

Coons has raised more than $6.8 million for his reelection bid, compared to $150,000 for his closest primary challenger. The other two, including Hansen, have not reported any fundraising.

Two Republicans are vying for the chance to take him on, although Delaware is a solidly blue state and Coons is expected to win easily in November. A Republican has not won a Delaware Senate seat since 1966, when the state elected J. Caleb Boggs to the upper chamber. Boggs was defeated six years later by a 29-year-old Biden, making him one of the youngest people ever elected to the Senate — nearly a half-century before Biden became one of the oldest people to serve as president.

U.S. House

Delaware's lone U.S. House member, incumbent Rep. Sarah McBride, is running for reelection and does not face any primary challengers. Democrats have held the seat since 2010.

McBride, the first transgender member of Congress, has become a lightning rod in Congress among Republicans in her first term. In November 2024, ahead of her arrival in Congress, House Speaker Mike Johnson announced that all House members would have to use the restroom corresponding to their biological sex. GOP Rep. Nancy Mace, who introduced the ban, said it was aimed at McBride.

McBride issued a statement at the time saying it was intended to "distract from the real issues facing this country," but she said she would comply with the rules.

McBride told The New York Times last year that there have been "folks who are coming after me" in Congress, saying they "were trying to bait me into a fight to get attention, and I refused to be used as a political pawn."

There are three Republicans running to take on McBride in November, including an opponent from her 2024 Democratic primary who has switched parties, Earl Cooper, and her opponent in the 2024 general election, John Whalen III.

World.title: Family blames Texas' "merciless" abortion ban for woman's death, sues Paxton, others
World.content:
The family of Tierra Walker, who died of preeclampsia at the age of 37 when she was 20 weeks pregnant, has filed a lawsuit in Texas, saying she was denied an abortion that could have saved her life as her health quickly deteriorated.

Lawyers for Walker's family filed the lawsuit Tuesday in Bexar County District Court accusing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, several of her doctors and others of "deliberate indifference, discrimination, and medical mistreatment [that] ultimately caused her horrific and tragic death" in 2024. Preeclampsia is a severe high blood pressure condition in pregnancy that can be fatal.

Walker's family alleges Paxton — a Republican who is currently running for Senate — and another defendant, Stephen Brint Carlton, executive director of the Texas Medical Board, stripped her of her right to life by imposing "a merciless blanket prohibition" on abortion, while the doctors allegedly failed to offer life-saving medical treatment.

Paxton has been outspoken in his defense of Texas' near-total abortion ban. He has filed lawsuits against doctors and organizations who ship abortion pills to Texas from out of state. His office did not respond to CBS News' request for comment.

"At every turn, Texas's political and medical establishments not only failed but actively harmed Ms. Walker," the lawsuit alleges.

"Tierra Walker is dead because not one of her … healthcare providers would give her the one medical procedure that would have saved her life," Michelle Maloney, an attorney representing the family, told CBS News. They refused, she said, because of "the immense culture of fear" around abortion in the state of Texas.

ProPublica was first to report on the circumstances of Walker's death.

Tierra Walker. Family photo

CBS News has reached out to all the parties involved in the lawsuit. University Health said in a statement that it could not comment on individual patients or litigation, but said, "Our priority is to provide medically appropriate and timely care, while safeguarding patient privacy and complying with all applicable laws and regulations."

Walker learned she was nearly eight weeks pregnant on Sept. 19, 2024, during an emergency room visit.

She had been working to get her health back on track after struggling with chronic health problems for years, including obesity, high blood pressure, asthma and Type 2 diabetes. Three years earlier, she had developed preeclampsia while pregnant with twins, which led to the stillbirth of her twins and "sent her into a health spiral," the lawsuit says.

By mid-2024, her health was improving — her blood pressure was lower and she was losing weight with the help of a GLP-1 drug.

An emergency room doctor noted in Walker's medical records it was "too early in pregnancy to have eclampsia" and she was sent home after her blood pressure medications were adjusted to account for her pregnancy.

She returned to the hospital hours later as she continued to have seizures, nausea, vomiting and complained of pain. Her medical records noted that her seizures may have been triggered by several factors, including pregnancy-related nausea, anxiety and stress.

She was hospitalized for most of October, where medical records show she received extensive testing for her seizures, which doctors noted were non-epileptic "functional seizures," unrelated to her pregnancy or preeclampsia.

Her records show she was surrounded by family members for nearly the entirety of her hospital stay, and that she was repeatedly offered mental health and psychiatric treatments for anxiety.

"They really treated her so bad because they thought she was crazy," her aunt LaTanya Walker told CBS News. "One day they told me to tell her husband, 'Can you go tell him that this is all in her head?'"

During the lengthy hospital stay in October, according to the lawsuit, Walker and her family told medical staff "that the pregnancy was going to cost Ms. Walker her life, and asked if she could terminate the pregnancy."

According to Maloney, Tierra Walker first asked for an abortion at another hospital on Oct. 12, and then asked at University Health on Oct. 30, when she would have been about 11 weeks pregnant.

"Despite the clear risk to her life in continuing the pregnancy, none of University Health's staff counseled Ms. Walker on the possibility of abortion as a life-saving medical treatment, offered her this treatment, or suggested that she leave the state. Instead, hospital staff kept insisting 'nothing is wrong with the baby' and continued to refuse the care that she needed on that basis," the lawsuit alleges.

In late October and early November, two doctors documented in Walker's medical records that she was at "high" risk of death.

Still, she was discharged from the hospital, only to be readmitted days later.

"I asked them time and time again to give her an abortion. And they would tell me … 'It's her, but it's not the baby,'" LaTanya Walker said.

The lawsuit claims hospital staff responded to her requests for an abortion by saying, "Your baby is fine," while allegedly "disregarding Ms. Walker's deteriorating health."

In a statement to CBS News, the Texas Medical Board said that under its current rules, "when addressing a condition that is or may become emergent, a physician is not required to wait until a mother's life is in immediate danger or her major bodily function is at immediate risk before providing necessary medical care" and noted that in some circumstances, that care "may include the termination of a pregnancy."

LaTanya Walker said her niece wanted to have the baby but was also thinking about her then 14-year-old son, JJ.

"She had to be here for JJ," LaTanya Walker said, recalling a conversation she had with her niece in the hospital.

Tierra Walker with her husband, Eric. Family photo

LaTanya Walker said she recalls her niece using the word "abortion" when asking doctors to terminate her pregnancy. But in the 6,500 pages of medical records reviewed by CBS News, doctors did not document any instance of Walker asking for an abortion, nor did doctors offer her one.

"They're going to hide whatever they need to hide," LaTanya Walker claimed.

Molly Duane, another attorney representing the Walker family, told CBS News that medical providers in Texas are "scared to even write the word in the medical chart."

"We have reviewed dozens of cases," Duane said. "And what is clear is that doctors are so scared to even write the word in their medical chart that it does not appear there."

Maloney said that in depositions with doctors involved in other cases, they have described conversations they've had with her clients about abortion that they do not document "because of repercussions from the state."

LaTanya Walker said she and her niece did not discuss traveling to another state for the procedure, but considered ordering abortion medication online. Her niece was open to the idea, but LaTanya Walker said she got cold feet about ordering it for her niece in case there were complications.

"Then that would have been something on me," she said.

Texas' state law banning nearly all abortions went into effect in 2022, shortly after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. The law had an exception if a pregnancy threatened the life of the mother. Anyone found guilty of providing an abortion faced up to 99 years in prison, fines and the loss of their medical license.

In 2025, Texas enacted legislation that sought to clarify the medical exemptions to the near-total ban after a ProPublica investigation found that several pregnant women in the state died after delays in their care. The changes included clarifying legal medical emergency exceptions, and enhanced legal protections for medical professionals who provide abortions as life-saving care.

A spokesperson for Bexar County District Attorney Joe Gonzales, who is named as a defendant in the lawsuit, told CBS News that Gonzales has not prosecuted any abortion cases, and his office "will carefully review all cases filed by law enforcement agencies and make informed charging decisions, as we are committed to ensuring that our assessments are grounded in fairness and justice."

Walker returned to the emergency room for the final time on Dec. 27, when medical records show that she was diagnosed with preeclampsia. Despite potentially fatal complications, her attorneys say she was never offered an abortion, and she was discharged by doctors later that night.

The lawsuit pointed out that her discharge paperwork from Dec. 27 states that delivery, meaning an abortion at that stage, may be the best treatment for preeclampsia.

"Medical guidelines say she should've been admitted, stabilized and given medicine to prevent seizures," explained Dr. Céline Gounder, CBS News medical correspondent and the editor-at-large for public health at KFF Health News. Under those guidelines, Gounder said, "her pregnancy should have been terminated since her baby was likely too young to survive. Instead, she was sent home."

Days later, Walker's teenage son found her unresponsive in her bed. It was his 15th birthday.

An autopsy found Walker died of hypertensive cardiovascular disease and preeclampsia. She also had an enlarged heart, as well as severe buildup of fluid in her lungs and kidney damage. The medical examiner found the fetus had normal development for 20 weeks' gestation, weighing less than a pound.

"For months, Ms. Walker had been asking for termination of her pregnancy — even though this was a wanted pregnancy — because she did not think she would survive the pregnancy. Tragically, she was right. An abortion at any point during her pregnancy would have saved her life," the lawsuit alleges.

Maloney and Duane denied that the timing of the lawsuit was political. Paxton is running in Texas' highly competitive Senate race as Republicans hope to retain control of the majority. The Walker family attorneys said the two-year statute of limitations is set to expire in the coming days.

"What he's doing in his office is using and abusing his role as attorney general to stoke a culture of fear," Duane said. "Our civil rights laws say that individual officials can be held liable in their personal capacity when their activity leads to the death of one of their citizens, and that's what happened here."

Asked about her message to Paxton, LaTanya Walker gave a pointed response.

"Honestly," she said, "go to hell."

World.title: FBI investigation thwarts "mass casualty attack" from man accused of ISIS allegiance
World.content:
A Pennsylvania man planned to carry out an ISIS-inspired "mass casualty attack" before an FBI investigation thwarted him, according to federal law enforcement officials.

Speaking at a press conference Tuesday, federal officials said Jonathan Kramer, 21, of Valencia, had pledged allegiance to the Islamic State of Syria. He was arrested Saturday outside of a hotel in Cranberry Township, around 25 miles north of Pittsburgh, with a rifle, ammunition and dozens of knives in his possession.

Suspect shared "radical ideology"

Richard Evanchec, special agent in charge for the FBI's Pittsburgh field office, called the planned attack an "imminent threat of violence inspired by ISIS."

"Let me be clear about this threat: Jonathan Kramer demonstrated a sustained devotion to the Islamic State of Syria," Evanchec said. "He recorded a pledge of allegiance to the same. Following that pledge, he made efforts to spread their propaganda and shared ways to kill all in the name of a foreign terrorist organization."

United States Attorney Troy Rivetti said it became clear that Kramer, a 2023 Mars Area High School graduate, was moving forward "with his radical ideology." But officials didn't elaborate on any specifics surrounding the alleged planned attack, including when or where it might have occurred.

Timeline of arrest

On the morning of Sept. 12, federal agents said they watched Kramer leave his home, carrying a backpack. He got into an Uber and went to a Walmart in Gibsonia. In the parking lot, they say he met another person and took something from the trunk — a long black bag that agents say could hold a rifle.

He then took an Uber to a hotel in Cranberry Township, where they said Kramer paid $450 in cash for a week. He then went to Dunham's Sports, where agents said they watched him at the firearms counter.

When he returned to the hotel, the FBI moved in and arrested him.

A photo shared with KDKA shows Jonathan Kramer at the hotel in Cranberry where he was arrested. (Photo: KDKA)

Investigators said a search of Kramer's hotel room and home led to the discovery of a semi-automatic rifle, loaded rifle magazines, a rifle scope and boxes of ammunition, along with 30 knives and a note. The note told people not to look for him, saying "I cant live In constant Fear," according to court paperwork. The FBI said he had roughly 190 rounds of ammunition.

The FBI said it also found social media correspondence that led investigators to believe an attack was being planned.

"This defendant made repeated attempts to encourage and coordinate violence through encrypted platforms such as advising others on attack methods, discussing chemical poisons, vehicle attacks, drone delivery explosives and firearms-based assaults," Evanchec said.

Authorities thank public for help

Rivetti referred to the FBI investigation that led to Kramer's arrest as being "covert."

"We want to thank the individual who first reported this defendant's dangerous and troubling behavior, as well as the other individuals who agreed to speak to law enforcement this weekend," Rivetti said.

Rivetti said that the cooperation of the public in investigations is key for law enforcement to be able to "prevent horrific crimes from being committed in our community."

"We hope this prosecution serves as a stark reminder to everyone of the importance of vigilance," Rivetti said.

Federal charges have been filed against a Pittsburgh-area man accused of plotting an attack in support of ISIS. KDKA Photojournalist Fred Williams

U.S. Congressman Mike Kelly (R-PA), whose district includes Butler County, said in a statement that he commends the diligent work of the FBI and law enforcement for apprehending Kramer before he could potentially follow through with an alleged attack.

"This disgusting, hate-filled extremism has no place in our nation," Rep. Kelly said.

Kramer has been charged with one count of receipt or transfer of a firearm or ammunition knowing or having reasonable cause to believe such firearm or ammunition will be used to commit a felony or a federal crime of terrorism.

Officials said that Kramer waived his right to a detention hearing, but requested a preliminary examination hearing that is scheduled for Wednesday.
