World.title: AI data centre provider could become one of Australia's biggest stock floats
World.content:
AI data centre developer Firmus Technologies is courting investors in Asia and Australia ahead of a widely expected multi-billion-dollar share market float next month.

The company has been making headlines over its expansions and resulting community concerns, as well as through its partnerships.

Last week Firmus announced it had signed a multi-year deal with OpenAI for two new AI factory sites in Malaysia.

Firmus' AI factory in Singapore, which uses the company's technology to submerge its data clusters. (Supplied: Firmus)

At the same time, the company has been growing its presence in northern Tasmania with three data centre projects and a flurry of sports sponsorships, including with the Tasmania Devils AFL team.

One AI data centre is currently under construction in Launceston, where its parent company is headquartered, and another near George Town has council approval while a site at Wesley Vale is still awaiting approval.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff is shown around Firmus's Launceston facility by Mr Rosenfield and Mr Curtis. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Plans are also underway for projects in Melbourne, Sydney, Perth and Canberra.

Firmus already has significant operations in Singapore, and over the next 24 months, it says it hopes to have seven AI data centres across four countries.

Data centre company's deal with AFL team defended by club boss The Tasmania Devils AFL club has signed a six-year sponsorship deal with a data centre builder. The AI company and club say it's a natural pairing — but not all are convinced.

This narrative of aggressive expansion will stoke interest in its expected float on the Australian share market next month.

Reports suggest Firmus intends to raise up to $7 billion from institutional and retail investors in an initial public offering (IPO), which could value the company at more than $50 billion, depending on what proportion of the company is sold.

If that pans out, it could make Firmus the second-largest float in Australian history, after the federal government raised $14 billion by selling a third of Telstra three decades ago, valuing the entire company at $42 billion.

Tim Rosenfield (left) and Oliver Curtis have sought to allay public concerns about the amount of energy and water the data centres would require. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Based on its share price yesterday, Telstra had a market value of $53 billion.

An important caveat for many of the figures being touted in the financial press for Firmus's float are that they are based on conjecture and hype.

The company's public offer document, the prospectus that potential investors will review, has yet to be lodged with the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX).

Firmus Technologies has plans for data centres across Tasmania. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

The valuation reports are based partly on an invitation for a "roadshow" in Asian and Australian capitals sent out to potential investors by investment banks handling the float for Firmus.

The roadshow will help determine how much demand there is for stock, based on forecast earnings.

A spokesperson for Firmus declined to comment on the likely size of the capital raising, or how much of the company might be sold, which will depend on the demand.

'Mum and dad investors' also likely for IPO, expert says

Sam Baker, private wealth adviser at Shadforth Financial Group, told the ABC it was widely known Firmus had been looking to debut this year on the ASX.

"It now appears as if the company is fronting investors both in Asia, and soon to be Australia, as a preamble to looking to do an initial public offering of up to $7 billion," Mr Baker said.

"They're telling the story of the business, providing details, which will largely be provided in any prospectus for the initial public offering.

" But it's about sort of gauging interest as to what or whether investors would be interested and at what price they would be potentially prepared to pay for any shares in an initial public offering. "

The data centre under construction at St Leonards, Launceston. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Mr Baker said investors in Australia and overseas would likely be interested.

"In an initial public offering, they tend to have cornerstone or institutional investors, but I would expect a raising of this size will also be looking to attract retail, or mum and dad, investors," he said.

Mr Baker said while IPOs could be used for the founders to "cash out," it seemed Firmus was raising funds to support the rollout of its AI data centres across Australia and South-East Asia.

From Bitcoin to AI

Firmus's most advanced project is at St Leonards in Launceston, and it has approval for another at Long Reach in the Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone.

The company is seeking approval for another at Wesley Vale in Tasmania's north-west.

A visualisation of the Firmus's AI data centre planned near George Town, in northern Tasmania. (Supplied)

Firmus has struggled to gain a social licence in Tasmania, but Mr Baker did not believe that would necessarily impact the IPO.

"Broader institutional investors are mainly focused on getting a return," he said.

" Whether or not there is some resistance across the retail shareholders, that will remain to be seen. "

Firmus began as a bitcoin miner in 2019, subsequently pivoting to data centre development.

Its co-CEO Oliver Curtis was sentenced to two years' jail in 2016 for conspiring to commit insider trading.

The trial heard how he shared in $1.4 million of illegal profits from insider trading using confidential information between May 2007 and June 2008.

Firmus co-CEO Oliver Curtis with his wife Roxy Jacenko. (Instagram: Roxyjacenko)

In October 2025, Mr Curtis was asked about his reflections on the ordeal and whether Tasmanians could trust Firmus.

"The experience of the past presents an opportunity for the future," he told ABC Radio Hobart at the time.

"It's all about resilience, it's all about how you get back on the horse, and it's all about basically making sure that you are completing what you believe you need to complete.

"For me, this is about more than an individual; this is about a company.

"I'm so fortunate we have a hugely amazing, talented team around us — and that's the story."

World.title: Epstein, FBI firings and bestiality: Key moments from Kash Patel's Senate grilling
World.content:
FBI Director Kash Patel has been grilled by the US Senate for nearly five hours over his controversial management of the agency, including the ousting of experienced agents.

Mr Patel's time at the FBI has been marred by his firing of veteran employees with little explanation.

Appearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee, Mr Patel defended his tenure, saying the US murder rate had fallen to a 20-year low, according to FBI data.

Here are the main takeaways.

Patel defends Epstein files rollout

Mr Patel defended FBI investigators who worked on the Epstein files release, as part of the Congress-backed Epstein Files Transparency Act.

Survivors of the notorious sex offender said the FBI failed to investigate Jeffrey Epstein in 1996 when the agency was notified of the first allegations.

More than 30 of Epstein's victims have now brought forward a lawsuit against the FBI, despite attempts by the Trump administration to dismiss the case.

With a unanimous Maxwell vote, the US Senate issues a warning to Trump The bipartisan vote is non-binding, but it reveals the sentiment surrounding Jeffrey Epstein within Donald Trump's own party. Here's how.

They've also criticised the administration for publishing unredacted personal information in the released files.

Mr Patel told the hearing that the FBI had complied with the Transparency Act and "produced three and a half million pages of documents for the first time ever".

"We've also repeatedly stated if there's new information, we want everyone to come forward so that we can analyse that information as to what is and isn't remaining," he said.

Probe into bestiality hiring change

One of the stranger moments was when Mr Patel confirmed the FBI had quietly lifted restrictions on hiring applicants who were victims of bestiality in their childhood

Similar changes were also made to those who had previously participated in prostitution.

Mr Patel denied the changes reflected a lowering of employment standards and insisted these were designed to prevent victims who had been forced to engage in that conduct from being automatically disqualified.

"We did not want to punish victims of bestiality, victims who were trafficked," he said.

"We did not want to make it an automatic disqualification for the FBI to consider you if you were a victim of these awful, heinous acts."

Loading...

The questioning spanned partisan lines, with Republican Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana grilling Mr Patel about the rationale for a change the FBI director said subordinates proposed to him.

"When you saw bestiality, I say this with respect: The person who recommended it, why didn't you just say what planet did you parachute in from?" Senator Kennedy asked.

Mr Patel later added that previous regulations disqualified "any individual who participated on either side of it".

"Either side of what, the bestiality?" Senator Kennedy probed further. "So you disqualified the animal?"

"We have great canines, but we're not going to disqualify them," Mr Patel said, laughing.

Patel rallies against 'weaponised FBI', amid reported firings

The main reason for the hearing was reports that Mr Patel had been gutting the ranks of longstanding FBI staff.

Connecticut Democrat Richard Blumenthal pressed Mr Patel, noting the agents had participated in an FBI investigation into Mr Trump's retention of classified documents at Mar-a-Lago.

Mr Patel was probed on his personal expenses. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

"Do you think firing the president's political opponents is more important than retaining the decades of experience and expertise monitoring intelligence threats from Iran?" Mr Blumenthal asked.

"I think what's most important is not to have a weaponised FBI, and I will endeavour every single day to make sure we have no one there who is doing that," Mr Patel said.

He later suggested that the scope of firings had been overblown, saying many agents had retired.

Mr Patel also later refused to pledge the FBI wouldn't interfere in mid-term elections.

"I pledge unequivocally that I will not participate in your charade of lies," he added.

Heated questioning over Olympics partying, magazine lawsuit

Mr Patel was probed on his personal expenses, including partying with the US hockey team as they celebrated their Winter Olympics win in Italy.

Trump seems to mock US women's hockey team while congratulating men on gold After the US men's hockey team won gold at the Olympics, Trump's locker-room joke about the women's team sparks backlash online.

"What you'll never understand is the players, who are my friends, invited me to the locker room," the FBI director said.

"What you'll never understand is that during that trip, where 300,000 Americans went to Italy to participate in the games and watch them, not a single security incident occurred."

Mr Patel also defended his decision to file a defamation lawsuit against The Atlantic after it printed a story alleging he has a drinking problem that has interfered with his ability to do his job.

"As a personal private citizen, I am allowed to participate in my own defence, especially when there's a smear campaign," he alleged, before becoming heated.

"Everyone sees you for the complete and total fraud you are," Mr Patel told Senator Peter Welch, who asked whether FBI resources had been used to investigate The Atlantic journalist.

World.title: Historic outback pub hits the market as restoration costs soar
World.content:
A heritage-listed hotel in Western Australia's Goldfields, infamous for its connection to the murders of two police officers a century ago, has hit the market, with an asking price of more than $1 million.

It is the second time the Cornwall Hotel in Boulder has been listed for sale in the past decade, in a sign that the overheated construction market and onerous heritage obligations could be turning off potential buyers.

The two-storey hotel was built in 1898, just five years after the discovery of gold at Kalgoorlie.

It takes its name from the 19th-Century Cornish miners who flooded into WA during the gold rush and built the pub from locally quarried stone.

The Cornwall Hotel received $992,090 from the WA government's $5 million Goldfields Earthquake Restoration Fund, but structural repairs did not begin until 2016. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Real estate agent James Brennan described the nine-bedroom hotel as a unique piece of Goldfields history, but concedes the interior of the building "needs a lot of love".

He said a mining company in need of workers' accommodation could be a potential buyer as the city faced ongoing accommodation shortages.

"A property like this, it needs the right owner, someone who can bring it back to its former glory," he said.

"It really is hard to put a price on that history, and obviously it's a beautiful building … heritage does scare people at times, but there's definitely been a lot of interest."

The Cornwall Hotel in Boulder circa 1926. (Supplied: Eastern Goldfields Historical Society)

Pub's famous link to murders

The Cornwall Hotel's most famous former licensee was Evan Clarke, who turned King's evidence following the brutal murders of detectives Inspector John Walsh and Sergeant Alexander Pitman, who were after gold thieves, in 1926.

It was rumoured that following the murders, the bodies were taken to the hotel where they were dismembered before being set alight and thrown down disused mineshafts.

Detective Inspector John Walsh (left) and Detective Sergeant Alexander Pitman were on the trail of gold thieves when they were murdered. (Facebook: WA Police Historical Society)

It was purchased in 1927 by the family of Jack Osmetti, a well-known local sportsman who ran the pub for around 50 years.

The hotel was badly damaged by fire during Kalgoorlie's 1934 race riots and again by a magnitude-5 earthquake in 2010, but has been extensively repaired.

Negotiations with insurers resulted in the building being propped up and fenced off for four years, until matters were finally settled in 2014.

The owners then applied and were granted $992,090 from the state government's $5 million Goldfields Earthquake Restoration Fund, but structural repairs did not begin until 2016.

Stonemason's old watering hole

In the era when the Cornwall Hotel was built, stonemasons constructed enduring public and commercial buildings by combining cheap, highly skilled manual labour with traditional lime mortars and hand-dressed masonry.

Today, retired Kalgoorlie stonemason Ken Ball reckoned his occupation of 55 years was a "dying trade" and the demise of historic buildings was a sign of the times.

Ken Ball (left) and Eastern Goldfields Historical Society member Arthur Ward with a photograph of the Cornwall Hotel after the 1934 race riots. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"I've got a lot of good memories here," he said, standing outside the Cornwall Hotel.

"I did a lot of work at the old Boulder cemetery, so I would often stop in for a drink on the way home … obviously not since the earthquake, though.

"It's a shame to see beautiful old buildings like this wasting away, and you'd love to see them get a new lease on life, but finding tradesmen is hard enough, let alone heritage-qualified tradesmen."

Heritage projects 'astronomically harder'

The City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder offers grants of up to $50,000 to private owners of heritage-listed buildings, but there has been little uptake in recent years.

While WA's shortage of skilled tradies is well documented, Kalgoorlie builder Tim Matthew said heritage projects were "astronomically harder" and typically required the use of a specialised heritage architect.

"Even if you had an infinite budget, most builders I know don't have the time to spend weeks and weeks researching the heritage requirements," he said.

"And honestly, some of these grants don't scratch the surface to do anything meaningful."

Tim Matthew outside the heritage-listed Lord Forrest site, which reopened as a public park in 2017. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Mr Matthew said a recent heritage project he consulted on was an historic WA pub seeking a roof replacement, which would involve replacing karri timber used for structural beams in the roof.

But karri timber has become much more expensive and harder to source since the WA government banned commercial native forest logging.

"Heritage projects are typically 100 per cent like-for-like replacement … if you use the wrong bolt that's a problem," he said.

An aerial view of the Kalgoorlie CBD. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Heritage must find relevancy

Eastern Goldfields Historical Society life member Scott Wilson said it was important heritage buildings in Kalgoorlie-Boulder were preserved for future generations, but they needed to remain functional as well.

"We would support anyone going down the road of heritage grants because it is an arduous process," he said.

"Whether that is a mining company renovating it for workforce accommodation, or someone turning it back into a pub, it needs to stay relevant."

That relevancy could come down to simple dollars and cents and what is possible in the current market.

A spokesperson for Heritage Minister Simone McGurk said more than $27 million had been awarded to nearly 930 projects since 1997, and a "high number" of development applications continued to be received.

World.title: Fishers fund independent review in last-ditch effort to overturn gillnet ban
World.content:
Commercial fishers in North Queensland are hoping a new report will convince the state and federal governments to reverse a planned ban on gillnets within the Great Barrier Reef.

Operators in the fishing zone have commissioned a report they say shows their netting practices are likely to pass international sustainability standards.

Temporary licences were introduced in 2024 to allow commercial fishers to continue using gillnets ahead of the planned phase-out in 2027.

The Queensland Seafood Industry Association, working with the operators, would not release the full report to the ABC, saying it was "commercial in confidence".

It did, however, release a summary of findings, which the ABC verified as being accurate by the report's authors, sustainable seafood consultants FishListic.

Townsville commercial fisher Nathan Rynn says results from the report are promising. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

Fisher Nathan Rynn said the association hoped to use the report to obtain a Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) "blue tick" on their boats and products to show the fishery was sustainable.

"I'm sort of positive about the net fishery moving forward, albeit the legislation issues," Mr Rynn said.

"I think we can overcome that and have the best-managed fishery on the planet … but we'll actually have the accreditation behind it, possibly."

Reef impact under review

According to the released section of the report, FishListic said it found the fishery would meet half of the MSC's standards without any conditions imposed and could pass others after further consultation.

The company reviewed the ecological risk of four threatened species that had interactions with the large mesh nets.

Great hammerhead sharks, scalloped hammerhead sharks, green sawfish and hawksbill turtles all returned a medium risk of being impacted by the nets, down from high risk under the current Queensland government assessment.

Several dolphin, marine turtle, and shark species listed as high risk under the 2021 study were not analysed in the FishListic report.

The company did not conduct site inspections but used public data, along with camera footage and data logs provided by fishers, to assess the MSC criteria.

Blue tick for consumers

The Queensland Seafood Industry Association's David Bobberman said the east coast inshore fishery produced between 200 and 300 tonnes of seafood annually.

Mr Bobberman said consultation and further research projects would likely be required before the fishery could receive a blue tick and "certified sustainable seafood" labelling.

"To be clear, it's not MSC-certified at the moment, but it's been pre-assessed, and the pre-assessor has given them a pass mark," he said.

Gillnets are anchored to the ocean floor and held vertically in the water. (Flickr: Virginia Sea Grant)

The MSC uses third-party auditors to conduct in-person reviews of fishing practices against international standards, following a pre-assessment.

Criteria include the sustainability of fish stocks, protection of marine species and habitat, and management strategy.

Mr Bobberman said the fishery impact had been greatly reduced since 2024 with fewer operators, and gillnetters now trained under a sustainable fishing program.

"We've gone from over 200 available licences to gillnet within the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park to 25," he said.

Mr Bobberman said he did not consider any alternative gear as viable replacements, with line fishing too limited, and tunnel nets "too selective" in when and where they could be used.

Wild barramundi and king threadfin salmon are target species for gillnet operators. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Minister investigating options

The office of Queensland Minister for Primary Industries Tony Perrett said in a statement it would "welcome" the opportunity to conduct a "robust review" of the report, but it was waiting to receive the full document.

It said Mr Perrett was investigating options available to Queensland that would comply with federal government bans.

However, the Federal Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water said the phase-out of gillnets was being led by the Queensland government.

Fishers 'making a real effort'

Leslie Roberson, a researcher at the University of Queensland, said governments should be taking notice of MSC certifications.

"I think it does mean something to consumers. To the government, I think it should mean something," Dr Roberson said.

"The fishery has paid for an independent assessment of themselves so, obviously, people are going to have questions of whether that's biased.

"[So,] they've taken steps to get that reviewed [by MSC auditors]. They are making a real effort."

Leslie Roberson has worked with other fisheries hoping to obtain MSC certification. (Supplied: Leslie Roberson)

Dr Roberson said gillnetting had a bad reputation partly stemming from a lack of data.

She said information about protected species interactions was previously filled out by fishers without a "third party" to check them.

East coast inshore fishery operators have been required to use onboard cameras and log interactions with threatened species since February 2024.

Queensland government data shows 188 fatal interactions with endangered scalloped hammerhead sharks and seven narrow sawfish deaths in that time.

No other threatened species deaths were reported.

World.title: Citizen scientists maintain dolphin watch amid bird flu threat
World.content:
As a boat full of tourists sets off to see dolphins in Victor Harbor early on Saturday morning, they are joined on board by a group of citizen scientists.

They head out regularly, collecting samples, data and observations that have proven to be invaluable for research into South Australia's harmful algal bloom.

Now, while continuing to monitor the water, they are also watching the wildlife for signs of bird flu, after the first Australian case in a dolphin identified locally at Goolwa Beach, which was followed by a new suspected case in a sea lion at Victor Harbor.

High alert for 'beloved' dolphins

Nedra Haines has been monitoring her beloved dolphins for 14 years, as part of the Victor Harbor Dolphin Watch Group.

Nedra Haines has been monitoring dolphins off the coast of the Fleurieu Peninsula for 14 years. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

She has helped to compile their catalogue of 140 bottlenose dolphins and 50 common dolphins, identifying them through the shape and markings of their dorsal fins.

Information collected on each dolphin and its environment is fed into the South Australian government's state biological database.

The dolphin watchers were, without realising it at the time, some of the first to see the very early signs of the algal bloom before it blew up spectacularly on local beaches.

Ms Haines said that while the days of the bloom had been depressing, she had watched over the dolphins, diligently recording any signs of irritation to their thick, rubbery skins.

The dolphin watch group spotted foam behind an island in March 2025. (Supplied: Samantha Sea)

Now she is watching to see if they show any signs of the viral infection.

"If they're swimming crazy, if they're off balance. Just any neurological defects, [we] definitely keep an eye out for things like that," Ms Haines said.

Today on the boat, there is no behaviour to suggest the dolphins are anything but healthy.

Those seen display playful antics including tail slapping, a lot of curiosity and even some carrying of seaweed, which apparently can be used to attract a mate.

Building knowledge

Also on board is Samantha Sea from the group Phytoplankton of South Australia, which formed as a response to the lack of data available to the public during the early days of the algal bloom.

Samantha Sea takes her water samples home and prepares them for analysis. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

She holds a degree in physics, but when the algal bloom appeared, she started attending community-led meetings, asking what could be done to help.

Since then she has pored over hundreds of samples, learning how to identify algae and other phytoplankton.

The information from Ms Sea and the network of volunteers now established across the state is being sent for use by researchers and government.

The group was recently awarded the title of South Australian Citizen Science Champions for 2026.

Wright Island, off the coast of Victor Harbor, is regularly monitored by citizen scientists, with the help of a local tourist boat operator. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Even though they now tend to record low levels of the Karenia algal species, which formed the harmful algal bloom, constant monitoring is still important.

"We don't understand the ocean. Not well," Ms Sea said, noting that before the bloom there was no baseline for normal levels of algae.

Now her samples are helping to build a picture of the recovering marine environment, used by the state government and Shauna Murray, the University of Technology Sydney researcher whose team identified the presence of the toxin-producing Karenia cristata within the bloom.

Buckets of help

When the bloom entered Gult St Vincent, Professor Murray reached out to friend and former fellow biology student Niko Streiber, now a scientist at the Adelaide Botanic Gardens and State Herbarium, who lived near the beach.

Dr Streiber collected water samples in 9-litre buckets from three different sites. She filtered them in her kitchen, filled tubes with the water and posted them off to Professor Murray's laboratory, where the Karenia was identified.

Nikola Streiber collected samples in buckets off the coast of Adelaide for months. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

While she is not currently sampling off the Adelaide coastline, Dr Streiber remains ready to start again when needed, aware that the bloom could recur given the right conditions.

"We can't predict it for certain because Karenia cristata is able to survive on the bottom of the ocean; it forms little cysts, and they can spring back to life," Dr Streiber said.

"That's why the ongoing monitoring is so important."

World.title: Rise in 'disgusting' attacks on WA police across state's far north
World.content:
Western Australia's Police Union says assaults against officers are becoming increasingly violent in the state's north and is calling for harsher penalties to be enforced.

Kimberley police say three officers in Broome, 2,200 kilometres north of Perth, were spat on while performing their duties on a single day last week.

Police statistics show 87 recorded assaults on police officers across the region to June 2026, up from 84 in the same period last year.

However, a new report by a former WA police sergeant has found rates of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) are rising within the force.

Union wants accountability

WA Police Union spokesperson Simone Taplin said there had been an uptick in needle-stick injuries, as well as officers being spat at.

"It's disgusting, to be honest, that people think they can just spit at police officers," she said.

"Our officers have to go and have blood tests and follow-ups in a month to ensure they've not caught any diseases."

Simone Taplin says assaults against police are unacceptable. (ABC South West: Anthony Pancia)

Under WA law, anyone charged with one of these attacks must be tested for contractible diseases.

But Ms Taplin said courts were not enforcing the tougher penalties available.

"There is a mandatory term of imprisonment for any assault on police that has an assault occasioning bodily harm element to it," Ms Taplin said.

"Instead, we're seeing offenders being given convictions that are suspended and therefore not doing time in jail."

Assaults on police across the Kimberley climbed steadily between 2019 and 2024, before decreasing in 2025. (ABC News: Rebecca Nadge)

Ms Taplin said offenders "deserved punishment" and the justice system needed to be "held to account" and get behind police.

Alarming PTSD rates

Former WA police sergeant and researcher Dan Talbot released a report yesterday tracking the impact of PTSD in the force.

The Blue Poppy Study, a collaboration between ECU, Murdoch University and UWA, surveyed 1,278 serving police officers, representing almost 20 per cent of the workforce.

It found more than 38 per cent of respondents had PTSD, "alarmingly" higher than previous recordings of around 20 per cent, Dr Talbot said.

" We kept going back to the data and checking it, making sure it was right because it was surprising to us all that it was so high. "

The Police Union says officers across the Kimberley are facing "disgusting" assaults. (ABC Kimberley: Esse Deves)

He said across five years of research, he saw a lot of "very damaged police officers".

The findings indicated officers were overwhelmingly getting their main source of support from partners or loved ones, followed by colleagues.

Support from the department was the lowest form, according to respondents at the time of the research.

"I look at my own experience, the trauma you faced wasn't as frequent, maybe not even as intense," Dr Talbot said.

"You had time to recover and re-centre a little bit between these things, whereas now they just seem to keep going, the load and the frequency of events."

Mr Talbot said he hoped this information would inform strategies about how the force responds to officers with PTSD.

Violence against police 'unacceptable'

The ABC sent questions to Police Minister Reece Whitby and Attorney-General Toni Buti, asking for their stance on the potential removal of suspended sentences in police assault cases.

The WA Police Union says the assaults against police are becoming increasingly violent. (ABC Kimberley)

In response, a state government spokesperson said they had invested significantly in supporting and equipping WA police with body-worn cameras and training.

"Police officers should always be shown the respect they deserve by the community and any violence is absolutely unacceptable," they said.

"More police are responding and arriving at incidents quicker, sometimes in the heat of the moment, which can lead to assaults."

The spokesperson said the mandatory six-month jail term for anyone guilty of assault occasioning bodily harm against a police officer was an appropriate penalty.

World.title: Live: ASX to recover from three-month low, surging oil prices drag Wall Street lower
World.content:
The ASX usually follows the lead of much larger share markets like Wall Street.

While US markets extended their sell-off this morning, it looks the Australian share market will do its own thing and start the day higher.

Yesterday, the ASX 200 fell to its lowest level since June 11. But today, it appears investors will 'buy the dip' as futures are pointing to a modest gain of 0.4% when the local market opens for business.

Wall of worry on US markets

A number of factors weighed on the New York Stock Exchange overnight including a rise in US government borrowing costs, mounting debt concerns and soaring oil prices.

The US Federal Reserve has begun for its two-day monetary policy meeting and it's widely expected to announce an interest rate hike tomorrow at around 4am (AEST), its first increase in three years.

Financial markets have priced in a 94.5% likelihood of a rate rise, up from 33% one month ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

As rate-hike bets increased, global bond yields resumed their upward climb, with benchmark US Treasury bond yields rising above 5%.

In other words, the US government's borrowing costs have lifted to their highest level since the global financial crisis in 2007.

Rising interest rates are increasing the pressure on heavily indebted borrowers, including companies that have placed big bets on AI.



Those worries exacerbated mounting fears over AI's destructive potential and growing opposition to the construction of data centres, leading to sharp falls in the share price of Oracle (-3.1%), SpaceX (-3.2%) and Amazon (-2%).

- with Reuters

World.title: ‘The world should trust us’: Silicon Valley billionaire’s plea as fight escalates
World.content:
Breaking TechnologyAI ‘The world should trust us’: Silicon Valley billionaire’s plea as fight escalates David Swan September 16, 2026 — 8:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has criticised the way that rival artificial intelligence companies have argued for an industry slowdown, saying the public should be able to trust AI firms to act responsibly without conditions attached. Speaking at the Dreamforce conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, the billionaire said he supported co-ordination on safety but objected to how the debate had been put to the public over the past week. OpenAI chief Sam Altman and Salesforce chief Marc Benioff speak at the conference. Bloomberg “The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing, and because we feel the magnitude of this,” he said. “But when there’s any implication that because of the commercial pressures in the race, some company, or between countries, some countries, might not do the right thing, I think that’s where people get very scared.” Altman said companies that qualified their commitments were part of the problem.



Related Article Opinion

AI These three kings of AI have a plan. It could blow everything up Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “You have companies saying things like, ‘we will only slow down if, or we will only be responsible if other companies are responsible’,” he said. “And then I think the public naturally says, ‘well, we’d really like to know that you’re going to do the safe thing and be responsible no matter what’. There should be no qualifier on that.” The comments follow an essay published on Saturday by Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei calling for a co-ordinated global slowdown, independent auditors to monitor safety work at AI labs, and regulatory approval for companies to co-ordinate on safety standards without breaching competition law. Altman publicly agreed with Amodei on Saturday, then began distancing himself a day later, warning in a social media post about the risk of “one lab ending up with too much power” without naming Anthropic, the New York Times reported. View post on X



On stage with Salesforce chief executive Marc Benioff, Altman detailed the July incident that triggered the debate. During an internal evaluation, an older OpenAI model broke out of its sandbox, hacked into a server belonging to the open-source company Hugging Face, moved laterally through its systems to obtain the answer to a benchmark test, and returned a perfect score. Related Article Analysis

AI ‘We must be stopped’: Why Australia needs to listen to the experts on AI “This is obviously a terrifying incident,” Altman said. “This was the worst accident we’ve seen.” He added that the episode had exposed a gap in how the models were trained. “Although we have aligned them in many ways, we have not taught them, hey, no matter how much we tell you to get the best score on this test you can, don’t break out, don’t hack in, don’t steal the answer.” Altman confirmed that Hugging Face, which employs about 200 people, was unable to obtain a cybersecurity model from another major lab to defend itself and had turned to Chinese open-source models instead.



He warned smaller companies to prepare for what was coming. “There is going to be this huge cyber threat that’s going to come,” he said. “So while there is this little period of advantage, please do something to defend yourselves.” Benioff, whose company has built its Dreamforce announcements around AI agents and the future of workplace software, pressed Altman on whether more occurrences of such incidents were inevitable, and whether the aviation industry was the right model for responding to them. Marc Benioff with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. Bloomberg “Accidents with any new technology are unavoidable, and we should have a great culture of transparent reporting about them,” Altman said. He also rejected the argument that technology is neutral. “It cannot be that a small number of companies building these models get to make the decisions that the world should get to make,” he said.



The industry is now visibly split. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, whose chips underpin the AI buildout, appeared at the same conference hours earlier and rejected any role for government. Assistant Technology Minister Andrew Charlton. Dale Wowk “Safety is paramount. In a lot of ways, it’s job one,” Huang said. “However, safety is an engineering problem.” He added: “The market forces are already there. We don’t need any new laws, we don’t need any new regulations.” Huang’s position aligns with the Trump administration. On Monday, the president telephoned Huang mid-interview at a conference in Los Angeles and told the audience that AI safety fears were “a hoax”, according to the New York Times. In Australia, the assistant minister for science, technology and the digital economy, Andrew Charlton, said governments should judge the industry on its conduct rather than its statements.



Related Article Updated

AI ‘Whoever wins with AI wins’: Trump hits back at tech chiefs’ calls to slow down “We’ve seen a lot of news in the last couple of days from some of these technology companies talking about their desire to slow things down. I take that at face value, but I don’t think we should care very much about what individual executives say or what individual executives claim they want to happen,” Charlton told an Australian Strategic Policy Institute event on Monday. “What’s actually happening is that we’re building the capability of these machines in a scaling environment which is not bending, and these companies have extremely strong financial incentives to continue that trajectory.” Charlton said Australia should assume the models would keep getting more capable, pointing to the digital duty of care, privacy reforms, automated decision-making rules and the work of the Australian AI Safety Institute. Hugging Face is not an Australian company, but the scenario has been raised locally. Asked at the same event what would have protected an Australian business in the same position, Charlton said Australia had “a lot of agency” and was working with overseas regulators, while declining to discuss specific conversations.



David Swan travelled to San Francisco as a guest of Salesforce. Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter every Friday. Sign up here.

World.title: Brisbane still the best place to sell a house despite slowing market
World.content:
NationalQueenslandProperty market Brisbane still the best place to sell a house despite slowing market Julius Dennis September 16, 2026 — 8:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane remains the best place to make a buck reselling property despite a declining market, with sales in the city returning the highest profit of any capital in the June quarter. The city has held that title for two years, with sellers pocketing a median profit of $525,000. This is $154,000 above the national median gain but down $5000 from the March quarter, according to new data from property research firm Cotality. The report found sellers in Brisbane were almost ensured to turn a profit, with 99.7 per cent of people selling houses and 99.1 per cent of those selling units getting more than they bought them for. Brisbane sellers are still making money. Robert Rough While the nation’s property market has fallen off record highs, Cotality’s head of research Gerard Burg said property owners looking to sell were still well-placed.



“Profitability is still exceptionally high by historical standards, but we are starting to see the impact of weaker housing market conditions flow through to resale outcomes,” Burg said. Related Article Queensland residential property Historic home on one of Brisbane’s best streets sells for $17m However, he said sellers looking to flip houses and units they bought recently could have trouble making a profit, with the best profits in Brisbane for the quarter made by people who had owned their houses for nine years. Things were tougher in the southern capitals, but still healthy, with 95.4 per cent of the 94,000 sales analysed turning a profit nationally. In Melbourne, 89 per cent of sales were for a profit, with a median gain of $278,000.



In Sydney 92.7 per cent made a profit, with a median gain of $404,000. Meanwhile, research conducted by Frank Knight highlighted Brisbane’s emerging luxury housing market, pointing to the city’s “more permissive” planning scheme compared to Sydney and Melbourne, and the upcoming spotlight of the Olympics. Related Article Queensland residential property How Brisbane just leapfrogged Sydney for property pain “Investment is spilling into hospitality, retail and residential property, underpinning the city’s emergence as one of Asia-Pacific’s fastest-growing luxury markets,” the report said. The report’s authors said Brisbane’s luxury real estate market had grown by 2.6 per cent in the year to June 2026, while Sydney and Melbourne’s had shrunk by roughly the same amount, signifying a shift to the city by wealthy people chasing high-amenity homes.



However, those homes still cost significantly more in Sydney in Melbourne. Luxury apartments in Sydney cost $74,500 per square meter compared to $29,000 in Brisbane and $33,000 in Melbourne. The report also noted the Gold Coast’s 34.7 per cent market growth over the past five years, placing it in the top 10 globally. World.title: Ed Sheeran’s US tour in chaos as supporting acts, band quit after Macklemore axed
World.content:
CultureMusicIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Ed Sheeran’s US tour in chaos as supporting acts, band quit after Macklemore axed Kayla Olaya September 16, 2026 — 8:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ed Sheeran’s opening acts and touring band have pulled out of his Loop tour after US rapper Macklemore was dropped for expressing support for Palestine on stage. Artists Finneas and Aaron Rowe, Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish folk quintet Beoga posted black-and-grey tiled carousel statements on social media overnight (AEST), supporting Macklemore and Palestine. Macklemore and Ed Sheeran, pictured in 2014. Four other of Sheeran’s opening acts have dropped out of his tour supporting Macklemore. Getty Macklemore himself posted a black carousel to Instagram on Tuesday (AEST), revealing his pro-Palestinian views led stadium owners to bar him from performing at their venues. Sheeran, referred to as “apolitical” in Macklemore’s post but who has publicly supported Ukraine in the Russia-Ukraine war, has responded to the US tour fallout and fan backlash with his own black carousel post on Instagram.



“Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s [Messina Touring Group] decision; it was not mine. Macklemore’s contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me,” Sheeran wrote. “I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living.” The controversy began at MetLife Stadium on September 4, when, during his support spot for Sheeran in New Jersey, Macklemore exclaimed “Free Palestine” while introducing his protest song Hind’s Hall alongside footage of the devastation in Gaza on a screen. Written after the 2024 campus protests supporting Palestinians, the song is named for Hind Rajab, a five-year-old Palestinian girl who was killed after Israeli forces opened fire on her family’s car in Gaza City. (Macklemore also performed the song during his 2024 tour of Australia.)



Artist and producer Finneas was one of the artists to drop out of Sheeran’s tour. AP Photo/Jordan Strauss Messina Touring Group said in a statement to Rolling Stone that venues had notified it that “they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the line-up, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans”. The following night, he returned to the stage and said: “To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, it in no way is criticism of you. This message is for peace, love, for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality.” New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium’s billionaire owner Robert Kraft was among the most vocal critics of Macklemore and led the push to remove him from Sheeran’s tour. Robert Kraft, the owner of the New England Patriots. Getty Images



In Macklemore’s Tuesday post, he said Sheeran told him Kraft called him to say Macklemore was banned from performing in a stadium owned by his business group. “Ed also told me that Kraft had rallied some of the other stadium owners, and collectively they gave him an ultimatum: if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues,” Macklemore said in the post. Sheeran, in his response overnight, confirmed that after Macklemore’s shows, “venues on my upcoming tour dates communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting”. “I was informed that this stance was based on how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance, rather than on everything that was said,” Sheeran wrote.



“I spoke with the venues at length all week to try and build a bridge. One of those people was Robert Kraft. I was also involved in direct talks with promoters, along with activists on both sides, to try and find a mutual resolution for all, but the venue’s and promoter’s decision was final.” Sheeran said he does not “use my professional platform for politics” regarding the war in Gaza. Macklemore performing in Melbourne in 2024. Getty “I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly. “My audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds. Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum.



“I respect Macklemore’s strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes. However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: peace.” Artist Finneas – brother and music producer of Billie Eilish – said on social media that he stood with Palestine and its people. “Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed. I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran,” he wrote. Meanwhile, traditional Irish quintet Beoga – who collaborated on Sheeran’s blockbuster album Divide, co-wrote the hit Galway Girl and toured numerous times with him – said it, too, decided to depart Sheeran’s tour following the “silencing of Macklemore by zionist lobbies”.



“We are Irish people who understand colonialism,” the post said, adding they had known Sheeran for more than 10 years and continue to be friends. “As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be.” Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Macklemore dumped from Ed Sheeran’s tour over pro-Palestine comments Irish musician Aaron Rowe also withdrew from the tour, saying he had also been friends with Sheeran for many years, but as “Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation”. “I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children. I would lose all respect for myself to carry on as normal.” A growing chorus of organisations and experts – including the United Nations – allege Israel’s wartime actions in Gaza amount to genocide. It’s an accusation Israel vehemently rejects.



Danish pop band Lukas Graham said it was also withdrawing from the tour. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Cameron Smith and LIV players warned of no immediate return to PGA Tour
World.content:
SportGolfPGA Tour Cameron Smith and LIV players warned of no immediate return to PGA Tour James Corrigan September 16, 2026 — 8:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The PGA Tour will not roll out the red carpet for Australian Cameron Smith and other LIV members who wish to return in 2027, as it becomes clear they will have to play at least a year solely on the DP World Tour. In a press conference on Tuesday, Brian Rolapp, the PGA Tour chief executive, did not need prompting before addressing the elephant in the room. “In terms of where we are today, we are not currently contemplating a returning-member program like the one you saw in January,” Rolapp said. Australian golfer Cameron Smith. Getty Images At the start of the year, Brooks Koepka was allowed to regain his card immediately, albeit with event entry restrictions and a $US5 million ($7 million) fine he had to pay to charity. The same deal was offered to Smith, Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau as major-winners from the past five years. However, that trio declined and a few months later they were perhaps left wishing they had not been so hasty after the Saudi Public Investment Fund announced that, after investing more than $US5 billion ($7 billion) into the breakaway league, it was pulling funding from LIV in August.



Last week, LIV went into bankruptcy, with Rahm its biggest creditor. It is believed the Spaniard is owed a nine-figure sum from his $US300 million ($420 million) contract. But as LIV tries to relaunch for a 2027 campaign, its lawyers are trying to get the courts to reject the remaining player signing-on deals. That motion is regarded as almost certain to be granted, at which point Rahm is expected to leave LIV, as is his Ryder Cup partner Tyrrell Hatton. There will be no instant route to the US circuit, but Rolapp did reveal that there would be a direct pathway through the DP World Tour – but only after a year on the circuit. Spain’s Jon Rahm is LIV golf’s biggest creditor after the golf league filed for bankruptcy earlier this month. Getty Images The issue is complicated by the fact that, at the end of the next campaign, the PGA Tour is splitting into two tiers – known as the Championship and Challenger Series. And from 2028 there will only be promotion and relegation on an annual basis and these first and second divisions will be kept separate. The DP World Tour is presently renegotiating its “strategic alliance” with its American counterparts and part of the bartering is how many US cards will be up for grabs on the European money list. For the past three years, the top players not already exempt have earned playing privileges on the PGA Tour, but Rory McIlroy on Tuesday explained why this system should be ripped up.



“I don’t see any reason why a DP World Tour player would go to the Challenger Series,” he said. “I don’t see that as an upward move in your career. I see it as a very lateral move. So it’s just OK, how many cards is reasonable to give to the DP World Tour for the Championship Series?” Related Video Video icon 1:20 Adelaide in limbo as LIV files bankruptcy It is understood that this figure could be up to five, and Rahm and Hatton would be confident of finishing high enough in next year’s order of merit. For now, the duo cannot comment on their plans as they remain under contract. “There’s a legal process they [LIV] have to go through before a lot of things fall into place,” Rahm said at Wentworth. Rahm and Hatton are two of six LIV members teeing it up on the West Course at the BMW PGA Championship, the DP World Tour’s flagship event, that begins on Thursday. McIlroy has been drawn alongside his fellow 2026 major winners, England’s Aaron Rai and New Zealand’s Ryan Fox. World.title: US delegation pressed Australia to end Port of Darwin lease, ramp up defence spending
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaForeign relations US delegation pressed Australia to end Port of Darwin lease, ramp up defence spending Michael Koziol September 16, 2026 — 8:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Australia is being pressured to hasten the termination of a Chinese company’s lease over the Port of Darwin, with a visiting US congressional delegation raising the issue – as well as defence spending – with top government ministers. Michael McCaul, a Republican congressman who co-chairs the Friends of Australia caucus, said the matter was raised by a member of the US delegation when they met last week with officials including Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles, Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy. Michael McCaul, the Republican co-chair of the Friends of Australia Caucus in Congress, who recently visited Australia. Bloomberg “That was something that was brought up by, frankly, our side … it’s an issue,” McCaul said during a debrief about the trip in Washington. “When we talk about critical minerals, I think it’s important that Australia own that port.” McCaul said the delegation accepted the Albanese government’s response that it was working to get out of the 99-year-lease to the China-controlled Landbridge Group, a decision made in 2015 by the Northern Territory government and waved through by the Turnbull government in Canberra.



Before the last election, both major parties promised to end the lease, either by finding an approved private buyer or direct intervention. “They can always exercise eminent domain over it in the national interest,” McCaul said. The US government has always disliked the deal, with then-president Barack Obama raising concerns about it with then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull at the time. Both parties have pledged to take control of the Port of Darwin from Chinese firm Landbridge. Alamy Stock Photo Much of the lithium exported from Australia for refining leaves from the Port of Darwin, and McCaul indicated this was of concern to the US, given the multibillion-dollar critical minerals deal between the two countries. China will resist moves to terminate the lease. This year, Landbridge lodged a legal challenge with the World Bank’s International Centre for Settlement of Investor Disputes, accusing Australia of discrimination and breaching the China-Australia free trade agreement.



A China hawk and chairman emeritus of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, McCaul visited Taiwan in August and said he was increasingly worried about Chinese aggression against the island – which Beijing claims as part of China. He said it was “absolutely critical” that Australia joins the US in any conflict with China over Taiwan, and had no doubt Australia would do so. “I don’t think it was even questioned. It’s just obvious,” he said. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Defence Minister Richard Marles at HMAS Stirling in 2024. Trevor Collens/Pool Asked about concerns that an increasing US military presence in Australia – particularly US submarines rotating through HMAS Stirling near Perth – made the country a target, McCaul said: “Australia is a target.” Defence spending was also discussed on the visit, McCaul said, making it clear that Washington still expected Australia to lift spending to at least 3.5 per cent of gross domestic product. That is despite President Donald Trump appearing nonplussed about the issue when Prime Minister Anthony Albanese visited a year ago.



McCaul said he recommended that Australia prioritise additional expenditure on pillar two of AUKUS, which involves developing and fielding emerging technologies. AUKUS was announced five years ago this week. Related Article Foreign relations ‘Force posture’: Marles, Hegseth back expanded US military presence in Australia “We appreciate your increase in defence spending. We’d like to see more as a percentage of GDP … I don’t sense that we would expect Australia to be off the hook.” Marles said following a recent meeting with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth in Washington that the Albanese government was spending an extra $117 billion on defence over 10 years. “We have a good story to tell,” he said. The government did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the Port of Darwin. During a visit to Darwin in July, Albanese said the government was continuing to “argue the case” to scrap the lease.



It had been a mistake to sell it, he said, noting he opposed the sale at the time. “I’m determined that it will come back into Australian hands, and we’re negotiating those issues through.” Last year, The Australian reported that US private equity firm Cerberus Capital Management was interested in acquiring the Port of Darwin, along with Australian freight company Toll Group and superannuation funds. McCaul said there was no discussion about potential buyers during the visit. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Nvidia boss rejects calls for AI regulation; Labor grows uneasy over interest rate rises, inflation; US reveals deployment of weapons in space

North Korea accused the US of expanding a “nuclear submarine alliance” that it said was undermining global nuclear security, as the fifth anniversary of its AUKUS defence pact with Australia and Britain arrives.

Kim Jong Un (third left) inspects a nuclear-powered submarine under construction, in a supplied photo from December 2025. AP

Washington was intensifying nuclear proliferation efforts, state media KCNA said, citing an international affairs analyst named Choe Ju Hyon who accused a senior US naval official of encouraging Japan and South Korea to pursue nuclear-powered submarines.

The commentary noted that AUKUS – under which the US and Britain are helping Australia acquire nuclear-powered submarines – has become a template that Washington is seeking to extend to other allies including South Korea and Japan. Those developments, it said, justified North Korea’s continued build-up of its own nuclear deterrent.

World.title: ASX eyes gains, Wall Street slips as oil prices, bond market crank up pressure; Bitcoin falls
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX eyes gains, Wall Street slips as oil prices, bond market crank up pressure; Bitcoin falls Stan Choe Updated September 16, 2026 — 6:33am ,first published 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks slipped after oil prices and the bond market cranked up the pressure on Wall Street. The S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 328 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.8 per cent. Wall Street lost ground on Tuesday. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.18am AEST pointing to a gain of 31 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.9 per cent on Tuesday as it closed at its lowest level in almost three months. The Australian dollar was lower at US71.31¢. Wall Street felt pressure as the yield on the 10-year Treasury, which is the centrepiece of the US bond market, climbed to 5.00 per cent from 4.97 per cent late Monday and briefly touched 5.04 per cent overnight. It’s been jumping to its highest level in years, and Monday was the first time it breached 5 per cent since 2023.



Higher yields mean everyone from the US government to households to businesses must pay more in interest to borrow money, which slows the overall economy. They also make people less willing to pay high prices for stocks because they can earn more from sitting in bonds, which are considered safer investments. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Trump set to explode if his man does his job Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “The result is a market that must work harder to generate earnings growth just as investors become less willing to pay premium valuations for that growth,” according to Darrell Cronk, president of Wells Fargo Investment Institute. The last time the 10-year yield was consistently above 5 per cent was around the turn of the millennium, and it’s been a long march back since it bottomed out below 0.50 per cent in 2020. The pace has accelerated since February, after the war with Iran sent oil prices much higher. That raised worries about high inflation potentially lasting for years, which are layering atop longstanding concerns about the US government’s massive debt level and other issues.



Oil prices rose further Tuesday following several sharp swings in the morning. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, climbed 2.9 per cent to settle at $108.75. It remains well above its $US72 level from early July and from before the war with Iran began in February, as doubt continues about whether the fighting will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf anytime soon through the Strait of Hormuz. Inflation remains high enough that the widespread expectation is that the Federal Reserve will announce on Wednesday that it will hike the federal funds rate for the first time in three years. Traders are still betting on a slight chance that the Federal Reserve could hold off on hiking interest rates, though. If it does, the market could swing because investors may see it as a sign that the Fed is less committed to getting inflation lower. Fed officials will also release forecasts for where they see interest rates heading in upcoming years, providing another opportunity to inject uncertainty into the market.



On Wall Street, stocks of companies that depend on customers having enough spare cash to spend on their products fell to some of the sharper losses. Related Article Opinion

Sydney Sweeney There’s a seriously bad industry behind Sweeney’s seriously bad ad Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Chipotle Mexican Grill dropped 5.9 per cent. Darden Restaurants, the company behind Olive Garden and Longhorn Steakhouse, sank 4.3 per cent. Dollar Tree, whose customers may have less financial cushion than others, fell 5.4 per cent. Dave & Buster’s Entertainment tumbled 19 per cent after reporting weaker results for the latest quarter than analysts expected.



Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks enmeshed in the cryptocurrency industry sank after the US Senate voted to block legislation creating a new regulatory framework for crypto, while demanding more limits on President Donald Trump’s investments. The price of Bitcoin slumped 4.2 per cent to $US75,920 at 6.50am AEST. Coinbase Global fell 10.1 per cent, and Robinhood Markets lost 3.4 per cent. Several artificial-intelligence stocks meanwhile held steadier following their worldwide slide the day before, after leaders of the AI industry called for a slowdown in development to address safety issues for humanity. Nvidia added 0.6 per cent a day after its 3.4 per cent drop was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500 index. Advanced Micro Devices climbed 2.2 per cent. Such stocks led the US market to records for years, but they’ve come under pressure recently on worries that their prices shot too high in the frenzy around AI.



All told, the S&P 500 fell 34.25 points to 7,585.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 328.09 to 52,093.11, and the Nasdaq composite fell 204.84 to 25,981.57. In stock markets abroad, indexes fell across much of Europe and Asia. But for several, the drops were not as sharp as Monday’s caused by the slide for AI stocks. South Korea’s Kospi index, for example, fell 0.9 per cent following Monday’s 3.3 per cent drop. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘The world should trust us’: Silicon Valley billionaire’s plea as fight escalates
World.content:
Breaking TechnologyAI ‘The world should trust us’: Silicon Valley billionaire’s plea as fight escalates David Swan September 16, 2026 — 8:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has criticised the way that rival artificial intelligence companies have argued for an industry slowdown, saying the public should be able to trust AI firms to act responsibly without conditions attached. Speaking at the Dreamforce conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, the billionaire said he supported co-ordination on safety but objected to how the debate had been put to the public over the past week. OpenAI chief Sam Altman and Salesforce chief Marc Benioff speak at the conference. Bloomberg “The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing, and because we feel the magnitude of this,” he said. “But when there’s any implication that because of the commercial pressures in the race, some company, or between countries, some countries, might not do the right thing, I think that’s where people get very scared.” Altman said companies that qualified their commitments were part of the problem.



Related Article Opinion

AI These three kings of AI have a plan. It could blow everything up Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “You have companies saying things like, ‘we will only slow down if, or we will only be responsible if other companies are responsible’,” he said. “And then I think the public naturally says, ‘well, we’d really like to know that you’re going to do the safe thing and be responsible no matter what’. There should be no qualifier on that.” The comments follow an essay published on Saturday by Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei calling for a co-ordinated global slowdown, independent auditors to monitor safety work at AI labs, and regulatory approval for companies to co-ordinate on safety standards without breaching competition law. Altman publicly agreed with Amodei on Saturday, then began distancing himself a day later, warning in a social media post about the risk of “one lab ending up with too much power” without naming Anthropic, the New York Times reported. View post on X



On stage with Salesforce chief executive Marc Benioff, Altman detailed the July incident that triggered the debate. During an internal evaluation, an older OpenAI model broke out of its sandbox, hacked into a server belonging to the open-source company Hugging Face, moved laterally through its systems to obtain the answer to a benchmark test, and returned a perfect score. Related Article Analysis

AI ‘We must be stopped’: Why Australia needs to listen to the experts on AI “This is obviously a terrifying incident,” Altman said. “This was the worst accident we’ve seen.” He added that the episode had exposed a gap in how the models were trained. “Although we have aligned them in many ways, we have not taught them, hey, no matter how much we tell you to get the best score on this test you can, don’t break out, don’t hack in, don’t steal the answer.” Altman confirmed that Hugging Face, which employs about 200 people, was unable to obtain a cybersecurity model from another major lab to defend itself and had turned to Chinese open-source models instead.



He warned smaller companies to prepare for what was coming. “There is going to be this huge cyber threat that’s going to come,” he said. “So while there is this little period of advantage, please do something to defend yourselves.” Benioff, whose company has built its Dreamforce announcements around AI agents and the future of workplace software, pressed Altman on whether more occurrences of such incidents were inevitable, and whether the aviation industry was the right model for responding to them. Marc Benioff with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. Bloomberg “Accidents with any new technology are unavoidable, and we should have a great culture of transparent reporting about them,” Altman said. He also rejected the argument that technology is neutral. “It cannot be that a small number of companies building these models get to make the decisions that the world should get to make,” he said.



The industry is now visibly split. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, whose chips underpin the AI buildout, appeared at the same conference hours earlier and rejected any role for government. Assistant Technology Minister Andrew Charlton. Dale Wowk “Safety is paramount. In a lot of ways, it’s job one,” Huang said. “However, safety is an engineering problem.” He added: “The market forces are already there. We don’t need any new laws, we don’t need any new regulations.” Huang’s position aligns with the Trump administration. On Monday, the president telephoned Huang mid-interview at a conference in Los Angeles and told the audience that AI safety fears were “a hoax”, according to the New York Times. In Australia, the assistant minister for science, technology and the digital economy, Andrew Charlton, said governments should judge the industry on its conduct rather than its statements.



Related Article Updated

AI ‘Whoever wins with AI wins’: Trump hits back at tech chiefs’ calls to slow down “We’ve seen a lot of news in the last couple of days from some of these technology companies talking about their desire to slow things down. I take that at face value, but I don’t think we should care very much about what individual executives say or what individual executives claim they want to happen,” Charlton told an Australian Strategic Policy Institute event on Monday. “What’s actually happening is that we’re building the capability of these machines in a scaling environment which is not bending, and these companies have extremely strong financial incentives to continue that trajectory.” Charlton said Australia should assume the models would keep getting more capable, pointing to the digital duty of care, privacy reforms, automated decision-making rules and the work of the Australian AI Safety Institute. Hugging Face is not an Australian company, but the scenario has been raised locally. Asked at the same event what would have protected an Australian business in the same position, Charlton said Australia had “a lot of agency” and was working with overseas regulators, while declining to discuss specific conversations.



David Swan travelled to San Francisco as a guest of Salesforce. Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter every Friday. Sign up here.

World.title: Brisbane still the best place to sell a house despite slowing market
World.content:
NationalQueenslandProperty market Brisbane still the best place to sell a house despite slowing market Julius Dennis September 16, 2026 — 8:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane remains the best place to make a buck reselling property despite a declining market, with sales in the city returning the highest profit of any capital in the June quarter. The city has held that title for two years, with sellers pocketing a median profit of $525,000. This is $154,000 above the national median gain but down $5000 from the March quarter, according to new data from property research firm Cotality. The report found sellers in Brisbane were almost ensured to turn a profit, with 99.7 per cent of people selling houses and 99.1 per cent of those selling units getting more than they bought them for. Brisbane sellers are still making money. Robert Rough While the nation’s property market has fallen off record highs, Cotality’s head of research Gerard Burg said property owners looking to sell were still well-placed.



“Profitability is still exceptionally high by historical standards, but we are starting to see the impact of weaker housing market conditions flow through to resale outcomes,” Burg said. Related Article Queensland residential property Historic home on one of Brisbane’s best streets sells for $17m However, he said sellers looking to flip houses and units they bought recently could have trouble making a profit, with the best profits in Brisbane for the quarter made by people who had owned their houses for nine years. Things were tougher in the southern capitals, but still healthy, with 95.4 per cent of the 94,000 sales analysed turning a profit nationally. In Melbourne, 89 per cent of sales were for a profit, with a median gain of $278,000.



In Sydney 92.7 per cent made a profit, with a median gain of $404,000. Meanwhile, research conducted by Frank Knight highlighted Brisbane’s emerging luxury housing market, pointing to the city’s “more permissive” planning scheme compared to Sydney and Melbourne, and the upcoming spotlight of the Olympics. Related Article Queensland residential property How Brisbane just leapfrogged Sydney for property pain “Investment is spilling into hospitality, retail and residential property, underpinning the city’s emergence as one of Asia-Pacific’s fastest-growing luxury markets,” the report said. The report’s authors said Brisbane’s luxury real estate market had grown by 2.6 per cent in the year to June 2026, while Sydney and Melbourne’s had shrunk by roughly the same amount, signifying a shift to the city by wealthy people chasing high-amenity homes.



However, those homes still cost significantly more in Sydney in Melbourne. Luxury apartments in Sydney cost $74,500 per square meter compared to $29,000 in Brisbane and $33,000 in Melbourne. The report also noted the Gold Coast’s 34.7 per cent market growth over the past five years, placing it in the top 10 globally.
