World.title: Tom Phillips inquiry exposes multiple mistakes by police and Oranga Tamariki
World.content:
Political Editor Jo Moir covers reaction to Phillips inquiry Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Analysis: "How on earth can this happen in New Zealand?"

Anyone who read Tuesday's final report into the almost four-year disappearance of Tom Phillips and his children would have been asking just that while "shaking their head", according to the minister in charge of the inquiry Louise Upston.

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers and Oranga Tamariki (OT) chief executive Amanda Malu repeatedly referred to the failures and mistakes rife in the report as "missed opportunities" and both confessed they had not offered their resignation, nor had anyone in their respective agencies been held accountable for the harm's way Phillips' three children were put in.

The report did not hold back on those agencies the public naturally looks to keep some of our youngest and most vulnerable safe.

Not only did it say the concerns of maternal whanau of the children were "minimised or overlooked by agencies for significant periods" but it even went as far as to say a more collaborative approach from OT and NZ Police "could have prevented the children's disappearance and brought them back sooner".

Louise Upston at yesterday's announcement. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Some of the specific findings and events are a grim and bleak read, such as the woman who had Phillips in her car in May 2023, took a photograph of him, sighted his children, and called police - but they never came.

Despite police being dispatched, they were diverted to a family harm incident before they got there and later recorded the initial callout as 'no further action required'.

Lillian Hanly reports on reaction to Tom Phillips inquiry Morning Report Download MP3 3m

To this day, police have been unable to explain to the inquiry why the callout was designated as not needing any follow-up.

Then in November 2023, a decision was made to downsize the core investigation team to just three people, despite the children still being unaccounted for.

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

On Tuesday, Chambers said at that point more resources could have been put into the search, but in the same breath he said, "there's no doubt over the course of the four years we threw everything at this".

Both of those things can not be true.

Chambers was appointed into the top job about 10 months before Phillips died in a shootout with police, after they were called to reports of a burglary in the early hours of 8 September 2025.

Tom Phillips. Supplied

Both he and Police Minister Mark Mitchell had spoken publicly on many occasions about the need to find the children safely, and arrest Phillips.

Many meetings were had over that period, and decisions were being made all the time about how to conduct the search.

Yet an Independent Police Conduct Authority (IPCA) report in August was critical of the communication between police leadership and the officers on the ground in the lead-up to Phillips being shot.

It found one of the local officers making judgement calls about how to pursue Phillips and one of his children - who had been spotted breaking into a warehouse before taking off on a quad bike - had to ask the senior commander on shift what the plan was three times before getting a response.

Separate to that, despite a communications plan being prepared about how to arrest Phillips if he was sighted, it was never communicated to police comms staff or passed onto officers on the ground who were most likely to encounter Phillips.

Those failures were on Chambers' watch and don't marry with assurances from the commissioner and the minister they were prioritising finding Phillips and getting the children out of the bush safely.

Oranga Tamariki also came up short on many occasions over the years with one of the most damning findings in Tuesday's report being the agency's failure to pass on warnings from the children's mother and older siblings.

Indeed, it did not even read an affidavit from one of the sisters that outlined serious concerns.

On Tuesday, Upston told RNZ the ministry had already done significant work ahead of the report's release to "improve the safety and wellbeing of children" and insisted change was already underway.

If that was the case, it seems unbelievable Malu oversees a ministry that as recently as March this year had staff [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/1384989/absolutely-appalled-labour-s-chris-hipkins-unleashes-on-oranga-tamariki-s-systemic-issues watch as a teenager was hit and slapped by his peers as he left a youth residence under OT's care.

Even worse, staff not only watched and seemingly condoned the physical assault ritual known as 'walking the line', but failed to even report it.

This is the same agency that just hours later its boss was insisting was doing everything it could to protect children in its care.

What is clear from Tuesday's events is that both NZ Police and Oranga Tamariki have systemic issues that still need to be resolved and people in positions of power who are prepared to tell the public one thing while doing another.

For all the mistakes however, Chambers and Malu should be credited for fronting up when it mattered.

World.title: Fiji declares HIV emergency as 1 in 60 Fijian adults live with HIV
World.content:
Fiji's Health Minister Dr Atonio Lalabalavu has formally declared a national HIV emergency in the country.

In a pre-recorded video press statement on Tuesday, Dr Lalabalavu said the decision was backed by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka and his Cabinet due to the "seriousness of the epidemic".

The health minister confirmed that the government's current estimates indicated that one in every 60 adults in Fiji is living with HIV.

"Five years ago, the estimate was one in 1667. In 2024, we recorded 2060 new HIV diagnoses," he said.

"HIV prevalence among women attending antenatal care reached around two percent. That means one out of 50 pregnant women now has HIV. These figures tell us the response must reach further and follow through more consistently."



This week, a health researcher told RNZ Checkpoint that a "horrendously high" number of newborns were dying due to HIV-related complications in Fiji.

The NZ government's SafeTravel website is warning people traveling to Fiji to avoid activities that could increase their risk of infection.

According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), Fiji has the second-fastest-growing HIV epidemic in the Asia-Pacific region behind Papua New Guinea (PNG).

An estimated 9000 Fijians were living with HIV as of March this year, and officials pointed to high-risk drug use contributing to the rapid rise.

The number of Fijians living with HIV had risen to at least 9000 as of March. RNZ Pacific

Dr Lalabalavu said every diagnosis must lead to care and every person starting treatment needed support to remain on it.

He said authorities would move quickly to introduce new interventions and scale up established services backed by evidence.

"That means expanding testing, treatment, and access to pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP. It also means accelerating the introduction of a formal needle and syringe programme and long-acting injectable prevention."

He stressed that treatment was central to the government's response.

"It helps people living with HIV stay well, and when it achieves and maintains an undetectable viral load, it prevents sexual transmission."

Fiji's Sexual Reproductive Health and HIV Programme Management Unit is expected to coordinate implementation, working through divisional and sub-divisional health services, and with community partners.

Dr Lalabalavu said Australia, New Zealand, the Global Fund, India, and the United Nations Joint Team on HIV and AIDS, and other partners are supporting the country with its HIV response.

The Fijian government has also proposed the establishment of a parliamentary standing committee on HIV and related matters, he said.

"To anyone who has been diagnosed with HIV, a diagnosis does not take away your future. Effective treatment can help you live a long and healthy life. Keep taking your medicine as prescribed, even when you feel well.

World.title: National vows to 'pursue' break up supermarket giant Foodstuffs
World.content:
National has made a supermarket break-up a key part of its election pitch, proposing to sever Pak'nSave from New World in a bid to drive down grocery prices.

The significant policy was announced with little warning on Wednesday morning, and on the same day that Labour promised to ban big companies from charging excessive prices.

National's plan would turn the company into supermarket chains: Pak'nSave, New World/Four Square and Woolworths.

The breakup, however, would be contingent on a six-month review by the Commerce Commission into whether the split would leave shoppers better off.

If the watchdog gave it the green light, National said it would legislate to force through the separation.

In a statement, finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said the shake-up could eventually save households up to $1320 a year, pushing down grocery prices about 5 percent lower than they would otherwise be.

The numbers came from a government-commissioned cost-benefit analysis also released today.

The modelling estimated prices would be about 3.5 percent lower in the first year of separation, with gains growing as the new chains bedded in. By 2035, the estimated annual household benefit ranged from $200 to $1320 depending on income and family type.

"That's real money back in the pockets of New Zealanders," Willis said.

"More competition means supermarkets have to work harder for every customer, on price, specials, range and service. That is how shoppers get a better deal."

The independent report also carried some hefty warnings, with the economists warning their analysis was "indicative rather than definitive" and flagging potential "insurmountable" legal and implementation hurdles.

Willis stressed that National would act carefully on the Commission's advice and not play "supermarket executive from the Cabinet table".

"There is a very high bar for this kind of intervention and National is not pursuing structural separation in any other sector," Willis said.

"However, after years of reviews and incremental reform, it's clear the status quo isn't working. It's time for change."

National said no individual Pak'nSave, New World or Four Square owner would be forced to sell or change brands.

Instead, the two Foodstuffs brands would be split into rival nationwide groups, with separate structures and incentives to compete against each other.

The Commerce Commission's latest monitoring showed Foodstuffs and Woolworths still controlled about 82 percent of the grocery market, with little movement in the core measures of competition over the past year.

World.title: Why schools are ditching Facebook photos of students
World.content:
Why schools are ditching Facebook photos of their students Nine To Noon Download MP3 8m

Social media has become a popular means of keeping school communities updated on events and student achievements.

But concerns over how the images could be used has seen two schools decide to no longer post photos of students on Facebook pages.

School leaders at Takaro School in Palmerston North and Pāpāmoa Primary School say the move was prompted by unease around children's privacy and the lack of control schools and families have over images once they're online.

Takaro principal Josie Woon said alarm bells went off for her about a year ago when she was at a Google-hosted course on AI.

"We were doing lots of manipulation of images and videos, and it just got me thinking about how much we can do to something that is not there. We could make a science experiment look like a bomb was going off on our field or a rocket ship landing and things like that.

"It then brought me back to our digital footprint and what could happen with the images we've got online. Over the last two terms, we've been thinking about the same thing as a senior leadership team and the safety of our children's images. I think with the way AI has boomed, we haven't been able to keep up with it... There's so much more that is happening with it that we're not ready for, and I want us to be in a space where we're ahead of the game - and that means we protect our children."

In the space of five years, AI has gone from being barely able to create recognisable still images of faces to generating video that can easily fool the untrained eye.

"I've just seen how easy it is to take a screenshot of a photo on Facebook to screen record videos. They can all be done within a second," Woon told Nine to Noon.

"You can superimpose people's faces on things, people could be seen to be in specific places that they're not. That's a worry... parents give permission for our children's images to go up, but it's a lifelong digital footprint that the children haven't given consent for."

She said photos the school uploaded in the past were being viewed all over the world - but the sheer numbers of views suggested it was more than just family checking in.

"I've been following schools overseas that have been doing the same thing, and actually have been doing it before we did anything here, and it's the same thing - it's the misuse of photos and being able to manipulate things and in spaces online that I would never want any of our children's images to be in."

The government banned students' use of mobile phones in schools in 2024. NurPhoto via AFP

Instead, Takaro School will only be using the popular school Hero app, which is only accessible by parents and family - not the wide world - to share images and video of its pupils. Facebook will only be used for events, reminders and the like, Woon said.

Matt Simeon, principal at Pāpāmoa Primary School, said while they had not had any reported incidents of misuse of images and video, another local school did.

"They posted a celebration of their kapa haka group, and that video was then taken off their site and used on other kind of Facebook sites that didn't reflect the values of the school."

He said the video was used for propaganda purposes. Facebook wouldn't do anything about it, he said, and neither Netsafe nor the police could.

"It just got me thinking and going, ah, look, the world's changed. We used to use Facebook for all the things that Josie said - celebrations, sharing information. But yeah, with AI, you can just manipulate and change things so quick and easy. A couple of strokes of the keyboard and you've got something that's completely not what you were planning to share."

He put a proposal to the school board, which approved the move "very quickly".

"Kudos to my colleague who posted it on, ironically, an internal principal's Facebook closed group to say, 'Hey, look, this is our experience. Just thought I'd share.'

World.title: Te Pāti Māori announces $1 billion fund for 'energy sovereignty'
World.content:
Te Pāti Māori wants to increase Māori and community ownership of new renewable energy assets, establishing a $1 billion Energy Sovereignty Fund in the process.

The party's 'energy sovereignty' election policy would set up a fund to administer grants, concessional finance, guarantees, equity investment, and co-investment so hapū, iwi, marae, Māori landowners, and communities can acquire permanent stakes in energy assets.

The fund would also invest in energy resilience projects, community batteries, Māori energy businesses, and workforce development, aiming to reduce household energy costs and increase resilience.

Co-leader Rawiri Waititi said replacing fossil fuels with renewables, but leaving the ownership and profits in the same hands would transform technology, but not the system.

Rawiri Waititi. (File photo) RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"Every party is talking about generating more electricity. We're asking the question they keep avoiding: who will own it?" he said.

Te Pāti Māori would establish a National Energy Independence Plan, to deliver "measurable reductions" in household energy costs and "measurable increases" to Māori ownership.

The party would also strengthen the powers of the Commerce Commission and Electricity Authority to investigate excessive pricing and profits and strengthen competition.

Like Labour, the Greens, and National, Te Pāti Māori said it supported the Ratepayer Assistance Scheme to increase access to solar.

The party's policy document said the transition to renewables must uphold tino rangatiratanga, and not reproduce an economic model where value was extracted from Māori communities, while the ownership, decision-making, and economic benefits accumulated elsewhere.

"Māori must have meaningful rights and interests in ownership, governance, investment, development, employment, procurement, benefit sharing and decisions affecting whenua, wai and other taonga," the document said.

World.title: Tom Phillips report: The missed opportunities to find the children
World.content:
Lillian Hanly reports on reaction to Tom Phillips inquiry Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Less than three months after disappearing with his children for the first time, Tom Phillips did it again. A public inquiry into the handling of the case has found Police and Oranga Tamariki missed opportunities to protect the children and bring them home sooner. National Crime Correspondent Sam Sherwood looks into what the report reveals about the second disappearance.

Eighteen days after Tom Phillips left his ute on the Kiritehere beach, disappearing with his children and making headlines throughout the country, he and his children suddenly reappeared.

He initially refused to speak to police, but the following day he gave them a statement. He said the disappearance was merely a spontaneous camping trip, and "not a deliberate act to take the kids away and avoid the Family Court proceedings".

He also said it was the "first time [he] had taken the kids camping like that".

As for why he had decided to return, the father-of-three said he "had a little supplies left… but couldn't [have] stayed for too much longer", and would not tell police where he had taken the children.

Less than three months later he took his children again. This time he spent 1358 days in the bush, the saga ending with Phillips dying following a shootout with police after they were called to reports of a burglary in the early hours of 8 September 2025.

Following his death, the Government announced an inquiry into the handling of the Phillips case by authorities and whether all "practicable steps" were taken to ensure the safety and welfare of the Phillips children as well as whether the agencies responded appropriately and in a timely way to locate the children once they had disappeared.

The final report of the inquiry, by Honourable Justice Simon Moore KC, was released on Tuesday.

The report says the harm Phillips caused in isolating the children as well as concerns from the maternal whānau were "minimised or overlooked by agencies for significant periods".

Lillian Hanly reports on reaction to Tom Phillips inquiry Morning Report Download MP3 3m

It also says that while agencies worked well together at times a more consistent and collaborative interagency approach "could have prevented the children's disappearance and brought them back sooner".

As for his explanation about his first disappearance, the report says it "sits uncomfortably with the known facts".

"It is incapable of belief for a variety of reasons. The plain inference to be drawn from all of the known facts is that Tom Phillips went into the bush with his children with the intention of not being found."

One of the campsites Tom Phillips used. RNZ / Supplied / Police

It says Marokopa was an area Phillips knew very well.

"In some ways it was his backyard"

Operation Marokopa

After Tom Phillips and his children were first reported missing in September 2021, police launched an extensive multi-agency search and rescue investigation dubbed Operation Marokopa.

Moore KC's report said as part of the investigation police built an "extensive and comprehensive profile" of Phillips by speaking to family, friends and searching the properties he and the children had been living in.

Police understood he had significant mental health issues and there were concerns regarding his alcohol use and "conspiracy views".

A person close to Tom Phillips said they were worried that, if cornered, he would turn "violent".

Another person close to him told police he had a dislike of government agencies, "meaning anyone that might try and remove his children from him".

A neighbour reported he had said "if [Covid-19] gets any worse I'm going to the bush". He had also been seen going into Ōtorohanga to purchase alcohol wearing "a full face army-style gas mask".

Moore KC's report said that police did not appear to accept his claims that the first disappearance was simply an impromptu camping trip.

"They appeared to see it for what it was; a father prepared to put his children at risk, and likely to have staged his own death and that of his children by accidental drowning, to defeat the Family Court's processes and deny their mother access."

Tom Phillips. Supplied

Police contacted Oranga Tamariki to make a report of concern on 30 September 2021.

Oranga Tamariki's record of the first phone call noted police as saying Phillips had not said anything to police about what happened while he was away with the children.

"There are concerns that Thomas has the potential to do this again and questions as to why his ute was stuck in the sand under the tideline. There are questions around Thomas's mental state."

The report also recorded that police had "no immediate concerns for the childrens (sic) safety".

On 1 October, police developed a "safety plan" to be followed by Phillips which said he would not leave the family farm, would have another family member present at all times, and that police were to be advised of any plans to leave the farm.

A day later police visited him and noted "there were no indications or comments from Tom that he would go bush again with the kids".

On 5 October, Phillips was charged with making a false report to police, and two days later a police staffer completed a report assessing his suitability to hold a firearms licence.

The report mentioned Phillips' "bizarre" behaviour, including mentions of doomsday prepping, telling family members he would "just take the kids and disappear" from authorities.

Police recommended temporary suspension of his licence on the basis he was not a fit and proper person. They issued the notice on 8 October, but it was not served on him for nearly two months.

Also on 5 October, a social worker and social work supervisor visited the children at the Marokopa home of his parents. Phillips told the social worker he "had no idea" a search and rescue operation was underway, and said he had been wanting to go camping for a while.

He said the trip was "spontaneous but somewhat planned", and that he "would never harm his children nor did he intend to".

Following the visit, Oranga Tamariki (OT) recorded that the family "presented well".

OT head Amanda Malu at the Tom Phillips Inquiry release. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"Tom did not present out of the usual, there were no obvious signs of drug use or mental health. Family was co-operative… Tom appeared to be upset when discussing the court process, but relieved that his family would support him and the children if the children needed to be placed elsewhere."

Phillips' first appearance on his charges was adjourned to January 2022 as a result of Covid-19 restrictions.

The second disappearance

The report says when Phillips took the children for a second time in December 2021, police led the efforts to try and locate them.

The report said some officers who spoke as part of the inquiry said they were worried for the children from the moment they were taken again.

"The then-district commander told the inquiry of his sense of 'foreboding' on learning that Tom Phillips had disappeared into the bush again with the children.

"In fact, such was his level of concern that he wondered whether Tom Phillips had caused himself and the children harm."

However, the report says the "dominant view" of the police on the ground was that there were no immediate concerns for the children's safety.

A senior officer originally assigned to the matter told the inquiry about the thought process.

"The information that I had and the assurance that I sought… from staff that were working on the [first disappearance investigation] was that the kids being away for the first period, there was no major concerns with them being in the bush…. So, I made the assessment at that point given that it had been a short period of time that there was no risk to their health and safety at that point."

Moore KC said this assessment was reflected by police in the following months in internal notes, including one from January 2022 which said "there is no evidence to indicate that the children are at any risk if Phillips has gone bush with them again".

"Given the lack of evidence indicating any concern for the welfare of the children, the need to act or direct resources into locating/arresting Phillips from a risk perspective is low"

The then-area commander told the inquiry that he felt the most effective response was to "softly bring him out" via the use of local staff who knew the rural community they lived and worked in.

The report quotes the area commander as saying it was a deliberate strategy not to "scare Tom because this is a guy that doesn't like the limelight".

Moore KC said the strategy was to "work softly within the community to get him and his children back".

"The sense was that Tom Phillips was likely fearful of the ramifications of a second disappearance and that escalating public interest might be counterproductive to a safe and voluntary return."

In January and early February there were two key sightings which confirmed Phillips was in the broader Marokopa area.

This included Phillips visiting his parents' home alone on 9 February about 12.30am.

The following day, about 3.30pm, police drove to the Te Kūiti Police Station to report the visit.

"His parents told police that the children were not with Tom Phillips when he visited. They said that their son did not disclose the whereabouts of the children but assured them they were safe."

Phillips asked his parents for cash, and he took a significant amount of food.

"He told them he was concerned about the charges against him, and about the children's mother having access to the children."

Minister for Social Development Louise Upston at the Tom Phillips Inquiry release RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Operation Curly

In April 2022, police reassessed their approach and formalised the investigation, Operation Curly.

Moore KC said during Operation Curly police "never gave up on trying to find Tom Phillips and the children", with about 1080 "taskings", such as reported sightings or offending attributed to him generated and followed up.

"They followed up on most reported sightings, even where the likelihood of obtaining a useful lead might have seemed tenuous. They tried to generate leads through media campaigns, area canvasses and, later, the offer of an $80,000 reward for information.

"They examined phone records, bank accounts and social media in an effort to identify any signs of activity. They actively investigated persons of interest who might have some knowledge of the whereabouts of Tom Phillips or who might be assisting him in one way or another."

Moore KC's report divided Operation Curly into four phases. He said that in May 2022, the area commander emailed the district commander and assistant commissioners that "all enquiries have been completed and have not yielded a result".

"Police hold no current intelligence that can be acted on or can enable a deployment of resources."

It was then decided to appoint a "highly experienced" Detective Senior Sergeant as day-to-day officer in charge.

In January, 2023, 13 months into the second disappearance the then-police commissioner made a request for the investigation team to reconsider the possibility of offering a reward.

An application for approval was submitted to the assistant commissioner.

However, the assistant commissioner repeated earlier concerns around "creating a precedent", Moore KC said.

"Currently the only offence committed by Mr Phillips is breach of a parenting order and failing to appear on charges relating to wasting police time post their initial disappearance.

"It is the lack of a serious offence that is causing concern and could potentially create an unruly precedent. This is also an investigative hindrance in terms of specialist investigative capability.

"To date the reward is not supported by either [the district commander] or [the assistant commissioner]."

They also noted the absence of Oranga Tamariki and their views as to the children's welfare.

"At this stage I agree with the decision in regard to the breach of a parenting order however if a Place of Safety warrant or OT has specific concerns then these may need to be factored into the considerations."

Moore KC said the inquiry had seen no evidence that this was put to OT. He said senior police staff "maintained an interest" in the progress of the investigation.

"Through the officer in charge and area and district commanders, requests were made for assistance from specialist police units and NZDF. However, the inquiry notes something of a pattern of these not being followed through in a timely way."

Richard Chambers at yesterday's media conference. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

The internal review

In October 2022, the area commander arranged for a police officer from outside the investigation team to review the investigation to date. Then, in March 2023, he asked a detective sergeant from Hamilton who had not been part of the investigation to undertake a more thorough review.

"The March 2023 review noted that the investigation had effectively stalled, relying as it had been, on new sightings reported to police or information provided, largely by the children's mother.

"It noted there were reputational issues for police through the investigation not advancing in the way the public believed it should. It identified that the investigation had been hampered by being carried out largely by uniform staff, with no single person having the necessary 'ownership'."

It also said relevant information was "also being split over different locations within various police databases," Moore KC said.

The review also identified leads that could be followed up from information already gathered, and noted concerns over Phillips' mental health and the children.

"The children are young and vulnerable due to their ages. Some of the information obtained about Thomas Phillips reveals he is an alcoholic. Taking the children in order to hide them from their mother is not in the best interests of the children. As time passes without any sighting of the children, concern for their welfare mounts. In my view Police are obligated to commit more resource to finding the children, hopefully safe and well...

"The paramount consideration is the safety and welfare of the missing children. In order to finalise this investigation and to achieve the safe return of the children it will be necessary to commit the resources needed to locate them."

From May 2023, the investigation was moved to the Major Crimes Unit at District Headquarters.

One of the the family's campsites. NZ Police / Supplied

The May 2023 sighting

Then, on 28 May 2023, a resident living on the main road out to Marokopa called police on the 105 line and reported a possible sighting of Phillips and his children.

The resident, referred to in the report as Rhonda, said that about 90 minutes earlier a man had knocked on her door and asked for a jump start for his car which he claimed was stuck on a forestry road.

She described him as Caucasian, in his late 30s to early 40s. She said he was wearing a black hat, black/grey shirt, black jeans, and work boots.

She said that he smelled strongly and like someone who had not had a shower in a very long time.

Rhonda and her mother-in-law drove the man along Te Anga Rd to a forestry road, where the man's car was parked. Rhonda took a note of the man's number plate, and said she saw a girl by the car as well as other children inside the car.

She expressed her concern about the man and the children because they seemed to be stuck in the middle of nowhere on a forestry road. Her and her mother-in-law suspected it was Phillips.

Following the report, police dispatched a unit about half an hour after receiving the call, but that unit was diverted to a family harm incident shortly after at a different address on Te Anga Rd. The report noted family harm incidents were usually given priority.

Not long after that, the unit advised no further action was required from police.

There was a brief follow up after this, by an "astute senior constable" but what followed was a "series of unfortunate mis-steps and circumstances" that together "conspired to compound the delay in police properly appreciating and investigating the significance" of the sighting.

There is no evidence that the first unit tasked with the report visited the woman's home or attempted to visit the location of the sighting. Police have not been able to explain to the inquiry why the report was designated as requiring no further action, Moore KC said.

The inquiry found police inaction on the day led to avoidable delays.

It said police should have recognised the sighting was credible, and investigated "more thoroughly and in a more timely way," and had there been no delay, "there might have been a real prospect of locating the children".

Phillips warned police 'would not take him alive'

In July and August 2023, detectives from the new investigation team went to the Phillips family farm to introduce themselves.

During one of the visits, police discussed Phillips' visit to the property in February 2022. Phillips' father said that during that visit Tom had warned that the police would not take him alive.

"The officer in charge at the time told the inquiry that this information materially changed the police assessment of the risk Tom Phillips posed.

"It also materially informed what actions were available to them. From that point on, police undertook no searches without Armed Offenders Squad or Special Tactics Group involvement."

In August, Phillips was also seen by his family on CCTV at his parents' farm, and the following day he was seen at Bunnings in Hamilton and on Kawhia Rd.

This led to him being identified as the offender in an armed robbery in Te Kūiti which happened several months earlier.

"There then followed a surge of activity in the Police investigation," Moore KC said.

Then in October 2024, Phillips and the children were photographed by pig hunters on open farmland near Marokopa.

Moore said NZ Police and the New Zealand Defence Force developed a "comprehensive strategy" using trail cameras and road cameras to narrow down the area the group was operating in. These cameras picked up three further sightings of the group over the next six months.

"While the use of cameras and the drone was successful in narrowing the location of the group and gathering intelligence about their habits, police were becoming increasingly concerned about what might happen if they were involved in a violent confrontation with Tom Phillips.

"Their greatest anxiety centred around avoiding any risk of harm to the children, police or the public."

On July 28 2025, a meeting was held between members of the investigation team, police district management, Technical Operations Group and Special Tactics Group to discuss the next stage of Operation Curly.

Moore KC referred to the minutes of that meeting which said the focus was on "identifying Phillips' resupply location to support STG in safely rescuing the children and arresting Phillips".

The following month there were several burglaries in the area which police believed were committed by Phillips.

Then on 8 September, Phillips died following a shootout with police after they were called to reports of a burglary in the early hours of the morning in Piopio.

The 'ripple effect'

In his findings, Moore KC said police had "limited options" to impose constraints on Phillips to "mitigate the risk of a second disappearance".

However, he said that police and Oranga Tamariki did not communicate again from 1 October 2021 until after the second disappearance in December 2021.

He also said police's report of concern to Oranga Tamariki was "commendable", but police should have ensured all information was provided and "critical discussions were ongoing".

In relation to Police action after the second disappearance, he said Police should have identified the serious risk to the welfare of the children from the time they were taken, and they should have developed a proactive investigation strategy at the outset.

"During the first two months, police missed specific opportunities to gather more information about where the children might be."

Operation Curly also should have involved more CIB staffing from the beginning and a review of progress and future options, should have occurred much sooner.

"In the inquiry's view this delay is likely a result of the initial and erroneous assessment that there were no concerns about the children...

"After April 2022, investigation efforts were stepped up incrementally, but slowly, from that starting point. This failed to recognise the seriousness of the risk to the children, and, as time went on, the ongoing harm from being alienated from their mother, siblings and wider families escalated."

He also said the police should have taken some steps "much earlier".

Moore KC said in his report that for the family of the children the four years "represented a long and harrowing ordeal".

"Every day that the children were missing added to a catalogue of fear and worry borne by the children's mother and older sisters. At times they wondered whether they were even alive."

He said Phillips' family also spoke of the "significant toll", and added that the "ripple effect" caused by the uncertainty also spread to those involved in trying to find them.

World.title: Man pleads not guilty over murder of two people in Auckland
World.content:
A man has pleaded not guilty over the murder of two people in the Auckland suburb of Wattle Downs.

Emergency services were called to a house on Gambare Place more than two weeks ago, and two people were found dead at the house.

Name suppression has lapsed for the victims, and they can now be named as Elaine Rudolph and Keagan Bell.

The 30-year-old accused entered not guilty pleas through his lawyer at the Auckland High Court on Wednesday, before Justice Michele Wilkinson-Smith.

The man has continued name suppression and is remanded in custody until trial next year.

Name suppression has lapsed for the victims, and they can now be named as Elaine Rudolph and Keagan Bell.

More than a dozen people observed in the public gallery and when the accused first appeared in the dock, a man in the public gallery yelled "d***head".

Justice Wilkinson Smith warned the man and asked him to contain himself.

She said if there's disturbance in the public gallery, she would close the court.

World.title: Labour pledges to ban big companies from charging excessive prices
World.content:
Labour has promised to ban big companies from charging excessive prices, if elected.

Leader Chris Hipkins said a handful of big businesses were guilty of price gouging - that is, charging more than necessary for essential items.

"Right now, a company big enough to dodge competition can charge excessive prices for the basics, like food and fuel, and there's no law against it," he said.

"Labour will change that, by making it illegal for big powerful companies to rip off New Zealanders on the essentials."

Commerce and consumer affairs spokesperson Arena Williams said 97 percent of New Zealand businesses were small, and would not be affected by the policy.

"It also only applies in markets for essentials, like food, power, fuel, transport, telecommunications banking, and insurance," she said.

Labour's policy document said the law would apply where a company had enough market power that customers could not realistically shop elsewhere, suppliers had nowhere else to go, or new competitors struggled to enter the market.

The full policy includes:

making it illegal for big companies with substantial market power to charge excessive prices for essential goods and services, or to pay unfairly low prices to suppliers

setting a legal test for price gouging: holding prices "well above what they would otherwise be in a competitive market, sustained over time"

requiring companies that gouge to pay penalties and hand back every dollar of excess profit

giving the Commerce Commission power to investigate price gouging and supporting consumer groups and suppliers to do the same.

World.title: PGA Tour not considering return program for LIV Golf players
World.content:
The PGA Tour is not considering a returning-member program that would allow players from LIV Golf to return to the US-based circuit the way Brooks Koepka did in January.

Speaking one week after LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection ‌in New Jersey, PGA Tour chief executive Brian Rolapp said accountability and discipline were essential elements for any sports league.

"In terms of where we are ‌today, we are not currently contemplating a returning-member program like the one ⁠you saw in January," he said.

"Everyone at the PGA Tour, myself included, has been focused on what is best for the organisation."

LIV Golf files for bankruptcy LIV Golf files for bankruptcy, flagging a restructure with a massive loan from the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia.

Rolapp added: "The PGA Tour is built on meritocracy. Every player, whether they are a member or want to become one, must earn their place."

LIV Golf's bankruptcy filing has left the playing futures of some of the breakaway circuit's biggest names in doubt.

Major ‌champions Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau, two of the sport's more popular players, were listed as the top unsecured creditors, with each ⁠owed more than $US5 million.

Five-time major champion Koepka ‌took advantage of a limited-time ‌returning member program in January to rejoin the PGA Tour after leaving LIV ‌Golf last December.

Koepka's return came at a cost, with the former world number one facing a five-year forfeiture of potential ‌equity in the PGA Tour's Player ⁠Equity Program, representing an estimated $US50-85 million loss depending on his performance and tour growth.

The Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia owns 100 per cent of LIV Golf's equity, according to its bankruptcy petition.

LIV Golf hopes to exit from bankruptcy by early 2027.

Reuters

World.title: Sturt versus Norwood stirs up 1978 controversy ahead of SANFL final
World.content:
Football Park was barely four years old when Sturt and Norwood last met in a famous grand final that included a brief tussle between players and officials in the Sturt dug-out.

The Redlegs came away with a one-point win in 1978 despite Sturt being favoured, but with both teams meeting again for this weekend's SANFL Grand Final, there are several controversies that remain front of mind for some.

First and foremost, there was the winning goal.

After kicking 5:9 to Norwood's 1:5 in the first quarter, Sturt was in front and living up to expectations, having only lost one game for the entire season.

But, 29 points down in the last quarter, the Redlegs mounted a comeback, briefly taking the lead before Sturt kicked another goal.

"Then there was a rough contest in Norwood's forward pocket, and [Redleg] Phil Gallagher took it out of the ruck, quickly slammed it on his boot, and it went straight to Sturt fullback Colin Casey," said SANFL senior media producer Zac Millbank.

"He kicked it straight back out of the area and then Phil Gallagher went to mark Casey's kick, but he actually dropped it."

Field umpire Des Foster blew his whistle and gave what commentators at the time assumed to be a weak free kick to Gallagher.

Foster later said that he actually called it a mark but admitted it was the wrong call, explaining that his field of vision had been obscured by players at the key moment when the ball came down.

In front of more than 50,000 spectators and a live television audience, Gallagher went back and kicked a goal, putting Norwood in front.

Sturt's Lucas Slade and Norwood's Alex Wright will compete for the SANFL flag on Sunday. (Supplied: Matt Talbot)

There were about three minutes left, however, and Sturt made several more 50-metre entries but only managed a point.

Mr Millbank pointed out that Sturt had kicked 14 goals and 25 points that day, so the upset loss could not be blamed on "the Des Foster blunder".

"Fourteen goals and 26 points is just horrendous kicking and some of the shots were very simple ones," he said.

Regardless, the moment went down in history as one of the most contentious free kicks or marks ever played at Football Park, the former stadium that was home to SA football between 1974 and 2013.

Mr Millbank said there had been a lot of commentary on the SANFL's social media pages about the 48-year-old moment since Sunday's match-up was confirmed, proving the incident was very much "still on people's minds".

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley and Sturt captain Tom Lewis are playing for the cup on Sunday. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Sturt captain Tom Lewis said he was reminded about the 1978 final by a pedestrian walking past his house on Monday morning.

"He reminded me at about 7am how disappointed he was at that grand final and asked us to right a few wrongs," he said.

"Both clubs have such a history; it does bring a lot of excitement, a lot of pressure.

"I'm thoroughly looking forward to it, and the boys are. Everyone's amped up; I know Norwood are as well, so hopefully we get a good turnout."

A dug-out scuffle

Another memorable moment occurred in the third quarter in 1978 when Norwood player John Wynne overran the ball on the boundary and ended up inside the enemy's camp, much to his own apparent amusement.

A skirmish ensued, with more players and officials from the Redlegs getting involved, until umpires quelled the situation and broke the parties apart — even as strong words continued to fly.

"Legend has it that master [Sturt] coach Jack Oatey was a bit ruffled after that incident," Mr Millbank said.

"I don't know how true it is, but there's a bit of thought that Wynne did it deliberately to try and stir him up a bit, put them off their game."

Norwood took the 1978 premiership after a long period of SANFL dominance for Sturt, in which they had won five flags in a row from 1966 to 1970, and then in 1974 and 1976 as well.

The fact they had only dropped one game for the entire season — a feat Sturt repeated in 2025 before winning the premiership — had made them the "raging favourites".

For this year's grand final, however, the shoe is on the other foot, and Norwood are the warm favourites going into the game.

Norwood beat Sturt by 19 points during the second semi-final earlier this month. (Supplied: Matt Talbot)

Having won the minor premiership and winning the second semi-final against Sturt two weeks ago, the team has only played one match in three weeks.

Coach Jade Sheedy said that after the team's main training session, they had another strong session on Saturday, "which put the boys through their paces and tried to replicate as much as we can to get them ready for a grand final," he said.

"Our preparation has been good … players are fresh."

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley said it was always a big game when Sturt and Norwood met, "so to be able to play in a grand final against them is a bigger deal".

"You can certainly feel the anticipation living in the eastern suburbs and knowing that rivalry, the history, the '78 grand final was obviously huge," he said.

"I've heard a lot about that even though it was 48 years ago now. That famous Gallagher mark, my former number 11, so I know a lot about the history."

Digging deep for a repeat

Sturt, which finished third on the ladder, has played three finals to get to the big dance, and will defend their 2025 premiership with a slightly different list to Sunday's preliminary due to injuries.

This includes midfielder Jared Dakin, who injured his hamstring in the opening quarter against Woodville-West Torrens; key defender Casey Voss, who dislocated his shoulder in the game; and ruckman Amos Doyle, who was a late withdrawal due to a neck injury.

The Superjesus will play a set before the SANFL Grand Final at Adelaide Oval on Sunday. (@they.muse)

Coach Marty Mattner said Doyle had been progressing and may still play on Sunday, depending on Wednesday's training, and there was still a window open for Voss, although his inclusion is considered unlikely.

"The positive is that everyone who hasn't been playing in the league side is fit and ready to go," he said.

"Realistically there’s probably seven or eight in that [reserves] group who have played league footy this year."

The 2026 SANFL Grand Final, which will feature Adelaide rockers The Superjesus in pre-game entertainment, will commence at Adelaide Oval from 2:30pm Sunday.

World.title: Rush to put Zverev in Alcaraz-Sinner tier premature despite twin titles
World.content:
When the latest edition of the ATP singles rankings dropped earlier this week, a 24-year streak came to an end.

After being bounced in the first round of the US Open, Novak Djokovic dropped out of the top-10 for the first time since 2018.

Djokovic's exit marks the first time since October 2002 that neither he nor Rafael Nadal nor Roger Federer is inside the top-10.

For tennis fans who wondered when the 'Big 3' era in the men's game would end, the end is now.

Novak Djokovic's first-round exit at the US Open caused him to drop outside the top-10 for the first time since 2018. (Getty Images: Mike Stobe)

With the Djokovic-Federer-Nadal triumvirate dominating the men's game for so long, the question of who their successors would be has been a popular one around tennis.

Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz have emulated Federer and Nadal's rivalry from the mid-2000s, exchanging grand slam titles while playing some spellbinding epics along the way, but would any other men's players on tour join them as Djokovic joined Federer and Nadal?

Alexander Zverev appears to be the third member of the party, having claimed two of the four available grand slam titles this year.

But questions remain as to whether Zverev's candidacy to join the very top tier of men's tennis is legitimate.

Alexander Zverev wins US Open without realising it Alexander Zverev wins his second grand slam title of the year with a dominant victory over American Ben Shelton in the men's US Open final.

Since first achieving a top-10 ranking in May 2017 as a 20-year-old, Zverev has been one of the most consistent performers on the men's tour.

Zverev has spent 414 weeks as a top-10 ranked player throughout his career, currently 15th all-time. He ranks second among active players in this metric, behind only Djokovic, with 959 weeks, just behind Federer's 968.

At the time of writing, Zverev has spent 102 consecutive weeks ranked inside the top 10 since his most recent streak began in September 2023.

Those numbers are not the problem when it comes to Zverev's bid to be considered the best player in the world.

It is this one.

Career wins against top-10 ranked opponents Wins % Novak Djokovic 69 66 Roger Federer 64 62 Rafael Nadal 55 67 Carlos Alcaraz 16 70 Jannik Sinner 14 50 Alexander Zverev 5 22

Despite being a constant presence in the top-10 rankings over the best part of the last decade, Zverev has consistently struggled to beat the other players ranked in the same vicinity.

The German owns an unenviable 5-18 (21.7 per cent) win-loss record against fellow top-10 opponents in grand slam matches. He has won 59 of his 146 matches against top-10 opponents overall, roughly a 40 per cent conversion rate.

Zverev's record pales in comparison to Alcaraz and Sinner, as well as Djokovic, Federer and Nadal.

Alcaraz has an astounding 16-7 record against top-10 opponents at grand slams, with his 69.6 per cent conversion rate by far the best among the elite cohort, while Sinner has gone 14-14 in such matches.

Zverev has been beaten by Sinner (pictured) in two of his six grand slam final appearances. (Getty Images/Frey)

Nadal, Djokovic and Federer all won over 60 per cent of their matches against top-10 opponents at grand slams, with Djokovic's 69 wins leading the way.

This record against the very best players helped make Zverev a perennial grand slam semifinalist and finalist before he broke through with his first title at Roland-Garros earlier this year.

While Zverev now has two grand slam titles to his name, the calibre of opponents he has overcome suggests he hasn't really gone up a tier.

The German claimed the French Open title without facing a single top-10-ranked opponent, with the runner-up Flavio Cobolli the top-ranked player at No.14.

US Open finalist Ben Shelton is the only top-10 ranked opponent Zverev has beaten en route to his two grand slam titles this year. (Getty Images: Simon Bruty/USTA)

Overall, the average ranking of the players Zverev beat en-route to his first grand slam title is 57.7, with his fourth-round opponent, world No.106, Jesper de Jong the lowest-ranked.

Zverev had a slightly tougher run to the US Open title, but still faced just one top-10-ranked opponent in finalist Ben Shelton (eighth).

On average, Zverev's US Open opponents ranked 45th overall, with his first-round opponent, Lorenzo Sonego, the lowest-ranked at No.89.

Zverev's victories offer hope for the rest of the non-Alcaraz and Sinner division on the men's tour, including players such as Australia's Alex de Minaur.

De Minaur, like Zverev, has struggled against top-10 opponents at grand slams, winning just two of 14 matches.

Zverev's breakthroughs offer hope for the likes of Australia's Alex de Minaur (pictured). (AP: Christinne Muschi)

Despite reaching a career-high ranking of No.5 this year, de Minaur has yet to win a grand slam quarterfinal.

The Australian has a 0-7 record in quarters, with six of those losses coming over the last three seasons.

De Minaur has looked downtrodden after his recent grand slam exits, but will hope that like Zverev, he too can capitalise on the bracket breaking just right for him at some point down the line.

For now, Zverev looks to have graduated above the class featuring the likes of Shelton, Daniil Medvedev, Felix Auger-Aliassime, de Minaur and others.

But for him to truly climb into the upper echelon of men's tennis, it is time he starts taking down the big names when it matters most.

World.title: Renshaw scores first ODI century as Aussies defeat Zimbabwe
World.content:
Matt Renshaw has scored his first ODI century, while Nathan Ellis took five wickets to guide Australia to a ​59-run win over hosts Zimbabwe in the first clash of their three-match series.

Australia chose to bat first, and the surprise decision from captain Mitchell Marsh was vindicated as ​the tourists scored 8-294 from ‌their 50 overs, setting Zimbabwe an imposing target at Harare Sports Club.

In reply, Zimbabwe was dismissed for 235 in 45.1 overs, showing good fight but always behind ‌the required run rate.

Renshaw, who last scored an international ton in ⁠a Test against Pakistan in 2017, made 109.

He featured ‌in some key partnerships, while Cooper ​Connolly made 51.

Renshaw put on 72 runs with Alex Carey for the fifth wicket and 75 with Ollie Peake for the sixth wicket, leaving Zimbabwe with a ​required ‌run rate of 5.90.

The 20-year-old left-arm quick Newman Nyamhuri finished with 5-62, only the second Zimbabwe bowler to take five wickets in ⁠an ODI against Australia.

Zimbabwe lost four ‌wickets quickly before Craig Ervine ‌and Sikandar steadied the innings with a 98-run partnership that offered the hosts hope ‌of victory on a surface that traditionally gets better for batting as the day wears on.

Ellis had taken two ‌wickets ​in his first spell and when he was reintroduced, took three balls to clean bowl Ervine for 59 and put the brakes on Zimbabwe.

Sikandar was dispensed by Spencer Johnson for 57 to leave Zimbabwe ⁠still significantly adrift.

Ellis finished with 5-31 in 9.1 overs, also cleaning up the tail.

The second ODI ‌will be played on ‌Friday in Harare, ​after which Australia moves to South Africa.

Reuters

World.title: SA school charged after student hurt in hammer-throw incident
World.content:
Criminal proceedings have been lodged against an Adelaide school after a student was seriously injured during an athletics training incident.

A Christian Brothers College student was struck in the head with a hammer-throw ball at St Albans Reserve at Clearview on September 5, 2024.

In a statement, SafeWork SA said a worker was also allegedly "exposed to the risk of being struck".

It said it had lodged the proceedings against Edmund Rice Education Australia Colleges Ltd, trading as Christian Brothers College (CBC), in South Australia's Employment Court earlier this month.

The safety watchdog said it had charged the school with a category two offence under the Work Health and Safety Act.

"It is alleged that workers and students participating in athletics training at St Albans Reserve, Clearview, were exposed to risks to their health and safety while undertaking javelin and hammer throw activities, in close proximity to each other, on 5 September 2024," SafeWork SA said in the statement.

"SafeWork SA alleges the school failed to provide adequate instruction or training to workers responsible for organising and supervising the athletics training and failed to ensure its safety policies and procedures were followed."

SafeWork SA says it lodged the proceedings against Christian Brothers College earlier this month. (YouTube: SafeWork SA)

The safety watchdog said it would be further alleged that the school "failed to perform an adequate hazard identification and risk assessment for the athletics training".

According to the statement, the school allegedly "failed to maintain a safe work environment" by failing to ensure the hammer throwing was not carried out in close proximity to students participating in javelin and by not using a safety cage that complied with the relevant industry safety standards.

"SafeWork SA alleges these failures exposed workers and students to a risk of death or serious injury from being struck by a hammer throw ball," SafeWork SA said.

The matter is expected to appear in the SA Employment Court at a later date.

World.title: Cowan warns BBL privatisation could 'spiral out of control'
World.content:
Former Australian Test opener Ed Cowan believes that the Big Bash League doesn't need to rush privatisation to compete with other T20 leagues around the world.

A Cricket NSW board member, Cowan told the ABC Cricket Podcast fears of a player exodus to rival leagues was premature, and a move toward privatisation could "spiral out of control".

Cricket Australia (CA) confirmed earlier this month that they would go ahead with an opt-in model that allows states to take their BBL teams to market with the option of selling stakes or entire franchises to private investors.

"[In previous seasons] they've been able to reshape scheduling, to reshape international stars and the salary cap around that. We've seen already there's no friction to attracting some of the world's best players," Cowan said.

Former England captain Ben Stokes will join the Adelaide Strikers for BBL16. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde-ICC)

"Ben Stokes is going to Adelaide, Finn Allen has just signed a mega deal. So the argument that is put forward is we're gonna lose players to the South African League. We haven't lost one yet.

"There's a view that the business could be run more effectively, which would enable some time to work out whether you actually do need to sell your star assets or not.

"Because when you start burning the furniture to warm the house, it can spiral quickly out of control from there."

The BBL has, in recent seasons, reshaped the fixture of the competition to make it shorter and in turn has increased viewership and attracted some of the games biggest names.

In the 2025/26 BBL season fans were treated to the likes of Colin Munro, Chris Jordan, Muhammed Rizwan and Sam Billings tearing up the competition. Coupled with Australian Test stars like Steve Smith, Alex Carey and Mitchell Starc who joined the tournament after their international duties finished.

Steve Smith has played 40 matches for the Sydney Sixers, including 6 in BBL15. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Compare that with recent seasons of The Hundred where Mitchell Marsh, Adam Zampa, Jos Buttler and Trent Boult were some of the biggest name players in that competition, all of whom have played in the tournament or are set to play in the upcoming BBL16 season.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

Cricket Australia believes that privatisation would allow the BBL to keep up with other T20 leagues around the world, like The Hundred in the UK and the SA20 in South Africa.

"There are opportunities now for our best Australian players to play in other leagues at the same time potentially with bigger salary caps. So when we talk about should we wait for two years or four years? No, we can't wait," CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said.

"Those challenges are on our doorstep today. So we've got to make some decisions about how we compete.

"We're a relatively small country in a big global sport. So it's incumbent on us to make decisions that we can compete with elsewhere and that's exactly what we're doing."

Cricket NSW has been the most vocally opposed to the current model, while Queensland Cricket has also said it will likely have further questions but intends to hold on to its BBL franchise for the time being.

Mitch March playing for the Leeds Sunrisers in The Hundred in the UK. (Getty Images: Annabel Lee-Ellis)

"We will closely monitor the sales process and at this stage, intend to retain 100 percent ownership of the Brisbane Heat, but of course remain open to private investment at the appropriate time," Qld Cricket Chair Kirsten Pike and CEO Terry Svenson said in a statement.

Meanwhile, Cricket Victoria is in support of the move, and will be the first to sell a license with the Melbourne Renegades set to be put to market to be sold in full.

"Private investment will unlock value for reinvestment across Victorian cricket, from the grassroots through to the elite game," Cricket Victoria Director Shaun Richardson said in a statement.

CA and the state's cricketing associations will continue negotiations ahead of the BBL16 and WBBL12 seasons starting, which are likely to be the last seasons involving the original eight franchises.

World.title: Dockers will not be 'ambushed' by 'galvanised' Swans, Longmuir vows
World.content:
Many see it as a golden opportunity for Fremantle to reach just their second AFL grand final, but Justin Longmuir insists there is no chance the Dockers will underestimate a Sydney side missing a host of star players in Friday night's preliminary final at the SCG.

Fremantle is set to enter the game as warm favourite, despite being away from home against a team which thrashed reigning premier Brisbane by 53 points in their qualifying final, with the Swans hard hit by suspension and injury.

When Sydney stood down Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice in the wake of the off-field scandal at a Melbourne hotel, Swans chairman Andrew Pridham said they had "effectively torpedoed" their season.

Remarkably since then, they have defied expectations, beating North Melbourne just days later before the stunning upset of the Lions.

Swans show what 'Bloods' culture is supposed to look like Many questions were asked about Sydney's famed culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. As the finals got underway, the players showed exactly what it is supposed to look like on the field.

That was despite losing Callum Mills during the game, with the captain joining the long list of absentees, ruled out for the season with a knee injury.

Longmuir has urged his side to put its full focus on the Sydney players who are taking the field, rather than those ruled out.

"Already done that. They dropped 141 points on Brisbane who were the flag favourites, it's a wake-up call," he said.

Errol Gulden and the Swans are undermanned but coming off a dominant qualifying final win. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"They didn't seem to miss those guys, so we just play what's in front of us.

"Clearly they haven't lost any of their scoring power, and all I can go on is what I see from the last two games, and playing like a really galvanised team, playing with great spirit, great physicality.

"It looks like whatever has happened has galvanised them, and they're playing a really tough brand of footy.

"We're definitely not going up there and getting ambushed by what they're trying to do. We've seen [it] in the last couple of weeks and we've seen it work really well.

"We've got to make sure that we don't just think it's going to happen for us, we've got to make sure we impose our footy."

Longmuir calls for no fear

The Dockers rebounded from their qualifying final loss to Hawthorn with a 14-point semifinal victory over Geelong, with Longmuir pleased with how his players took the contest on against the Cats.

Luke Jackson was instrumental in Fremantle's semifinal win and shapes as a big factor against Sydney. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

He urged his side to not to be afraid of making mistakes on the big stage, and to always be prepared to move on to the next contest.

"If we're going to make mistakes, let's make sure we make mistakes playing our way and playing with the right mindset, because usually those mistakes you can move on from a little bit quicker," he said.

Dockers show they have the steel to be AFL's best Fremantle booked a spot in the AFL preliminary finals with a stirring win over Geelong, breathing life into the club's premiership dream.

"At times we didn't make those mistakes the right way against Hawthorn and we stood still after, because we didn't move on from them.

"It's been a message for a long time because we play such an imperfect game, players who have played their best games would've been full of mistakes. It's just the nature and the scrappiness of our game, so let's make them with the right mindset."

The Dockers are set to fly to Sydney on Wednesday, with the two clubs naming their teams on Thursday ahead of the clash.

World.title: The moment this Knights finals rookie will hold on to forever
World.content:
Last Friday's semifinal win over South Sydney was one of the great nights in Newcastle's recent history, and nobody enjoyed it more than Jermaine McEwen.

In his first finals match, the 21-year-old had the game of his young life, inspiring the 20-10 upset victory that has the whole Hunter dreaming big ahead of Sunday's sudden-death clash with the Warriors.

McEwen scored the first double of his NRL career and ran for 187 metres, the best mark of his 37 first-grade matches, and set the tone for the Knights' right-edge defence with a physical brutality that would make a mafia kingpin proud.

Knights win is proof the future has come Stars were born under the finals lights as Newcastle knockout finals win over South Sydney announced the dawn of a new tomorrow.

On a night of many highlights, McEwen's personal favourite was his second try that helped Newcastle kick clear in the second half, as he backed up winger Dom Young to score right in front of the Knights faithful.

McEwen crawled the last few metres before slamming the ball down so hard it's a wonder they could dig it out of the turf.

"The only reason I slammed it was because my parents and my family were right in front of me. I just looked at them, and I was like, 'hell yeah,'" said McEwen.

"That was the best moment I have ever had in my footy career. That moment right there, that's something I will hold forever. So I am just super grateful and so happy."

McEwen's first try of the evening helped get things started as he again trailed Young after the Englishman claimed a bomb inside the first five minutes.

It brought Newcastle into the match and gave the team the start they needed en route to their first away finals win since 2013 and just their third since their last premiership 25 years ago.

Repeating the dose in Auckland is a tall order, but even before the win over Souths, McEwen and his teammates did not lack for belief.

"The Knights have given me everything, and I believe in the coach, Justin (Holbrook). He's allowed me to be the greatest version of myself on that field," said McEwen.

"But when I put the ball down and looked up and saw all the fans, I was (thinking) how happy I am to be a Knight. I'm just so grateful.

"We just wanted to go out there and play with energy and lift each other up."

Newcastle's right edge did a fine job shutting down South Sydney's attack. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

McEwen spent much of the week thinking about how the Knights would shut down South Sydney's left edge, which is just about the most dangerous attacking weapon in the NRL.

Between them, Alex Johnston, Latrell Mitchell, Tallis Duncan and Cody Walker scored 63 tries in 2026, two more than Newcastle managed as an entire club last season.

But McEwen, Sandon Smith and Dane Gagai rose to the occasion magnificently, locking onto the superstars and refusing to let go, moving and defending as one.

Souths did end up scoring down the left through Jye Grey, but only after McEwen had left the field late on.

"When you have challenges, you get more prepared for it. You think about it more. When you're at home or training, you get flashbacks of what you have to do," said McEwen.

"When I have Cody Walker and their left edge — they do it the best in the whole comp. Cody Walker, he is just so good at that stuff.

"Us in D, we had a big job to do, and we just went out there and did it."

Jermaine McEwen and the Knights will look to pull off another finals ambush this Sunday against the Warriors. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The journey through this year to Sunday's knockout final has not always been smooth for McEwen.

He was suspended for one match in June after being charged with low-range drink driving, an incident for which he apologised unreservedly and left him "deeply ashamed".

At the time, McEwen said he let his community down, and he's been trying to make amends ever since.

"Bro, at the end of the day we're all human and just because I play footy doesn't mean I'm special," said McEwen.

"In those circumstances, with the rollercoaster (of this year), that has taught me a lot in life.

"I feel like people can either shy away from it or own up to it. I wanted to show up for the fans and show them what I could do, and repay them in that way."

"Because I know how much the town speaks to this club and the hold this club has on the town. I wanted to repay them with good footy."

A sellout crowd is expected at Eden Park on Sunday, and a win would send Newcastle to just its second preliminary final in the last 25 years.

They'll again be underdogs against a Warriors side that beat them just three weeks ago, and the match marks the biggest game of McEwen's career, as it is for several of his teammates.

But the same was true last Friday, and by leaning on the experience of men like Gagai and prop Tyson Frizell, McEwen was inspired to make a difference, and all he wants is to do it all over again.

"These are experienced boys who have been in the game for a lot of years, and when you have them talk to you, it makes you more comfortable," said McEwen.

"You're not nervous. You're going out there to do a good job."

Tech.title: Microsoft announces Windows and Surface event for October 7th
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s been more than two years since the last major Windows event, so Microsoft is heading to San Francisco next month to outline the future of Windows and Surface devices.
